p.h: Prester John between Gog and Magog on the old sea charts
p.g: Ramusio notes that Marco Polo called the northern lord Uncan 'Prester John' and put his seat in two regions, Og and Magog. He adds that on all the sea charts made 200 and 300 years earlier, Prester John is placed in the north above India, between the Ganges and the Indus, with no mention of an Ethiopian Prester John; on the next page he calls these 'the provinces of Gog and Magog, that is, of the Tartars'.
p.q: oue dice Messer Marco Polo che sotto la Tramontana v'era vn gran signore detto VmCan che vogliono alcuni questo nome dire Preti Ianni, nella nostra lingua: & che la sua principale sedia era in due regioni, Og & Magog, è da sapere, che in tutte quelle carte da nauigare che si vegghono hoggidi fatte già 200 & 300. anni, v'è posto questo Prete Ianni sotto la Tramontana & sopra l'India
p.s: Giovanni Battista Ramusio, Dichiaratione on Marco Polo
p.pe: Tartars identified with Gog and Magog; 'Uncan' as Prester John
p.t: where Messer Marco Polo says that in the north there was a great lord called Uncan, whose name some take to mean Prester John in our language, and that his principal seat was in two regions, Og and Magog: it should be known that on all those sea charts one sees today, made 200 and 300 years ago, this Prester John is placed in the north and above India
p.c: Ramusio is reporting legend and old maps, not asserting the facts himself; useful for the maps team.

p.h: Royal tombs with poisoned children and arrow traps
p.g: Huc passes on a lurid report about Tartar kings' burials: a brick building with statues, a central cavern full of treasure, children killed with mercury to keep their faces fresh and set up around the corpse holding the king's pipe and snuff, and a spring-loaded battery of bows to shoot any grave robber. He says bow-makers sold such traps and that Chinese sometimes bought them to guard their houses.
p.q: These monstrous interments sometimes cost the lives of a great number of slaves. They take children of both sexes, remarkable for their beauty, and make them swallow mercury till they are suffocated; in this way they preserve, they say, the freshness and ruddiness of their countenance, so as to make them appear still alive.
p.s: Évariste Huc (translated by William Hazlitt, 1852)
p.c: Huc did not see this; 'they say' marks it as hearsay, and it echoes older Chinese tomb legends.

p.h: The 'piebald horde' of Siberia
p.g: A 'piebald horde' was famous in 16th-century Siberia, and some doubted it existed because people thought its members were themselves spotted. Klaproth says the name only described their horses, and quotes the explorer Messerschmidt's diary: in 1721 the governor of Tomsk still claimed the Kistym Tatars had been piebald people who slowly 'degenerated' into white ones.
p.q: la horde bigarrée, … dont on a souvent révoqué en doute l'existence, parce qu'on croyait que les hommes qui la composaient étaient eux-mêmes bigarrés, tandis qu'il ne s'agissait que de leurs chevaux. … le woiewode de Tomsk assura: « Qu'on appelait les Tartares de Kistym la horde bigarrée (piegaga ou piestra orda), qu'ils étaient bigarrés, mais qu'ils avaient successivement dégénéré, en devenant blancs.
p.s: Julius Klaproth, quoting D. G. Messerschmidt's manuscript journal (10 October 1721) reporting the voevoda of Tomsk
p.t: the piebald horde, … whose existence has often been doubted because people believed that the men who made it up were themselves piebald, whereas it concerned only their horses. … the voevoda of Tomsk asserted 'that the Kistym Tartars were called the piebald horde (pegaya or pestraya orda), that they had been piebald, but had gradually degenerated by becoming white.'
p.c: Klaproth himself rejects the spotted-people story as an 'extravagant idea'; the voevoda was repeating local lore.

p.h: Heaps of monster bones across Tartary and Siberia
p.g: Discussing why lions are carved on Tibetan buildings though none live nearby, Turner remarks that if lions ever lived there wild, it was in the age of the huge animals whose bones lie in heaps in Tartary and Siberia. He takes the bones (mammoths) as proof of a great convulsion of the globe. This is Turner's own speculation, a common idea in his day.
p.q: it must have been at the same time with those vast monsters, whose bones are found in huge heaps in various parts of Tartary and Siberia at this day, and clearly point to some great convulsion, and change, in the order of our globe.
p.s: Samuel Turner (1800)
p.c: Turner's own inference from reports of mammoth bones; he did not see them.

p.h: The hare, the owl and the fortress of wind
p.g: Riccoldo's origin tale: the Tartars lived shut in by mountains whose only pass held an empty fortress that roared with the noise of horses, men and trumpets, a trick of the wind. A hunter chasing a hare followed it in, saw an owl singing on the gate, reasoned that no one lives where a hare runs and an owl sings, and led his people out. So, Riccoldo says, Tartars honour the hare and paint it on arms and tents, and nobles wear owl feathers and owl skins, which Western merchants now sell them for up to twenty pounds each.
p.q: Non est habitacio hominum, vbi lepus fugit et bubo cantat. Et sic fiducialiter intrans neminem inuenit.
p.s: Riccoldo of Monte Croce, Liber peregrinationis, ed. J. C. M. Laurent (Leipzig, 1864)
p.pl: Mountains beyond the Caspian (Caucasus in the legend)
p.t: 'There is no dwelling of men where a hare flees and an owl sings.' And so, entering confidently, he found no one.
p.c: A legend Riccoldo heard; Hayton of Corycus (W229) tells a different owl story in which the bird saves Genghis Khan in a bush.

p.h: Yermak's armour and the Tatars' vow of silence
p.g: In 1651 the Tobolsk officer Ulian Remezov took Yermak's famous mail coat, reclaimed from Tatar princes, as a gift to the Kalmyk ruler Ablai, who kissed it and raised it to his head. Ablai then told his own version of Yermak's death: drowned at the ford, found and shot at, his blood flowing, his armour divided up, miracles from his armour and clothes, and a Tatar oath 'on pain of death' not to tell the Russians about him. Ablai said that as a sick child he was given earth from Yermak's grave to drink and was cured.
p.q: И нача Аблай повѣсти дѣяти о немъ по своей исторіи, какъ пріѣхалъ въ Сибирь, и отъ Кучюма на перекопѣ побѣжа, и утопе, и обрѣтенъ, и стрѣлянъ, и кровь течаше, и пансыри раздѣлиша и развезоша, и какъ отъ пансырей и отъ платья чюдесъ было, и какъ Татара смертной завѣтъ положиша, что про него Русакамъ невѣщати
p.s: Kungur (Brief Siberian) Chronicle, Remezov tradition (reporting Ulian Remezov's embassy), 1880 edition
p.pl: Camp of the Kalmyk taisha Ablai
p.pe: Ablai, Kalmyk (Oirat) ruler; Ulian Remezov, Tobolsk envoy; Siberian Tatars
p.t: And Ablai began to tell stories about him, according to his own history: how he came to Siberia, and fled from Kuchum at the ford, and drowned, and was found, and was shot at, and blood flowed, and they divided up his armour and carried it off, and how there were miracles from the armour and the clothing, and how the Tatars made a vow on pain of death not to tell the Russians about him
p.c: A family story of the Remezovs, told half a century later; the miracles are Tatar and Kalmyk beliefs as Russians reported them.

p.h: Flood geology and the 'Plateau of Tartary'
p.g: Humboldt explains how a geographic guess became a myth. If the highest lands had been the first to emerge from the waters, they must also have received the first seeds of civilisation; 'diluvial' geology built on ancient myths encouraged this, and so the vaguely named Plateau of Tartary gained a 'moral interest'. Travel, measurement and the study of Asian languages, he says, have corrected these exaggerations.
p.q: Les hautes régions qui les premières avaient été abandonnées par les eaux, devaient aussi avoir reçu les premières des germes de civilisation. Des systèmes de géologie diluvienne, fondés sur des mythes anciens et sur des traditions locales, favorisaient ces aperçus. … donnait à ce grand massif, à ce plateau continu, vaguement appelé Plateau de la Tartarie, un intérêt moral et une importance particulière.
p.s: Alexander von Humboldt
p.t: The high regions that had been the first to be left by the waters must also have been the first to receive the seeds of civilisation. Systems of diluvial geology, founded on ancient myths and local traditions, favoured these views. … gave this great massif, this continuous plateau vaguely called the Plateau of Tartary, a moral interest and a special importance.

p.h: A great stone ghost city near Lake Dalai
p.g: Describing Lake Dalai (Hulun Nur) from what the local peoples told him, Spafarii reports a great stone city a day's ride from the lake, 'with every kind of building', its stone halls still whole. Some said its people all died of plague and left their goods behind, so that no one dared enter and people only looked at it from afar; others said war had emptied it. On the same page he repeats that the lake is so deep it holds whales and seals.
p.q: Отъ Далая днище есть городъ великой каменной со всякимъ строеніемъ, и палаты въ немъ каменныя цѣлы; и говорятъ, что въ томъ городѣ отъ мору люди всѣ пропали, и осталось имѣніе ихъ все тамъ; и иноземцы въ тотъ городъ иттить не смѣютъ, а смотрятъ все издали; а иные говорятъ, что отъ войны запустѣло.
p.s: Nikolai Spafarii (ed. Yu. V. Arsenyev, 1882)
p.pe: Mongols nomadising around the lake; the city's builders are not named
p.t: A day's journey from the Dalai there is a great stone city with every kind of building, and the stone halls in it are whole; and they say that in that city the people all perished of plague, and all their goods remained there; and the natives dare not go into that city, but look at it all from afar; and others say that it was laid waste by war.
p.c: Rumour from local informants; a gap in both manuscripts cuts off the sentence just before, so the river it stood on is lost.

p.h: Telebuga lost in the mountains: a hundred thousand dead
p.g: Returning from a raid on Hungary, Nogai went by Brasov, while Telebuga tried to cross the mountains. A three-day crossing became fifty days of wandering. Famine set in, the soldiers began to eat people and then to die, and 'eyewitnesses said' a hundred thousand perished. Telebuga came out on foot with his wife and a single mare. The chronicler presents it as God's punishment.
p.q: Телебуга поиде поперекъ Гору; што бяшеть переити треими деньми, и ходи по 50 дній блудя въ горахъ, водимъ гнѣвомъ Божіимъ. И бысть въ нихъ голодъ великъ; и начаша люде ѣсти, потомъ же начаша и сами измирати, и умре ихъ бесчисленое множьство; самовидци же тако рекоша: умершихъ бысть сто тысячь.
p.s: Hypatian Chronicle, PSRL vol. 2 (1843)
p.pe: Golden Horde army of Nogai and Telebuga
p.t: Telebuga went across the Mountain; what should have been crossed in three days, he wandered for 50 days lost in the mountains, led by the wrath of God. And there was a great famine among them; and they began to eat people, and then began themselves to die, and a countless multitude of them died; eyewitnesses said this: the dead were a hundred thousand.
p.c: The figure of 100,000 is hearsay attributed to eyewitnesses; the cannibalism report is part of the same account.

p.h: Ox-footed men with dogs' faces
p.g: Telling of Mongol campaigns in the far north, Carpini says the army passed the Samoyeds, who lived by hunting in tents of hide, and came to a land by the Ocean where they found monsters, 'as we were firmly told', with human bodies but ox feet and dogs' faces, who spoke two words like men and barked at the third.
p.q: Indè ultrà procedentes venerunt ad quandam terram super Oceanum, ubi invenerunt quædam monstra, ut nobis firmiter dicebatur, quæ per omnia formam humanam habebant sed pedes desinebant in pedes bovinos, et humanum caput habebant sed faciem habebant ut canis; duo verba loquebantur more humano et tercio latrabant ut canis
p.s: John of Plano Carpini
p.t: Going on further they came to a land on the Ocean, where they found certain monsters, as we were firmly told, which had human form in every way except that their feet ended in the feet of oxen, and they had human heads but faces like dogs; they spoke two words in the human way and at the third barked like a dog
p.c: Carpini marks it as hearsay ('ut nobis firmiter dicebatur'); it echoes the dog-headed races of classical and medieval lore.

p.h: Electric shocks at the khan's court taken for magic
p.g: After a fireworks show for the khan's birthday, de Tott staged 'a little chamber fire-work' of electrical experiments. The courtiers thought it sorcery; the khan asked to be shocked himself, and next day the whole town talked of nothing but electricity.
p.q: The first effects of this phenomenon excited such astonishment, that I had some difficulty in destroying the opinion of magic I saw arising in their minds… The Kam, however, had the air of comprehending me, and was himself desirous of being electrified. I gave him the stroke very moderately, but I handled the courtiers in such a manner as to obtain the Prince's approbation.
p.s: Baron de Tott (English translation, 1785)
p.pe: Crimean Tatars (Khan Maksud Giray and courtiers)
p.c: A self-flattering anecdote; only de Tott tells it.

p.h: The lamb that grows from the ground
p.g: Among the marvels Chang De heard of is the 'furrow-planted sheep': a sheep's navel sown in the ground and watered sprouts when it hears thunder, grows up still tied to the earth by its navel, and is freed by a scare so it can graze. This is the Chinese form of the 'vegetable lamb of Tartary' (barometz) that European books later placed on the Volga steppe.
p.q: 壠種羊岀西海羊臍種土中溉以水聞雷而生臍系地中及長驚以木臍断嚙草至秋可食臍内復有種
p.s: Liu Yu, Record of an Embassy to the West, from Chang De's report (Qiujian ji juan 94 = Yutang jiahua juan 2; Sibu congkan text, Kanseki Repository transcription)
p.pe: Hearsay about peoples of the far west
p.t: The furrow-planted sheep comes from the Western Sea. A sheep's navel is planted in the soil and watered; when it hears thunder it comes to life, its navel still tied into the ground. When it has grown, they startle it with a piece of wood; the navel snaps and it grazes. By autumn it can be eaten, and inside its navel there is seed again.
p.c: Liu Yu himself closes the list by saying such strange things 'cannot all be recorded'; it is hearsay.

p.h: Bone skates, but no monsters
p.g: From informants at Mongke's court Rubruck learned of northern peoples: the Orengai, who tied polished bones under their feet and sped over snow and ice fast enough to catch birds and beasts. He also asked about the monstrous races described by Isidore and Solinus; his informants said they had never seen any such thing, which, he writes, 'we much wonder whether it is true'.
p.q: Sunt etiam ibi Orengai, qui ligant ossa limata sub pedibus suis, et impellunt se super nivem congelatam, et super glaciem cum tanta velocitate ut capiant aves et bestias. … Quesivi de monstris, sive de monstruosis hominibus, de quibus narrat Ysodorus et Solinus. Ipsi dicebant michi quod nunquam viderunt talia, de quo multum miramur si verum sit.
p.s: William of Rubruck
p.t: There are also the Orengai, who tie polished bones under their feet and push themselves over the frozen snow and over the ice so fast that they catch birds and beasts. … I asked about the monsters, or monstrous men, that Isidore and Solinus tell of. They told me they had never seen such things, at which we much wonder whether it is true.
p.c: Rubruck's doubt runs both ways: he is surprised the monsters of the old books were not confirmed.

p.h: The Field of White Bones
p.g: South of the Altai, Chen-hai warned that the road crossed the 'field of white bones', a plain strewn with black stones where a whole army had once died of exhaustion and where the Naiman army had lately been destroyed (by Chinggis, Bretschneider notes). Anyone who crossed by day in the sun would die with his horse, so the party marched all night, past more than a hundred great sand hills that 'seemed to swim like big ships in the midst of the waves', and reached a small Hui-ho (Muslim) town the next morning.
p.q: Chen-hai replied: "That is an old battlefield … a field of death. At one time a whole army perished there by exhaustion; no one escaped. A short time ago, at the same place, the army of the Nai-man was destroyed. Whoever crosses the desert in the daytime and in clear weather (i.e., exposed to the sun) will die from fatigue, and his horse also."
p.s: Chen-hai (Chinqai), as reported by Li Zhichang (translated by E. Bretschneider, 1888)
p.pe: Naiman army; the travellers' Mongol escort
p.c: The story of the older lost army is Chen-hai's hearsay; the diarist saw only the desert.

p.h: A stone sphinx from a Siberian grave
p.g: In the new mining museum at Barnaul, Ledebour was struck by a crudely carved stone 'sphinx' on a squared block, said to have been found in a Chud grave. He found it remarkable to meet 'this form of the highest antiquity' in Siberia. He reports the find-spot as he was told it and gives no further detail.
p.q: Im Vorzimmer stand eine aus Stein gehauene Sphinx, auf einem viereckigen behauenen Block ruhend, beinah 4 Fuß lang … mir höchst interessant, da dies Denkmal in einem tschudischen Grabe gefunden worden. Die Arbeit war zwar roh
p.s: Carl Friedrich von Ledebour
p.pe: the legendary Chud (ancient builders of Siberian graves)
p.t: In the anteroom stood a sphinx hewn from stone, resting on a squared, dressed block, almost 4 feet long … most interesting to me, since this monument had been found in a Chud grave. The workmanship was indeed crude
p.c: Ledebour saw the object in a museum; its grave origin is the museum's claim. 'Sphinx' is his word for a crouching beast figure.

p.h: Towers built of the heads of 'white Tartars'
p.g: Outside Damghan the envoys saw towers of mud and human heads. They were told these were the heads of 'white Tartars', nomads from between Turkey and Syria whom Timur had deported to Damghan; when they tried to ride home, plundering as they went, his army killed them, and Timur ordered every white Tartar found to be put to death. Locals said lights burned on the towers at night.
p.q: These towers, which are made of heads, are built of the heads of a race of people called "white Tartars," natives of a country between Turkey and Syria. … The people of the city say, that they often see lights burning on the top of these towers in the night.
p.s: Ruy González de Clavijo (translated by Clements R. Markham, 1859)
p.w: 1404 (towers seen); event a few years earlier
p.c: The towers were seen; the story, the figure of 60,000 dead and the lights at night were told to the envoys.

p.h: The devil's claws on the moon
p.g: Muraviev says that even the court astronomer who could calculate eclipses believed, like everyone in Khiva, that an eclipse happened when the devil grabbed the sun or moon, and that shouting and firing guns would drive him off. They called the North Star the 'iron point' at the end of the earth's axis and compared the earth to a watermelon.
p.q: he does not even know the cause of an eclipse, but believes with the rest of the people that it is brought about by the devil fastening his claws on to the sun or moon, and thinks a loud noise and the firing off of guns necessary to get rid of this dreadful enemy. The earth they believe to be round and compare it to a water-melon.
p.s: Nikolai Muraviev (translated by W. S. A. Lockhart, 1871)
p.c: Muraviev writes condescendingly about Khivan learning.

p.h: A holy fool cries: 'Tatars will not live here'
p.g: Among the omens of Kazan's fall the author lists a Tatar holy fool who walked the streets shouting that Tatars would not live there, only Russians. The khan forbade killing him and had him shut in an empty house, but he broke out. The next chapters tell of a calf born in human shape that turned into an armed man, and a fish-net that brought up a live old man who urged surrender to Moscow.
p.q: Нѣкто Татаринъ въ Казани уродивъ, по граду ходя, нача напрасно вопити и непрестанно глаголати: «не жить здѣ Татаромъ, но Рускимъ людемъ». Татарове же хотяху убити его; не повелѣ имъ царь убити его, но въ праздну храмину повелѣ затворити его.
p.s: Anonymous author of the History of the Kazan Tsardom, PSRL vol. 19 (1903)
p.t: A certain Tatar in Kazan, a holy fool, walking through the city, began suddenly to cry out and say without ceasing: 'Tatars will not live here, but Russian people.' The Tatars wanted to kill him; the tsar did not allow them to kill him, but ordered him shut up in an empty house.
p.c: Prophecies written after the event to show that Kazan's fall was fated.

p.h: Gog and Magog in Tartar speech
p.g: Strahlenberg says the Tobolsk Tartars told him they call peoples on this side of the mountains 'Ma-Tschudi' and those beyond 'Ja-gougi and Ma-gougi', and he concludes that these words are the same as the biblical Gog and Magog. Elsewhere he suggests that Gog was the Tartars' legendary ancestor Oghuz Khan. It is a learned attempt to find the Bible's northern nations among the Tartars.
p.q: The same Tartars have also told me, that they use, in the like Manner, the Name Ma-Tschudi, … And when they, at the same Time, would denote the Heathen roving Scythian Nations, who inhabited the other Side of that Mountain, they call them Gaed-Tschudi, Ma-schudi or Ja-gougi and Ma-gougi; And these Words then signify the very same as Gog and Magog,
p.s: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (English translation, 1738)
p.c: The informants' words are filtered through his own etymologies, which are speculative.

p.h: The 'tailed Tatars' of Turkestan
p.g: The interpreter Aralov, who had often been to the town of Turkestan, told Rychkov of a despised clan of under a hundred families nicknamed the 'tailed Tatars'. The story went that their ancestors killed the son of a local saint, who cursed them so they could not ride horses, and they grew a tail-like mark. Aralov swore he had seen such a mark on a naked child. Rychkov leaves it to the reader: 'whether this is true or not'. His real point follows: there the name Tatar is an insult, and the Tatars of Orenburg and Kazan are called Nogais.
p.q: заклялъ ихъ молитвою, дабы они неспособны были къ верховой ѣздѣ на лошадяхъ, и будтобъ съ того времени получили они на тѣлѣ знакъ подобной хвосту … Помянутой Переводчикъ объявляетъ, яко бы онъ изъ тѣхъ людей одного робенка самъ видѣлъ нагова, и увѣряетъ, что у него назади такой знакъ подлинно былъ. Правдаль сіе, или нѣтъ, остается въ произвольномъ разсужденіи.
p.s: Pyotr Rychkov, reporting the interpreter Aralov (1762)
p.pe: A despised clan near Turkestan called 'tailed Tatars'
p.t: he cursed them with a prayer, so that they should be unable to ride on horseback, and supposedly from that time they received on their bodies a mark like a tail … The said interpreter declares that he himself saw one child of those people naked, and assures that it really had such a mark behind. Whether this is true or not is left to free judgment.
p.c: A second-hand legend; Rychkov explicitly declines to vouch for it.

p.h: A cemetery of giants at Umbarr
p.g: Passing an abandoned walled town, Abbott's interpreter told him it had been a Kalmyk capital, and that the late Khan stopped rebuilding it when diggers found huge human bones. The interpreter claimed to have seen skulls too big to hug that crumbled to powder in the air. Abbott doubts the giants but thinks the bones deserve study.
p.q: He said, it was supposed to have been the capital of Khaurism, under the Culmauks, whom we call Calmucks. That these were slain, in an invasion by Russia. That the late Khaun purposed rebuilding this city, and had walled it accordingly ; but that, in digging, some monstrous human bones were found, which proved it to have been a cemetery of giants.
p.s: Ali Muhummud, Abbott's interpreter, as reported by James Abbott
p.pe: Khivans, Turkmens; Kalmyks (as former rulers in the story)
p.c: Hearsay. Abbott did not see the bones and on the next page says few would accept the giants theory.

p.h: Bearded 'Alimenes' guarding the Tartar passes
p.g: Cruz reports that the king of China keeps salaried soldiers to guard the weak passes and walls facing the Tartars: big, bearded men in cut breeches and caps, with curved swords. A Portuguese captive heard the Chinese call them 'Alimenes', which Cruz takes to mean Germans (Alemanes), concluding that China must border Upper Germany. He tells the same story on an earlier page (n25). The identification is his own leap.
p.q: dizem os chinas que tẽ el Rey da China muita gente darmas salariada, que lhe guarda os passos fracos e os muros da bãda dos tartaras: dizẽ q̃ sam homẽs grãdes e barbaçudos, e q̃ trazẽ calças cortadas e gorras e espadas rõbas, e disse me hũ portugues q̃ pola terra dentro fora leuado catiuo, q̃ ouuira dizer aos chinas q̃ lhe chamauã a estes Alimenes
p.s: Gaspar da Cruz, O.P. (Tractado, Évora 1569)
p.pe: Hired guards on the Tartar frontier, called 'Alimenes' by the Chinese
p.t: the Chinese say that the King of China has many salaried men-at-arms who guard for him the weak passes and the walls on the side of the Tartars; they say they are big, heavily bearded men who wear cut breeches, caps and curved swords; and a Portuguese who had been taken captive inland told me that he had heard the Chinese call these people Alimenes.
p.c: Third-hand report; the leap from 'Alimenes' to Germans is Cruz's guess.

p.h: Forty Christian Tartar princes buried at Derbent
p.g: On the hills around Derbent the 1746 embassy saw many ancient graves and tombstones six to nine feet long, with inscriptions no one could read. Persians told them forty of these belonged to Christian Tartar princes who died for their faith, and that each stone was cut to the exact height of the dead man. The diarist warns that the Persians 'deal much in the marvellous'. (These are probably the Kirkhlyar, the 'Forty' cemetery linked to the early Arab conquest.)
p.q: …the Persians report, that of these are not less than 40 belonging to Christian Tartar princes, who have died fighting for their religion. There are many antient tomb-stones, from 6 to 9 feet long, … with inscriptions not intelligible to any of the present inhabitants. The Persians, who deal much in the marvellous, endeavoured to persuade us, that these stones were cut in length exactly to the stature of the deceased
p.s: Anonymous journal of the Russian embassy to Persia of 1746, extract printed by Jonas Hanway (1753)
p.c: Local Persian tradition, which the diarist himself doubts. The identification with the Kirkhlyar cemetery is ours, not the source's.

p.h: The wind that dried the sea for Möngke
p.g: In the Chinese biography of Möngke, the Kipchak chief Bachman fled to an island in the sea. When Möngke arrived, a strong wind drove the water off the shallows and his army crossed; Möngke declared that Heaven itself was opening the road. Bachman, captured, refused to kneel, saying 'I was the ruler of a state' and 'am I a camel, that I should kneel?', and warned that the water would soon return. The next sentence says Möngke then marched with Batu against Rus ('Oros').
p.q: По счастію, сильный вѣтеръ согналъ морскую воду съ мелкихъ мѣстъ, такъ, что можно было переправиться. Ханъ, обрадовавшись, сказалъ: »Само Небо открываетъ дорогу мнѣ.« … Ханъ приказалъ ему стать на колѣна: но Бацимакъ сказалъ: »Я былъ обладателемъ государства и могу ли дорожить жизнію? Сверхъ сего я не верблюдъ: для чего мнѣ становиться на колѣна?«
p.s: Yuan shi (biography of Möngke), translated by Iakinf Bichurin, 1829
p.t: By good fortune a strong wind drove the sea water off the shallow places, so that it was possible to cross. The khan, delighted, said: 'Heaven itself opens the road for me.' … The khan ordered him to kneel; but Bachman said: 'I was the ruler of a state, and can I value my life? Besides, I am not a camel: why should I kneel?'
p.c: An official dynastic history that presents the wind as a sign of Heaven's favour; not an eyewitness account.

p.h: Raiding the Land of Darkness on mares with foals
p.g: Far to the north, Polo says, lies a Land of Darkness where no sun, moon or stars are seen. Tartars raid it riding mares whose foals they leave at the border, trusting the mares to find the way back to their young. The pale inhabitants hunt sables, ermine and black fox for the fur trade. Yule suggests the story garbles the Arctic winter night.
p.q: The Tartars however sometimes visit the country, and they do it in this way. They enter the region riding mares that have foals, and these foals they leave behind. After taking all the plunder that they can get, they find their way back by help of the mares, which are all eager to get back to their foals
p.s: Marco Polo (translated by Henry Yule, 1871)
p.pe: Tartars (Golden Horde raiders) and northern fur hunters
p.c: Pure hearsay; the mare-and-foal trick is an old travellers' tale also told of Alexander the Great.

p.h: Mammoth tusks shown in Moscow
p.g: Among Siberia's riches Avril lists a fine ivory from creatures the Russians called 'Behemot', found along the Lena and the shores of the 'Tartarian Sea'. He was shown teeth in Moscow ten inches long, finer than elephant ivory. On the next page he says the ivory was believed to stanch bleeding, was prized by Persians and Turks for dagger hilts, and came from a creature 'as big and as dangerous as a Crocodile'.
p.q: Several teeth of this Monster were shewn us at Moscow, which were ten Inches long, and two in Diameter at the Root ; Nor are the Elephants Teeth comparable to 'em
p.s: Philippe Avril (English translation, 1693)
p.c: He saw the teeth; the living 'monster' is hearsay. This is fossil mammoth (or walrus) ivory; the page OCR is badly garbled around it.

p.h: The sorcerer, the snakes and the dragon on Kazan's coat of arms
p.g: In the same Tatar tradition, the site of the new Kazan was infested with snakes. A sorcerer gathered them all in autumn, piled wood on them in winter and burned them in spring, while pigs were driven off by setting the forest alight. A two-headed winged serpent, 'or rather a dragon', fled to Snake Hill and was finally killed by the sorcerer's arts; the khan took it for his arms, and Georgi notes it is still the city's coat of arms.
p.q: Die Schlangen versammlete ein Zauberer des Herbstes alle an einen Ort, lies im Winter Holz auf denselben führen und verbrannte sie im Frühlinge. … Eine zweyköpfige geflügelte Schlange oder vielmehr ein Drache entflohe nach dem Dshilantau (Schlangenberge) und war daselbst fürchterlich, sie ward aber doch endlich durch die Künste des Zauberers getödtet und zur Erinnerung vom Chan zum Wapen erwählt.
p.s: A Tatar written tradition, translated for Georgi
p.t: A sorcerer gathered all the snakes in one place in autumn, had wood carted onto them in winter and burned them in spring. … A two-headed winged serpent, or rather a dragon, fled to Dzhilantau (Snake Hill) and was terrible there, but it was finally killed by the sorcerer's arts and chosen by the khan as his coat of arms in remembrance.
p.c: Legend, reported as the Tatars' own account; Georgi does not endorse it.

p.h: Friars look for Alexander's enclosed nations and find nothing
p.g: Scholastic histories said Alexander the Great had the Jews (in other versions Gog and Magog) shut up between the Caspian mountains, to break out at the end of the world. Vincent reports that Dominicans who lived seven years in Tiflis asked Georgians, Persians and Jews about it, and all said they knew nothing of it. The margin says the story 'appears to be a fable', and the next page adds that only Alexander's gates exist, one of which the Tartars broke.
p.q: Cum enim dicant historiæ nostræ scolasticæ, quod Alexander magnus Rex Macedonum oratione impetrauit à Domino reclusionem Iudæorum inter montes Caspios, ipsosque circa finem mundi prædicent exituros, Fratres nostri … per 7. annos commorati sunt, diligenter à Georgianis & à Persis, & etiam à Iudæis de inclusione illa inquisierunt, & dicunt omnes etiam Iudæi, quod nihil penitus inde sciunt
p.s: Vincent of Beauvais, Speculum historiale (Douai 1624), from material he says he received from Simon of Saint-Quentin
p.pe: Dominican friars in Georgia; the legendary peoples shut behind the Caspian mountains
p.t: For whereas our scholastic histories say that Alexander the Great, king of the Macedonians, obtained from the Lord by prayer the shutting up of the Jews between the Caspian mountains, and predict that they will come out near the end of the world, our brothers [of the Order of Preachers, in the Georgian city of Tiflis near the Caspian mountains] stayed seven years, and diligently asked the Georgians and Persians, and even the Jews, about that enclosure; and all, even the Jews, say that they know nothing at all of it
p.c: The friars tested a legend and found no support; the passage does not itself call the Tartars the enclosed nations.

p.h: A gold sphinx from a Siberian kurgan, and Egyptians in Siberia?
p.g: Witsen describes a small beaten-gold figure sent to him from Siberia, dug from an old burial under a kurgan: a lion or tiger body with a human head and spread wings. On the same page he wonders whether Egyptian idol-worship somehow reached Siberia, or whether Chinese settlers of Chinggis Khan's time left such things. A striking early report of Scythian-style gold from Siberian mounds, wrapped in pure speculation.
p.q: Een ander Afgoden-beeld, groot twee vinger-breet, van geslagen Goud, is my uit Siberien toegezonden, 't geen mede uit een oude Begravenis-plaets, daer men Menschen doods-beenderen by vond, onder een Kurgan, of groote heuvel is geligt, vertoont het Lichaem van een viervoetig Beest, als van een Tyger of Leeuw, heeft het hooft van een Mensch, en twee vleugelen
p.s: Nicolaes Witsen
p.t: Another idol, two fingers' breadth in size, of beaten gold, was sent to me from Siberia; it too was lifted from an old burial place, where human bones were found with it, under a kurgan or great mound; it shows the body of a four-footed beast, like a tiger or lion, has the head of a man, and two wings
p.c: The object is real evidence; Witsen's Egyptian and Chinese explanations are his own guesses, which he himself calls a riddle.

p.h: The Mongols as Gog and Magog
p.g: At Selenginsk, where by his reckoning the Siberian realm ended and the 'Mongol state' began, Spafarii offers a learned identification: the Mongols are the Gog and Magog of the Bible, 'because they call themselves Mogol'. It is an old pun on the name from biblical geography, not something the Mongols told him. He then describes them as a very great people stretching from the Amur to Bukhara and India.
p.q: И здѣ скончается Сибирское государство, и начинается государство Мунгальское. Мунгалы суть, о которыхъ пишетъ въ Библіи - Гогъ и Магогъ, потому что они называютъ себя Маголь. И тотъ родъ Мунгальской зѣло великой
p.s: Nikolai Spafarii (ed. Yu. V. Arsenyev, 1882)
p.t: And here the Siberian state ends and the Mongol state begins. The Mongols are those of whom the Bible writes, Gog and Magog, because they call themselves Magol. And that Mongol race is very great
p.c: A bookish word-play, repeated from the European and Byzantine tradition. The printed dash is shown as a hyphen.

p.h: Genghis Khan descended from a grey deer and a white she-wolf
p.g: Visdelou compares the Mongol origin stories. A Chinese abridgement says the Mongols' 'secret memoirs' traced Chinggis's family to the mating of a grey deer and a white she-wolf, whose monstrous child was his twenty-fourth ancestor; on the same page is the story of the widow Alan-kouo conceiving by a golden light through the tent's smoke-hole. Visdelou notes the official Chinese genealogy says none of this and calls the wolf tale 'shameful and impossible'.
p.q: les mémoires secrets des Moumgols témoignent que la famille de Ki-o-uen étoit sortie de l'accouplement d'un cerf gris & d'une louve blanche, & que l'enfant monstrueux qui en nâquit fut le vingt-quatrième Ayeul de Tchim-khis-khan … elle ne parle nulle part de la dernière, qui est également honteuse & impossible.
p.s: Claude de Visdelou, citing Yuan Liaofan's Chinese abridgement ('Tuen-leao-fan'), which cites the Mongols' 'secret memoirs'
p.t: the secret memoirs of the Mongols testify that the family of Ki-o-uen came from the coupling of a grey deer and a white she-wolf, and that the monstrous child born of it was the twenty-fourth ancestor of Chinggis Khan … it [the official history] nowhere mentions the last story, which is both shameful and impossible.
p.c: Visdelou reports the legend at third hand and rejects it.

p.h: Walking dead for forty days
p.g: Holderness reports a startling belief: the spirits of wicked people walk for forty days after death, and then the grave must be opened and the corpse shot, beheaded or have its heart removed. She follows it with a Tatar neighbour's gentle answer on why every dead person got a good 'passport'.
p.q: The Tatars believe that the spirits of the bad walk for forty days after death. In this case, they say, it is requisite to uncover the grave, and either shoot the dead body, cut off its head, or take out its heart.
p.s: Mary Holderness
p.c: Reported belief; she does not say she saw a grave opened.

p.h: No monsters, but hairy little men who cry 'chin, chin'
p.g: Rubruck asked priests at Karakorum about the dog-headed and one-eyed monsters described by Isidore and Solinus. They told him they had never seen any, which surprised him. Then a priest from Cathay told him of tiny hairy creatures with stiff knees living among rocks east of Cathay, caught by leaving out mead to get them drunk, whose blood made a red dye.
p.q: They told me they had never seen such, which astonished me greatly, if it be true. … in the countries east of Cathay there are high rocks, among which dwell creatures who have in all respects human forms, except that their knees do not bend, so that they get along by some kind of jumping motion
p.s: William of Rubruck (translated by W. W. Rockhill, 1900)
p.pe: Priests at the Mongol court; Cathay
p.c: The creature story is hearsay from a single informant; the denial of monsters is a useful check on older book-learning.

p.h: A petrified city on the Aral Sea
p.g: In Bukhara Burnes heard tales of an enchanted, petrified city on the south-west shore of the Aral Sea called Barsa-gil-mis, Turkic for 'go and never return', because curious visitors never came back. He files it with Bukharan belief in magic and remarks that 'distance gives countenance to most of the fables'.
p.q: tales of an enchanted and petrified city which was described by the Bokharees as lying on the south-western corner of the Sea of Aral, and between Orgunje and Orenburg. They call it "Barsa-gil-mis;" which, in Toorkee, means, to go and never return; since such is said to be the fate of the curious.
p.s: Alexander Burnes (1834)
p.c: A local legend that Burnes reports with open scepticism.

p.h: The Tatar tale of Chinese who fled when the forest grew
p.g: Müller reports a story still told orally by the Tobolsk Tatars: Siberia was once a bare steppe where the Chinese lived, but when forest began to grow everywhere the people took fright, 'as the land became as if horned', and moved away to their present home. He says it was also written down in 1670 on the orders of the Tobolsk governor Pyotr Godunov. Müller calls it a false tale that no reasonable person can believe, and notes that forest could easily grow over abandoned sites in 450 years without any miracle.
p.q: Сказываютъ, якобы сперва вся Сибирь была голая степь безъ лѣсу, а какъ въ оное время Китайцы тамъ жительство свое имѣли, то помалу по разнымъ мѣстамъ началъ лѣсъ расти, чего народъ испужавшись, понеже земля подобно какъ рогатая стала, на нынѣшнее жилище переселился. Сію повѣсть еще и нынѣ у Тобольскихъ Татаръ изустно слышать можно.
p.s: Gerhard Friedrich Müller, reporting Tobolsk Tatar oral tradition (Russian edition, 1787 issue)
p.pe: Siberian Tatars of Tobolsk (tellers); 'Chinese' (in the tale)
p.t: They say that at first all Siberia was a bare steppe without forest, and when at that time the Chinese lived there, forest little by little began to grow in various places, at which the people took fright, because the land became as if horned, and moved to their present dwelling. This tale can still be heard by word of mouth from the Tobolsk Tatars.
p.c: Müller records the tale in order to reject it; the next page adds the claim that ruined towns between the Irtysh and Tobol are overgrown with forest.

p.h: Cannibal famine, mice and two suns: omens of the Tartar war
p.g: The same 1618 memorial explains the defeat by heaven's anger and lists recent prodigies: no rain in the capital province, famine so bad in another province that people ate one another, a plague of mice in Nanjing, fires in the palace and two suns in the sky, one eclipsing the other. It shows how the Ming court read the Tartar war as a sign of cosmic disorder.

p.h: 'The sea once lay at the foot' of the cliffs
p.g: The house of the chief minister's sister stood below extraordinary rocks full of springs. On their summits, Craven says, were marks where huge cables had 'certainly passed and been tied', and the Tatars insisted the sea had once reached the foot of the cliffs and ships were moored there. At dinner she found Tatar cooking 'much grease and honey', and her hostess served two quarts of sherbet, coffee and sweets.
p.q: The Tartarians insist upon it that the sea once lay at the foot of them … and ships were fastened to them
p.s: Elizabeth Craven (letters published London, 1789)
p.c: The belief is the Tatars'; the 'cable' marks were probably natural weathering grooves, but Craven gives no more detail than this.

p.h: Khan Janibek's giant cooking pot
p.g: The buildings of the Russian saltpetre works at Selitrennoe, Gmelin notes, were mostly built from the rubble of the Tatar ruins. Among the old boiling kettles of the works lay one so huge that the local Tatars told a tale about it: that it was a relic of their past, in which Khan Janibek had twelve oxen cooked at once for his feasts. Gmelin says flatly that it is a Crown saltpetre kettle.
p.q: einige hier wohnenden Leute, sind meistens von tatarischen Trümmern erbauet … In der Siederey sind noch Oefen und Keßel. Unter letztern liegt einer … Die Tataren fabeln, daß er ein tatarisch Ueberbleibsel sey und daß Chan Dschanibek in demselben, bey seinen Schmausen, 12 Ochsen zugleich kochen laßen. Es ist aber gewiß ein der Krone gehöriger Salpeter-Keßel.
p.s: Samuel Gottlieb Gmelin (part 4, compiled by P. S. Pallas, 1784)
p.t: [the dwellings of] some people living here are mostly built from Tatar rubble … In the boiling works there are still furnaces and kettles. Among the latter lies one … The Tatars tell a fable that it is a Tatar relic and that Khan Janibek had 12 oxen cooked in it at once at his feasts. But it is certainly a saltpetre kettle belonging to the Crown.
p.c: A local legend that Gmelin rejects on the spot.

p.h: A cliff of unknown writing on the Yenisei
p.g: Before the great rapids of the Yenisei, Spafarii was told, a stone cliff carries carved writing in an unknown script, with crosses among the letters and carved men holding maces, and 'many other such works'. Nobody knew what it said or who made it. The upper Yenisei is famous today for its rock art and early Turkic runic inscriptions, but Spafarii could only report the mystery.
p.q: А до болшого порогу не доѣзжая есть мѣсто, утесъ каменной по Енисѣю. На томъ утесѣ есть вырѣзано на каменю невѣдомо какое писмо и межъ писмомъ есть и кресты вырѣзаны, такъ же и люди вырѣзаны, и въ рукахъ у нихъ булавы, и иные многіе такія дѣла. … А никто не вѣдаетъ, что писано и отъ кого.
p.s: Nikolai Spafarii (ed. Yu. V. Arsenyev, 1882)
p.t: And before one reaches the great rapids there is a place, a stone cliff along the Yenisei. On that cliff there is carved in the stone some unknown writing, and among the writing crosses are carved too, and men are carved as well, and in their hands they hold maces, and many other such works. … And no one knows what is written or by whom.
p.c: Hearsay ('as they say'); he did not travel that stretch of the Yenisei.

p.h: A twelve-cubit giant of Gog and Magog at Bulghar
p.g: Frähn summarises a tale Ibn Fadlan heard from the Bulghar king: traders found a man twelve cubits tall floating in the flooded Volga, with a head like the largest cauldron, a nose over a span long and fingers a span long. The Wisu people told the king he belonged to Gog and Magog, who lived three months away across a sea. The giant died, and the speaker claims to have seen his dreadful bones. Yaqut already refused to vouch for it, and Frähn suggests in a footnote that mammoth bones were the likely source.
p.q: der eine Höhe von 12 Ellen gehabt, einen Kopf so gross wie nur der grösste Kessel sey, eine Nase über eine Spanne lang, grosse Augen und Spannenlange Finger;… dass dieser Mensch zu den Jog und Magog gehöre,
p.s: C. M. Frähn, summarising Ibn Fadlan's report of the Bulghar king's story (1823)
p.t: who was twelve cubits tall, with a head as big as the biggest cauldron, a nose more than a span long, large eyes and fingers a span long; … that this man belonged to Gog and Magog,
p.c: An editor's paraphrase of a story told to Ibn Fadlan; Yaqut himself doubted it.

p.h: Siberian inscriptions that look European
p.g: Klaproth admits that the letters on the inscribed stones of South Siberia look more European than Asian, with shapes like Greek and Slavonic letters. He warns that this does not mean they were carved after the Russian conquest, since many stand on ancient gravestones. The script was still undeciphered in his day.
p.q: En examinant les caractères de ces inscriptions, on ne peut pas se dissimuler qu'ils ont plutôt un air européen qu'asiatique. On y reconnaît facilement plusieurs lettres grecques et esclavonnes. Cependant on ne peut raisonnablement conclure pour cela que ces inscriptions soient postérieures à la conquête de la Sibérie par les Russes
p.s: Julius Klaproth
p.t: On examining the characters of these inscriptions, one cannot hide from oneself that they look more European than Asian. One easily recognises several Greek and Slavonic letters. Yet one cannot reasonably conclude from this that these inscriptions are later than the Russian conquest of Siberia
p.c: These are the Yenisei runic inscriptions, later shown (1893) to be in an Old Turkic script; the likeness to Greek letters is only in shape.

p.h: A widow warlord with four thousand women archers
p.g: A powerful Tartar widow named Sadur Melik came to Edigü with four thousand women and girls to avenge her husband. Her women rode to war with sword and bow like men. When the kinsman who had killed her husband was captured, she beheaded him herself. Schiltberger says he was there.
p.q: He was brought before the woman ; she ordered him to kneel, and drew her sword, and cut off his head at one blow, and said : " Now am I revenged." I was present there, and I also saw this.
p.s: Johann Schiltberger (translated by J. Buchan Telfer, 1879)
p.c: The number of women (four thousand, on p.37) is likely inflated.

p.h: The camel's tower and a pipeline of mare's milk
p.g: Pallas was told of a great heap of bricks on the steppe, called by Russians the 'hill of the house of prayer' and by Kalmyks 'the camel's tower'. The Kalmyks said that Janibek Khan (who ruled the Golden Horde 1342 to 1357) kept mares here and piped their milk to his residence. Pallas dryly replies that the burial mounds all around show what the building was really for.
p.q: …there is a large heap of bricks, called by the Russians, Metshetnoi Bugor, or the hill of the House of Prayer, and by the Kalmuks, Temahne Balgasum, or the camel's tower. The Kalmuks give the following account of this place: Dshanibek-Khan kept here a number of mares, whose milk was conveyed by tubes, from this tower to his residence.
p.s: Peter Simon Pallas (English translation, 1812 edition)
p.pe: Kalmyk tradition about Janibek Khan of the Golden Horde
p.c: A Kalmyk legend that Pallas reports and rejects.

p.h: A hill heaped over a Tartar emperor by soldiers' helmets
p.g: Below Samara the Russians pointed out a round hill called Sanol Kiergan and told de Bruyn it was the tomb of a Tartar emperor named Mammon, who came up the Volga with seventy other Tartar kings to conquer Russia and died there. His soldiers filled their helmets and shields with earth to raise the mound. The name may echo Mamai, the Golden Horde warlord of the 1370s; Struys (W249) heard a version in 1669.
p.q: Les Russiens nous dirent que c'étoit le tombeau d'un Roi, ou d'un Empereur de Tartarie, nommé Mammon, qui avoit monté le Wolga avec 70. autres Rois Tartares, pour s'emparer de toute la Russie. Que ce Prince étant mort en ce lieu-là, les soldats … remplirent leurs casques & leurs boucliers de terre, pour lui dresser un tombeau, dont cette montagne avoit été formée.
p.s: Cornelis de Bruyn (French translation, Voyages de Corneille Le Brun, 1718)
p.pe: a legendary 'Emperor of Tartary' called Mammon
p.t: The Russians told us it was the tomb of a king or emperor of Tartary named Mammon, who had come up the Volga with seventy other Tartar kings to seize all Russia. That this prince having died in that place, the soldiers … filled their helmets and shields with earth to raise him a tomb, from which this mountain had been formed.
p.c: A folk legend told by Russian boatmen; the hill may be natural.

p.h: Silent trade with unseen people in the Land of Darkness
p.g: At Bulgar he was told of a Land of Darkness forty days north, reached only by dog-sledges over ice, where there were no trees, stones or houses. Merchants left their goods and withdrew; next day they found sable and ermine in their place, and could take the furs or leave them. Nobody ever saw the other party, so the merchants did not know if they traded with men or demons. He did not go.
p.q: each man, leaving what he has brought with him, goes back to his appointed station. On the morrow they return to look for their goods, and find, instead of them, sable, ermine, and the fur of the sinjab. … for the merchants know not whether it is with mankind or demons that they have to do ; no one being seen during the transaction.
p.s: Ibn Battuta (translated by Samuel Lee, 1829)
p.pe: Unknown northern peoples; Golden Horde merchants
p.c: Hearsay; he says he decided not to make the journey. Modern scholars also doubt that he reached Bulgar itself.

p.h: The ancient people who 'taught us everything except their name'
p.g: Humboldt says the high plains of Tartary are no longer seen as the cradle of human civilisation and of the arts and sciences. He borrows d'Alembert's joke about the vanished ancient people imagined by Bailly: they taught us everything except their name and the fact that they existed. Solid research, he adds, has shown that learning reached the lands between the Pamirs, China and the Altai late.
p.q: Ces plaines élevées de la Tartarie ne sont plus regardées comme le berceau de la civilisation humaine, le site primitif des sciences et des arts. Il a disparu, ce peuple ancien qui, selon une expression heureuse de d'Alembert, « Nous a tout appris, excepté son nom et son existence. »
p.s: Alexander von Humboldt, quoting Jean d'Alembert's letter to Voltaire
p.pe: an imagined lost people of Tartary
p.t: These high plains of Tartary are no longer regarded as the cradle of human civilisation, the original home of the sciences and arts. It has vanished, that ancient people which, in d'Alembert's happy phrase, 'taught us everything except its name and its existence.'

p.h: A Tatar commander buried alive in a Polovtsian kurgan
p.g: When Prince Mstislav crossed the Dnieper and beat the Tatar vanguard, the survivors fled with their commander Gemyabeg into a Polovtsian kurgan (burial mound). Unable to hold out, they buried him alive in the earth to save his life. He was found, and the Polovtsy begged him from Mstislav and killed him. The steppe was already dotted with mounds that the chronicler credits to the Polovtsy.
p.q: а прокъ ихъ въбѣже съ воеводою своимъ Гемябегомъ въ курганъ Половьчьскыи, и ту имъ не бы мочи, и погребоша воеводу своего Гемябега жива въ земли, хотяще животъ его ублюсти, и ту й налѣзоша, испросивъше Половьци у Мьстислава, и убиша й.
p.s: Novgorod First Chronicle (PSRL vol. 3, 1841)
p.t: and the rest of them fled with their commander Gemyabeg into a Polovtsian kurgan, and there they could not hold out, and they buried their commander Gemyabeg alive in the earth, wishing to save his life; and there they found him, and the Polovtsy, having begged him from Mstislav, killed him.

p.h: The long-haired forest goblin who boiled two children
p.g: Among the Karachay's many tales of mountain demons, Klaproth records the Ssalmasti, a long-haired female spirit of the woods. A villager caught one and enslaved it by hiding its cut hair, until his children revealed the hiding place; the spirit threw them into the boiling pot and fled back to the forest.
p.q: A malignant spirit in female shape, and having very long hair, which they call in their language Ssalmasti, is reported to reside in a certain wood. About twenty-five years ago one of the inhabitants of the village caught this goblin, carried it home with him, and cut off its hair, which he carefully hid, and by which means he rendered the spirit subservient to him.
p.s: Julius Klaproth (English translation, 1814), from an Armenian informant who lived among the Karachay
p.c: A folk tale passed on through an informant.

p.h: Were the Tartars the lost tribes shut up by Alexander?
p.g: Matthew Paris repeats the belief that the Tartars were the ten lost tribes of Israel, whom Alexander the Great walled up in the Caspian mountains, the peoples who would break out at the end of the world (the Gog and Magog legend). Interestingly, he admits a doubt: these Tartars speak no Hebrew and do not know the law of Moses.
p.q: having forsaken the Mosaic law, followed after the golden calves, and whom Alexander the Macedonian endeavoured at first to shut up in the rugged mountains of the Caspians with bitumen-covered rocks. … There arises, however, a doubt whether the Tartars now coming from there be really they, for they do not use the Hebrew tongue
p.s: Matthew Paris, Chronica Majora, quoted in W. W. Rockhill's introduction (1900)

p.h: 'Om-om': the sound of bells beyond the Pesida
p.g: Tungus sent east by the Russians met strangers who, by signs, said that thunder and a great noise of people were often heard across a river they called Pesida, repeating 'om-om'. The Muscovites decided this must be the sound of bells, and Massa guessed it was the edge of Cathay. A lovely example of how rumour pushed the map of 'Tartary' eastward.
p.q: only by signs and gestures, they made out so much that thunder was often heard on the other side by their saying: om-om; and also a dreadful noise and rumour of human beings; they pointed to the river, saying: Pesida … From the words om-om, the Muscovites afterwards came to the conclusion, that it must be the sound of bells
p.s: Isaac Massa's description of Siberia, as printed by Hessel Gerritsz in 1612 (English translation by F. J. Millard in the 1878 facsimile edition)
p.pe: unknown people reported by Tungus and Tartar guides
p.c: Third-hand rumour interpreted by signs; nothing was found.

p.h: The biggest army since Adam marches on Beijing
p.g: Pinto says that while he was a captive in China, news came at midnight that 'the King of Tartary' was before Beijing with the largest army any king had gathered 'since the time of Adam': twenty-seven kings and 1,800,000 men, 600,000 of them cavalry, with 80,000 rhinoceroses carrying supplies, and the Chinese emperor had fled to Nanjing. The numbers are fantastic and the event cannot be matched to 1544.
p.q: auia noua certa de estar el Rey da Tartaria sobre a cidade do Pequim, co mais grosso poder de gente q nenhum outro Rey nũca ajuntara no mundo, desde o tempo de Adão até aquella hora, no qual se affirmaua que vinhaõ vinte & sete Reys, & q se dezia q trazião comsigo hũ conto & oitocentos mil homẽs, de q os seiscẽtos mil eraõ de cauallo
p.s: Fernão Mendes Pinto (Peregrinaçam, Lisbon 1614)

p.c: Pinto reports this as rumour in the city; the numbers are impossible, and no such siege took place in 1544 (Altan Khan's raid on Beijing was in 1550).

p.h: A hill made of the bones of a Tartar emperor and seventy kings
p.g: Passing a hill called Sariol-Kurgan, Struys records a Russian tradition: the place was once a plain where an Emperor of Tartary came with seventy kings and a countless army to seize Muscovy, and was beaten there with all his men. The mountain, the story ends, is made of their bones (the OCR of those last words is damaged). Cornelis de Bruyn heard a version of the same legend in 1703 (W251).
p.q: l'une appelée Sariol-Kurgan, si l'on en croit la tradition des Moscovites, a été faite d'une manière fort étrange. Ce lieu disent-ils, étoit autrefois une vaste plaine, où un Empereur de Tartarie étant descendu avec soixante & dix Rois & un armée innombrable pour se s'emparer de la Moscovie, il y fut battu & défait avec tous ceux qui l'accompagnoient
p.s: Jan Struys (French translation by Glanius, Amsterdam 1681)

This place, they say, was once a vast plain, where an Emperor of Tartary came down with seventy kings and a countless army to seize Muscovy, and was beaten and defeated there with all who accompanied him

p.h: Breaking into a Kalmyk tomb
p.g: Adèle describes how the party tricked their Kalmyk camel-drivers, broke into a satza (a small tomb-shrine for a high priest's ashes) through a window, 'took possession' of it with a silk handkerchief, and carried off two clay statues and some images. She knows the Kalmyks would see it as the worst sacrilege and treats it as a lark. A startling reminder of how European travellers collected 'curiosities'.
p.q: Like generous victors we contented ourselves with taking two small statues, and a few images. According to the notions of the Kalmucks, no sacrilege can compare with that of which we were now guilty. Yet no celestial fire reduced us to ashes
p.s: Adèle Hommaire de Hell (English translation, 1847)

p.h: Hunting the vegetable lamb
p.g: German authors claimed that a 'Tartarian lamb' (barometz) grew as a plant near Astrakhan, half animal and half vegetable, eating the grass around it. Bell walked many miles with local Tartars to find it and found only a dry prickly bush. The Tartars themselves, he reports, laughed at the story. A rare case of a traveller testing a legend on the spot.
p.q: In search of this wonderful plant I walked many a mile, accompanied by Tartars who inhabit these deserts; but all I could find out were some dry bushes, scattered here and there, … After further enquiry of the more sensible and experienced among the Tartars, I found they laughed at it as a ridiculous fable.
p.s: John Bell (Travels, 1763)

p.h: Skeletons sitting on horseback in the old graves
p.g: Near an old burial ground of hollow-topped stone mounds, Kazakhs told Eversmann that a hundred or more years earlier they had opened some graves to learn whether Muslims or unbelievers lay there. They said they found human skeletons sitting on horseback with silver sabres and stirrups, and women with necklaces of pearls and precious stones laid in their mouths. The Kazakhs believed the dead were Kalmyks; Eversmann classes the mounds with the so-called Chud graves.
p.q: sie erzählen, dass sie vor hundert oder mehreren Jahren nicht gewusst hatten, ob dort Muhamedaner oder Ungläubige begraben lägen, deshalb habe man beschlossen einige Gräber zu öffnen, wo man alsdann Menschengerippe zu Pferde sitzend gefunden habe, so wie auch viele Geräthe von Silber, als Säbel, Steigbügel etc. auch habe man Weiber vorgefunden, denen ihr Halsgeschmeide, bestehend aus Perlen und kostbaren Steinen, in den Mund gelegt gewesen wäre.
p.s: Eduard Eversmann, reporting Kazakh informants
p.pl: Kuvandzhur stream, Kazakh steppe north of the Aral Sea
p.pe: Kazakhs (Kirghiz) as tellers; the dead said to be Kalmyks
p.w: late October 1820 (story set a century or more earlier)
p.t: they relate that a hundred or more years ago they had not known whether Muslims or unbelievers were buried there, so it was decided to open some graves, where human skeletons were then found sitting on horseback, as well as many implements of silver, such as sabres, stirrups and so on; women too were found, whose necklaces of pearls and precious stones had been laid in their mouths.
p.c: Pure hearsay about a dig long before Eversmann's visit; he saw only the stone mounds.

p.h: A living god in Lhasa, and relics made of his excrement
p.g: Kircher says traces of the famous Prester John survive in the 'Tanchut' kingdom that the Tartars call Barantola and the locals Lassa (Lhasa). There are two kings there: one governs, the other, the Grand Lama, sits hidden in his palace and is worshipped as God the Father, so much that people believe even his dung cures all ills. The Jesuits were refused access to him and drew only his portrait.
p.q: Sunt & in hoc Regno duo Reges, prior administrationi Regni totius incumbit; alter, quem & Deum patrem sive cœlestem, aut etiam Magnum Lamam, sive sacrificulorum Pontificem vocant, in ultimis Palatii sui recessibus Numinis instar residens, ab omnibus divini cultus recipit cerimonias; tantoque eum in honore habent, ut vel ipsius sordes & excrementa ad omnes infirmitatum adversitates plurimum conducere stultè sibi persuadeant
p.s: Athanasius Kircher, S.J. (China illustrata, Amsterdam 1667), from the oral report and drawings of Johann Grueber and Albert Dorville

p.c: Hostile missionary framing; the Prester John link is Kircher's own speculation, and the excrement relics are hearsay the Jesuits did not see.

p.g: In his account of Mongol campaigns Carpini passes on marvels: far north, beyond the Samoyeds who live by hunting and wear only skins, the Tartars met at the Ocean monsters shaped like men but with ox feet and dogs' faces, who spoke a few words and then barked. On the facing page are the Parossites, with tiny mouths, who live only on the steam of boiled meat.

p.h: The Kazakh chief who ordered prayers in a jar
p.g: The Kirghiz told Wood joke stories about their Kazakh neighbours as simple folk. In one, a Kazakh chief sent to Kokand to buy Muslim prayers for his horde and was given a sealed jar of bees, to be opened by the fire in a closed tent with all the elders undressed. Wood repeats it as a comic tale, not as fact.
p.q: A jar carefully covered, containing a swarm of bees, was delivered to the dull Kazak, with instructions to his chief not to open it till all the head men of the horde were assembled. … The chief himself, literally stung to madness, swore that never again should a Mussulman's prayer issue from a Kazak kirgah.
p.s: Kirghiz storytellers, as retold by John Wood
p.pe: Kazakhs, as described by Kirghiz storytellers
p.c: A folk joke told by one people about another.

p.h: A Russian envoy guesses that ancient Russians lay under the mounds
p.g: Continuing the argument about the robbed mounds, Unkovsky told Darzha that in pagan times, over seven hundred years earlier, Russians had buried their dead with war-gear under great earth mounds, so perhaps some of 'our peoples' had once lived here. He blamed the digging on Kalmyks, Ostyaks or Kazakhs, and said Russian law punished grave-robbers with death. Darzha, doubtful, replied that his people had only had writing for a hundred years and could not know. A striking early example of a claim about who once lived on the steppe, made on the spot and without evidence.
p.q: У насъ погребаются люди съ богатствомъ, а паче что въ древнія времена еще до христіанского закона, лѣтъ слишкомъ за семь сотъ погребалися со всѣмъ военнымъ уборствомъ, и насыпали на нихъ великіе бугры земли, и можетъ быть, что въ древнія времена нѣкоторые изъ нашихъ народовъ въ сихъ мѣстахъ жили … сказалъ, что у насъ де только сто лѣтъ какъ грамота началась
p.s: Ivan Unkovsky, recording his own words and the reply of the Dzungar envoy Darzha (ed. N. I. Veselovsky, 1887)
p.pl: Irtysh steppe between Semey (Semipalatinsk) and Yamyshevo
p.t: Among us people are buried with their wealth, and especially in ancient times, before the Christian law, more than seven hundred years ago, they were buried with all their war-gear and great mounds of earth were heaped over them; and it may be that in ancient times some of our peoples lived in these places … [Darzha] said that among them writing began only a hundred years ago.
p.c: Unkovsky offers this as a guess in a diplomatic sparring match, not as knowledge; he himself calls it 'perhaps'.
