p.h: A poor old blacksmith and the white knight
p.g: Hayton's origin legend of Genghis Khan: a poor old blacksmith named Canguis saw in a dream a white knight on a white horse, who told him that God willed him to rule the seven Tartar nations called Mogols and free them from servitude. The chiefs laughed at him until they saw the same knight the next night. A second vision later sends him west over the mountain.
p.q: un veillart, povre home fevre, qui avoit non Canguis, vit en songe un avision; car il vit un chevalier armez sur un cheval blanc qui l'apela par son non, et luy dit: « Canguis, la volenté de l'inmortel Deu est tel que tu doies estre governeor e seignor sur les VII nacions des Tartars qui sunt dites Mogols
p.s: Hayton of Corycus, La Flor des estoires de la terre d'Orient (French text, 1307), ed. Ch. Kohler (1906)
p.t: an old man, a poor smith, named Canguis, saw a vision in a dream: he saw an armed knight on a white horse who called him by his name and said: 'Canguis, the will of the immortal God is that you should be governor and lord over the seven nations of the Tartars, which are called Mogols'
p.c: A legend; the 'smith' idea echoes Genghis's personal name Temujin, which was linked with 'smith' in later tellings. Hayton says this part comes from the Tartars' own histories.
p.tg: genghis khan vision white knight blacksmith legend

p.h: The vegetable lamb of the Volga
p.g: Herberstein's most famous marvel: a Russian informant said his father, on an embassy to the Tartar king, saw a seed that grew into a lamb-like plant called 'boranetz' (little lamb) with wool, blood and hoofs, which grazed until the grass around it ran out. Herberstein admits it sounds incredible but repeats it because trustworthy people vouched for the wool. Editor Major adds that it was a fern (Polypodium baromez) trimmed to look like a lamb.
p.q: he had seen in the island a certain seed, somewhat larger and rounder, but not unlike the seed of a melon, from which, when planted, grew up something very like a lamb, of the height of five palms, and that it was called in their language " boranetz", which signifies a lambkin
p.s: Sigismund von Herberstein, reporting Dimitry Danielovich (translated by R. H. Major, 1851-52)
p.pl: Lower Volga (lands of the Savolha khans)
p.c: Thirdhand (informant's father); Herberstein calls it 'almost incredible'.

p.h: The Khazar king's tomb under a river, its builders beheaded
p.g: The Khazar excerpt says that when the supreme king died, a great building with twenty rooms was raised over a river, with a grave dug in every room, so that no one would know which held the king. The men who buried him were then beheaded. The tomb was called 'paradise'. A page later (n30) it adds that a king was killed if he reigned a day beyond forty years.
p.q: Regi supremo mortuo magnum exstruatur palatium in viginti divisum conclavia, inque singulis sepulchrum fodiatur… Sepulto Rege, colla eorum, qui eum composuere, amputantur, ne quis sciat, in quonam eorum conclavium ejus sepulchrum sit.
p.s: Ibn Fadlan as quoted by Yaqut (Latin translation by C. M. Frähn, De Chasaris, 1822)
p.t: When the supreme king dies, a great palace divided into twenty rooms is built, and a grave is dug in each one… Once the king is buried, the necks of those who buried him are cut, so that no one may know in which of the rooms his grave lies.
p.c: Hearsay about a court the author had not seen.
p.tg: khazars royal tomb secrecy sacral kingship

p.h: Twenty thousand killed on the road to a khan's grave
p.g: Polo says all the Great Khans were carried, however far away they died, to a mountain called Altay for burial, and the funeral escort killed everyone they met on the road to serve the dead ruler in the next world, along with his best horses. He claims more than 20,000 people died this way on Möngke's funeral journey. Yule notes Rashid al-Din reports the same custom for Chinggis.
p.q: When they are carrying the body of any Emperor to be buried with the others, the convoy that goes with the body doth put to the sword all whom they fall in with on the road, saying : "Go and wait upon your Lord in the other world !" … when Mongou Kaan died, more than 20,000 persons, who chanced to meet the body on its way, were slain
p.s: Marco Polo (translated by Henry Yule, 1871)
p.pl: Altai mountains (burial ground of the khans)
p.c: Möngke died in 1259, years before Polo arrived; the figure is hearsay and likely exaggerated.
p.tg: burial funeral human sacrifice altai atrocity rumour

p.h: A Mongol official's belief about Genghis Khan's houses
p.g: A Mongol officer (the zakiroktchi) told the Russians he was sure several European kings descended from Genghis Khan, since Genghis had reigned in Russia, and that ruins of Genghis Khan's houses still stood in Mongolia and probably in Russia too. Timkovsky dismisses the royal descent as absurd but records the belief. It is an early example of a local legend crediting ruins to Genghis Khan.
p.q: The zakiroktchi was persuaded that several sovereigns of Europe must be descendants of Gingis Khan, … because he had reigned in Russia, and other foreign countries; a conjecture of which it seems unnecessary to shew the absurdity. He informed us that there still existed in Mongolia ruins of houses that belonged to Gingis Khan, and he supposed there must be some in Russia.
p.s: George Timkowski (English translation, 1827)
p.pl: Mongolia (on the road south of Urga)
p.c: Hearsay from a Mongol official; Timkovsky himself rejects part of it.

p.h: The khan who wanted no gold: the Khiva massacre
p.g: Bruce tells how Prince Alexander Bekovich, sent to find gold on the Amu Darya, was lured into quartering his men among the Uzbeks. The khan assured him he had no use for gold or silver, since his people owned only herds and tents and had no castles or towns to lose. That night the troops were massacred and Bekovich cut to pieces. The story reached Peter through a surviving captive officer.
p.q: for his own part, he neither valued gold nor silver, as it was of no use in their country, for they lived without that, or even bread, consequently had no use for either ; their whole riches consisting in herds of cattle, which, with their tents, they could remove at pleasure ; and, consequently, could not fear having either castles, towns, or villages, rifled or taken from them
p.s: Peter Henry Bruce, reporting the khan's words via a surviving officer (published 1782)
p.c: Hearsay and dramatised; the khanate of Khiva in fact had walled towns, so the khan's speech (if spoken) was a ruse.

p.h: Five doors in the cliff and a hidden king
p.g: Along the dry old bed of the Amu Darya, Muraviev passed five neat openings cut in a cliff, called Besh Dishik. The Turkmens said they led to caverns where a king with his family and treasure had lived since ancient times, and that intruders were strangled by an unseen hand. When one man doubted, another pointed to the cliff's echo as proof.
p.q: The nomadic Turcomans of the surrounding country are all assured that these apertures are the approaches to vast caverns in which from time immemorial there has dwelt a King with a numerous family, countless treasure, and beauteous daughters, but that once when some inquisitive persons tried to intrude into the caverns, they were immediately seized by an unseen hand and strangled.
p.s: Nikolai Muraviev (translated by W. S. A. Lockhart, 1871)
p.c: A local legend; Muraviev tried to climb up but could not reach the openings.

p.h: Miracles at the enemy's grave
p.g: After Yermak drowned in the Irtysh, his body was first abused on Kuchum's orders, but then, Coxe says, the Tatars came to revere him: they buried him with pagan rites, and stories spread that touching his body cured all illness and that a flame hovered over his tomb. A footnote adds that a Kalmyk prince, Allai, was said to have been cured by drinking earth from the grave.
p.q: Many miraculous stories were soon spread abroad, and met with implicit belief. The touch of his body was supposed to have been an instantaneous cure for all disorders; and even his clothes and arms were said to be endowed with the same efficacy. A flame of fire was represented as sometimes hovering about his tomb
p.s: William Coxe (compiling Müller's Siberian history)
p.pe: Siberian Tatars; later a Kalmyk prince
p.c: Legend preserved in Russian Siberian chronicles; Coxe calls these 'idle fables'.

p.h: Hunting the vegetable lamb around Kazan
p.g: Chappe searched everywhere around Kazan for the famous Borametz, the 'vegetable lamb' described in Abbe Lambert's natural history: a plant shaped like a lamb, with fleece, a little blood and flesh, that grazed the grass around it and died when the grass dried. He could not find it, nobody in Kazan knew it, and he calls it a ridiculous fable.
p.q: Je cherchai par-tout dans les environs de Cazan la fameuse plante nommée Borametz, dont parle M. l'Abbé Lambert dans son Histoire Civile & Naturelle. … cette plante ressemble à un agneau, elle en a toutes les parties avec une toison délicate, dont les femmes se servent pour couvrir leur tête. … Malgré mes soins je ne pus jamais me procurer cette plante inconnue à Cazan.
p.s: Jean Chappe d'Auteroche, summarising the Abbe Claude-Francois Lambert
p.t: I searched everywhere around Kazan for the famous plant called Borametz, of which the Abbe Lambert speaks in his Civil and Natural History. … this plant resembles a lamb; it has all its parts, with a delicate fleece which women use to cover their heads. … Despite all my efforts I could never obtain this plant, which is unknown at Kazan.
p.c: Chappe tested the legend and rejected it. He adds that a plant shown under that name at the King's Garden in Paris, which some authors class among the mosses, has nothing to do with the fable.

p.h: Mongolia: land of the race of Gog and Magog
p.g: Sketching the borders of the Mongol lands from Lake Khövsgöl to the Argun, Ides says that this is what 'hath been formerly said' to be the realm of the race of Gog and Magog, the wild nations of the Bible and the Alexander legends. He then gives an accurate current picture: three ruling brothers, the chief being the Khutughtu, the Buddhist high priest, who had placed themselves under the Chinese emperor after suffering from the Kalmyk (Dzungar) ruler in 1688 and 1689.
p.q: is the circumference and boundary of the whole Mongalian Territories, or as hath been formerly said of the Jurisdiction of the Race of Gog and Magog, which is governed by three Regents, the chief of which is the Kuttugt, who is also the High Priest of the Nation.
p.s: Evert Ysbrants Ides (English translation, 1706)
p.c: Ides repeats the old Gog and Magog label as something said by earlier writers, not as his own claim.
p.tg: gog and magog mongols khutughtu legend

p.h: The khan who died to music, poisoned by his doctor
p.g: De Tott tells how Krim Giray, suffering 'hypochondriac' fits, took a draught from the Greek physician Siropolo despite de Tott's warnings. The khan sent for his friend, said farewell, and had six musicians play as he went to sleep; he died within the hour. The doctor left freely, and de Tott says embalming showed clear signs of poison.
p.q: Prince breathed his last to the sound of music… Siropolo obtained, without difficulty, a passport, and the necessary order for post-horses, to return quietly to Wallachia. The symptoms of poison appeared very manifest, however, on embalming the body; but the present interest of that Court, stifled every idea of vengeance, and of the punishment of the offender.
p.s: Baron de Tott (English translation, 1785)
p.c: De Tott was present at the death, but the poisoning is his suspicion and a report from the embalming; no trial followed.

p.h: The lost ten tribes, shut in the Caspian mountains by Alexander
p.g: Matthew reports the belief that the Tartars were descendants of the ten tribes of Israel who abandoned the Law for golden calves, and whom Alexander the Great tried to wall up in the Caspian mountains with stones cemented with bitumen; when the work proved too great, God made the mountain peaks close together. On the next page he admits a problem: these Tartars do not speak Hebrew or know the Law of Moses, which he explains as divine punishment.
p.q: Creduntur isti Tartari, quorum memoria est detestabilis, fuisse de decem tribubus, qui abierunt, relicta lege Mosaica, post vitulos aureos; quos etiam Alexander Macedo primo conatus est includere in praeruptis montibus Caspiorum molaribus bituminatis. Quod opus cum videret humanos labores excedere, invocavit auxilium Dei Israel; et coierunt cacumina montium adinvicem
p.s: Matthew Paris, Chronica majora, ed. H. R. Luard (vol. 4, 1877), drawing on Peter Comestor's Historia scholastica
p.pe: Tartars as imagined by Matthew Paris
p.t: These Tartars, whose memory is detestable, are believed to have come from the ten tribes who went away, abandoning the Law of Moses, after the golden calves; whom Alexander of Macedon first tried to shut up in the steep Caspian mountains with millstones set in bitumen. When he saw that the work was beyond human labour, he called on the help of the God of Israel; and the peaks of the mountains came together
p.c: A medieval legend (Alexander's gates and the enclosed nations, linked to Gog and Magog), taken from Peter Comestor; Matthew himself notes the difficulty that the Tartars are not Hebrew speakers.
p.tg: ten tribes alexander gog and magog caspian gates legend

p.h: Fair Manchus with blue eyes and bushy beards
p.g: Barrow noticed some Manchu men and women who were very fair, with blue eyes, straight or aquiline noses, brown hair and big beards, 'more the appearance of Greeks than of Tartars'. He guesses at Greek ancestry from Sogdiana, notes that the Qianlong Emperor boasted of descent from Genghis Khan, and stresses these were exceptions.
p.q: The Man-tchoo Tartars would appear to be composed of a mixed race: among these we observed several, both men and women, that were extremely fair and of florid complexions: some had light blue eyes, straight or aquiline noses, brown hair, immense bushy beards, and had much more the appearance of Greeks than of Tartars.
p.s: John Barrow
p.c: Barrow himself calls these exceptions; the Greek-descent explanation is pure guesswork.

p.h: Shambhala placed in 'Great Tartary' on the maps
p.g: Joao Cabral, writing in 1628 after travelling in central Tibet (U-Tsang), says the kingdom is bounded on the north by the Tartars, with whom the king sometimes fights, and that many Tartars come there who say their religion is the same. He then decides that the famous kingdom of 'Xembala', which his companion Cacella had hoped was Cathay, is really the 'Great Tartary' of European maps. Xembala is the European spelling of Shambhala, the hidden kingdom of Tibetan Buddhist tradition, so here a legendary land is being matched to a map label.
p.q: Pollo norte confina com os Tartaros com os quaes este Rei as vezes briga, e aqui vem muitos os quaes dizem que a sua Lei he a mesma. … Xembala que a meu ver não he o Catayo, mas aquella que nos Mapas chamão gram Tartarea fica mais desviada para o Norte.
p.s: Joao Cabral, S.J., Portuguese letter from Hugli, 17 June 1628, printed in Wessels's Appendix III
p.t: On the north it borders on the Tartars, with whom this king sometimes quarrels, and many of them come here who say that their religion is the same. … Xembala, which in my opinion is not Cathay but that which on the maps they call Great Tartary, lies further off to the north.
p.c: The identification of Xembala with Shambhala is a modern one; Cabral himself treats it as a real kingdom he has only heard of. The 'same religion' remark refers to Mongol Buddhists.
p.tg: shambhala xembala great tartary maps buddhism

p.h: A bird cries 'Chinggis!' and a jade seal appears
p.g: The chronicle explains Chinggis Khan's title with a marvel: for three mornings a never-before-seen bird with rainbow feathers sat on a stone in front of his palace and called 'chinggis, chinggis', so his officials gave him the name. Then the stone split open by itself, revealing the old imperial jade seal. The author adds that the name is mispronounced in Tibetan as 'Jingir'.
p.q: rief lange mit lieblicher Stimme ‘c'ihgis, chhgis’. Die Beamten fassten dies als ein wunderbares Zeichen und glückliches Omen auf und gaben daher dem Könige den Namen Pogta C'ingis
p.s: Jigme Namkha (translated from the Tibetan into German by Georg Huth, 1896)
p.t: ...[the bird] called for a long time in a lovely voice 'chinggis, chinggis'. The officials took this as a wonderful sign and a lucky omen, and therefore gave the king the name Bogda Chinggis.
p.c: A legend taken from Mongolian chronicles such as Sagang Sechen.
p.tg: chinggis omen bird jade seal legend

p.h: The myth that Hungarians came from Madzhar
p.g: Klaproth traces a legend: in 1728 Gerber saw 'handsome stone houses' at Madzhar and guessed from the name that the Hungarians (Magyars) came from there, a notion copied onto maps. Klaproth calls it absurd: the name is Tatar for stone buildings, and the ruins are Golden Horde.
p.q: It is yet called Madshar, an appellation which is given by the Poles and Turks to the Hungarians, and by which the latter commonly distinguish themselves. It is probable that the founders of the kingdom of Hungary were originally from this country. Thus we see that Gerber was the first who broached the absurd opinion that the Hungarians derived their origin from Madshar
p.s: Johann Gustav Gerber (1728), quoted by Klaproth, followed by Klaproth's comment (English translation, 1814)
p.c: A name-based origin legend that Klaproth rejects.

p.h: The Baraba steppe, 'this earthly Tartarus'
p.g: Holman crossed the marshy Baraba steppe in the rain, having been told of poisonous lakes, fevers, swarms of stinging flies and a disfiguring local disease. He calls it 'this earthly Tartarus', playing on the old pun between Tartary and Tartarus, the Greek underworld. On the next page he describes it as fit only for wild animals, reptiles 'and a few sickly Tartars', and compares it to the land of the legendary poison tree, the Upas.
p.q: The above, however, is one of the minor evils of this earthly Tartarus; the insalubrious quality of its atmosphere, loaded with malaria, or miasmatic impregnation, is not only abundantly productive of typhus and intermittent fevers, but gives rise to a disease peculiar to this horrid Steppe.
p.s: James Holman (1825)
p.pe: 'A few sickly Tartars' of the Baraba steppe
p.c: Much of this is what Holman was told in advance; he admits his imagination was 'excited by the accounts it had previously imbibed'.

p.h: Prester John's son cut to pieces, his daughter wed to Chinggis
p.g: Sanudo tells how the Tartars, once tributaries of 'David, son of Prester John, king of India', rose against him under Chinggis. Their best weapons were clubs with bows and arrows; most fought on foot, some rode oxen, a few rode asses and colts. David was cut limb from limb with all his family except one daughter, whom Chinggis took as wife. A blend of the Prester John legend with the real defeat of the Kereit ruler Toghrul.
p.q: Potiora eorum arma, fuere claua cum arcubus, & sagittis: pedites in maxima parte erant; pars minor in bobus sedebat; minima asinis & iumentis & pullis equorum. Rex itaque Dauid eorum aduentum audiens … & cum tota familia, exceptâ vnicâ eius filiâ, membratim truncatur: quam quidem filiam, Cyngis Chaam vxorem accepit.
p.s: Marino Sanudo Torsello (Liber secretorum fidelium crucis, c. 1321; ed. Bongars, Hanau 1611)
p.pe: Mongols under Chinggis Khan; 'David, son of Prester John'
p.t: Their best weapons were clubs, with bows and arrows: for the most part they were on foot; a smaller part sat on oxen; the smallest on asses and beasts of burden and colts. So King David, hearing of their coming ... was cut limb from limb with his whole family except his only daughter: which daughter Chinggis Khan took as his wife.
p.c: A legend repeated from older crusade-era books; the Mongols were famously mounted archers, not ox-riding foot soldiers.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image; long s normalized.

p.h: The poet who carried his own head
p.g: Local legend held that the Sufi poet Attar was captured when the Mongols sacked Nishapur and later beheaded by his owner. His headless body then picked up its head, ran a mile to the site of his tomb and wrote its own epitaph in blood. The tomb's guardians, Fraser adds, told of villagers who stole lead from it and died.
p.q: he drew his sword, and smote off the sheikh’s head ; but no sooner had it rolled to the ground than the body taking it up, ran with it a full mile, to the spot where the tomb now is, and with its own finger for a pen, and its blood for ink, wrote upon a stone the epitaph which has since been engraved upon the tomb.
p.s: Local tradition, as retold by James Baillie Fraser
p.pe: Sheikh Farid al-Din Attar, captured when the Tartars (Mongols) took Nishapur
p.c: A saint's legend, reported as such.
p.tg: attar legend miracle tomb mongol conquest

p.h: The two-headed serpent of Kazan
p.g: Before the town, 'many say', the site was a serpents' nest ruled by a huge two-headed serpent: one head a snake's, which ate people, cattle and beasts, the other an ox's, which ate grass. The khan's sorcerer drew a line around all the snakes, heaped hay, reeds and wood on them with sulphur and pitch and burned them, and the stench killed many of the army's horses and camels. Then the khan built Kazan there. The author reports it as hearsay.
p.q: живяше ту вгнездився змій великъ, страшенъ, о двою главу, едину имея змиеву, а другую главу волову; единою пожираше человѣки и скоты и звѣри, а другою главою траву ядяше; а иныя змія около его лежаша, живяху съ нимъ, всяцеми образы.
p.s: Anonymous author of the History of the Kazan Tsardom, PSRL vol. 19 (1903), reporting what 'many say'
p.t: there lived, having made its nest, a great and terrible serpent with two heads, one a serpent's head and the other an ox's head; with one it devoured people and cattle and beasts, and with the other head it ate grass; and other serpents of every kind lay around it and lived with it.
p.c: A founding legend (related to the Zilant dragon of Kazan's later coat of arms); the author marks it as hearsay.
p.tg: serpent dragon sorcerer founding legend zilant

p.h: The Assassins' paradise
p.g: Describing the Ismaili state the Mongols destroyed in 1256, Chang De repeats the story that its soldiers were all assassins, trained by being drugged, shown music and women in a hidden chamber, and told they would enjoy such bliss after death. It is the Chinese version of the 'Old Man of the Mountain' legend that Marco Polo tells, and it is hearsay.
p.q: 其國兵皆刺客俗見男子勇壯者以利誘之令手刄父兄然後充兵醉酒扶入窟室娱以音樂羙女縱其慾數日復置故處既醒問其所見教之能爲刺客死則享福如此
p.s: Liu Yu, Record of an Embassy to the West, from Chang De's report (Qiujian ji juan 94 = Yutang jiahua juan 2; Sibu congkan text, Kanseki Repository transcription)
p.t: The soldiers of that country are all assassins. Their custom is that when they see a brave, strong man, they lure him with gain and make him kill his own father or elder brother with his own hand; then he is enrolled as a soldier. They make him drunk, carry him into a cave chamber and entertain him with music and beautiful women, indulging his desires for several days, then put him back where he was. When he wakes, they ask what he saw and teach him that if he can become an assassin, at death he will enjoy bliss like that.
p.c: A hostile legend about the Ismailis, told by their conquerors; not an eyewitness account.

p.h: The Tsar feeding the khan's horse from his cap
p.g: Fletcher says the Crimean khan claimed Moscow itself as his right, and repeats a Russian story that the Russian ruler once had to stand on foot and feed the khan's horse with oats from his own cap as yearly homage. On the next page he says this homage was later turned into a tribute of furs.
p.q: that tell of a certeine homage that was done by the Russe emperour every yeare to the Great Chrim or Cham, the Russe emperour standing on foot and feeding the Chrims horse (himselfe sitting on his back) with oates out of his owne cap, in stead of a boule or maunger
p.s: Giles Fletcher (1591; ed. E. A. Bond, 1856)
p.c: A story Fletcher gives 'by the report of the Russes themselves'. Margin notes break the OCR of this passage and have been removed; check the page image.

p.h: A being of light enters through the tent's roof opening
p.g: The widowed princess Alancu refused to remarry. One morning, she said, a shining orange-coloured man came down through the opening at the top of her chamber (in a felt tent, the smoke-hole), lay with her and vanished. In Mongol tradition the sons born after this were the ancestors of Chinggis Khan. The English margin calls it a 'Fable of an Incubus'.
p.q: having slept all Night long, she saw something as she awak'd in the Morning, as bright as the Sun, fall into her Chamber thro' the Opening a-top, and approach her in the Form of a Man, of an Orange Colour, with Eyes of a singular Beauty
p.s: Abu'l Ghazi Bahadur Khan (English translation, 1730)
p.pe: Alancu (Alan Qo'a), ancestress of Chinggis Khan
p.c: The Alan Qo'a legend, known from the Secret History of the Mongols; a sacred origin myth, not history.

p.h: A 13th-century poem calls the Tartars cannibals
p.g: In his notes d'Avezac prints lines, copied by Thomas Wright from a Cotton manuscript, of John of Garland's poem On the Triumphs of the Church. It paints the Tartars as Satan's household and the Church's plague who eat human flesh: no lion eats a lion and no wolf tears a wolf, but these men roast human limbs on spits. D'Avezac traces the poet's 'reliable' information to atrocity letters from priests in central Europe.
p.q: Gens est sæva nimis, Sathanæque domestica, pestis Ecclesiæ, fidei dissona, cædis amans. … Esuriens hominem corrodit homo; leo nullus Carne leonina viscera laxa replet; Non lupus ungue lupum lacerat; gens ista colurnis In veribus vertit membra veruta foco.
p.s: John of Garland (De triumphis Ecclesiae, 13th century), quoted by Thomas Wright in Armand d'Avezac's notes
p.t: A people exceedingly savage, of Satan's household, a plague to the Church, at odds with the faith, in love with slaughter. … Hungry, man gnaws man; no lion fills its slack belly with lion's flesh; no wolf tears a wolf with its claw; this people turns limbs spitted on hazel skewers over the fire.
p.c: War propaganda built on rumour; Garland never met a Mongol. The poem's Latin is quoted from a single manuscript copy and the OCR is rough.
p.tg: cannibalism atrocity rumour propaganda invasion of europe

p.h: Venetian treasure-hunters dig a kurgan
p.g: Tipped off by a story that a Tatar woman in Cairo had told of Alan treasure, Barbaro and six partners hired 120 men and dug into a great mound. Instead of gold they found layers of ash, millet husks and fish scales, then stone vessels, glass-covered brick beads and part of a silver ewer. The dig was so big that locals renamed the mound 'the cave of the Franks'.
p.q: we founde in the botome certein vessels of stone, some of them with asshes, some with coles, some emptie and some full of fishe back bones. We founde also v or vi beadestones as bigge as oranges made of bricke and covered with glasse … We founde also halfe the handle of a little ewer of sylver, made with an adders hedde on the toppe.
p.s: Giosafat Barbaro (Tudor translation by William Thomas, c. 1550)
p.c: The treasure story came at third hand; Barbaro repeats the local explanation that the Alan lord Indiabu faked a grave to hide his wealth from the Tartar emperor.

p.h: An exiled Englishman as the Tartars' envoy
p.g: In a letter Matthew copied under 1243, a cleric named Ivo of Narbonne says that among eight Tartars captured in Austria was an Englishman, banished from England for some crimes, who had twice come to the king of Hungary as envoy and interpreter for the Tartar king, threatening disaster unless Hungary submitted. The letter goes on (next page) to give his account of how he drifted east, learned many languages, and was recruited by the Tartars because they needed interpreters.
p.q: Ex ipsis vero fugientibus princeps Dalmatiae cepit octo, quorum dux Austriae novit unum, Anglicum natione, sed propter quaedam maleficia de regno Angliae perpetua banniatione proscriptum. Hic ex parte regis nequissimi Tattarorum, bis venerat ad regem Hungariae nuntius et interpres, mala, quae postmodum contigerunt, satis manifeste praemuniendo comminatus est, nisi se et regnum suum Tattareae dederet servituti.
p.s: Letter of Ivo of Narbonne to the archbishop of Bordeaux, copied by Matthew Paris under 1243 (Luard, vol. 4)
p.pe: Mongol army and its English interpreter
p.t: Of those fleeing, the prince of Dalmatia captured eight, one of whom the duke of Austria recognised: an Englishman by nation, but banished from the kingdom of England for ever for certain crimes. He, on behalf of the most wicked king of the Tattars, had twice come to the king of Hungary as envoy and interpreter, and had openly threatened the evils that afterwards happened, unless he surrendered himself and his kingdom to Tattar servitude.
p.c: Ivo's letter is a contested text and its author admits a shady past; the Englishman's story cannot be checked. The same letter includes lurid cannibalism stories.

p.h: A Tartar emperor buried under his soldiers' helmets of sand
p.g: Near Samara the Russians showed Olearius a sand hill called Sariol Kurgan. They said a Tartar emperor named Momaon, who meant to invade Muscovy with seven kings, died there, and his soldiers heaped sand over him with their helmets and shields until the grave became a hill. A tale about a burial mound, told to him by Russians.
p.q: The Muscovites call it Sariol Kurgan, and affirm, that a certain Tartarian Emperour, named Momaon, who had a design to enter Muscovy, together with seven Kings of the same Nation, dy'd in that place, and that his Soldiers, instead of burying him, fill'd their Head-pieces and Bucklers with Sand, and so cover'd the body that it became a Mountain.
p.s: Adam Olearius (English translation by John Davies, 1669)
p.c: Russian folk explanation of a natural or man-made hill; 'Momaon' may be a memory of Mamai, the Horde commander of the 1370s, but the source does not say so.

p.h: A magic head on a Tartar banner, breathing smoke at the Poles
p.g: In the history of the Polish kings Guagnini tells how the Poles were winning against the Tartars until a Tartar standard-bearer came forward with a banner marked with a Greek X and, on top of the lance, a terrible head made by magic art that breathed foul smoke over the Poles. Bewitched, they lost their strength and were cut down 'like grain by hail', and the Tartars cut off every dead man's right ear and filled nine great sacks.
p.q: sed quidam Vexillifer Tartarorum, cum vexillo, in quo erat scripta litera Graeca tali modo, X, processit: superius vero in cuspide hastae erat caput quoddam terribile infixum, arte magica confectum, ore fumum vaporemque sordidum in Polonos evomens: quo velut peste quadam infecti, & incantationum vi fascinati, vires amiserunt.
p.s: Alessandro Guagnini, Sarmatiae Europeae descriptio (Speyer, 1581), lives of the Polish kings, following Polish chroniclers
p.t: but a certain standard-bearer of the Tartars came forward with a banner on which was written a Greek letter in this manner, X; and above, on the point of the lance, was fixed a terrible head, made by magic art, spewing smoke and foul vapour from its mouth over the Poles, by which, as if infected with a plague and bewitched by the force of spells, they lost their strength.
p.c: A battle legend from Polish chronicles (Dlugosz tells it of Legnica); Guagnini dates the reign from 1243 and does not name the battle. Some historians suspect a smoke or incendiary device behind the tale.

p.h: The mammoth that hides under the water
p.g: Bell saw many 'mammon's horns' (mammoth tusks) in Siberian towns and brought one home to Hans Sloane. He thought they were elephant teeth and could not explain how they got so far north. His Tartar informants, however, said the mammoth was a living beast the size of an elephant that appears at dawn by lakes and dives into the water when seen, and tunnels under marshes with its horns.
p.q: The Tartars tell many fables of its having been seen alive. But to me it appears that this horn is the tooth of a large elephant. … I have been told by Tartars … that they have seen this creature, called mammon, at the dawn of day, near lakes and rivers; but, that on discovering them, the mammon immediately tumbles into the water,
p.s: John Bell (Travels, 1763)
p.pe: Tartars of the Baraba; Siberian peoples

p.h: A golden 'Russian god' in a cup
p.g: Yermak's men besieged Prince Demyan's big hill-town on the lower Irtysh, held by 2000 Tatars, Voguls and Ostyaks. A Chuvash who had been Kuchum's captive told them the defenders prayed to 'a Russian god, cast in gold, sitting in a cup'; they poured water in the cup and drank it, called it Christ, and said it had come from Vladimir's baptism of Rus. Sent to steal it, he reported that it stood on a table surrounded by burning fat and sulphur fumes. The Cossacks never found it.
p.q: Одинъ же въ нихъ Чювашенинъ былъ у Кучюма, руского полону, сказалъ: молятся де они рускому богу и тотъ де руской богъ литой золотой, въ чашѣ сѣдитъ, и въ ту де чашу наливши воды пьютъ, и зовутъ его Христомъ, а сказываютъ де привезенъ отъ Владимерова крещенія
p.s: Kungur (Brief Siberian) Chronicle, Remezov tradition, 1880 edition
p.pe: Tatars, Voguls and Ostyaks of Prince Demyan's town; a Chuvash informant
p.t: One of them, a Chuvash who had been with Kuchum, a Russian captive, said: they pray, he said, to a Russian god, and that Russian god is cast of gold, sits in a cup, and they pour water into that cup and drink it, and call him Christ, and they say he was brought from Vladimir's baptism
p.c: Third-hand: a captive's report retold a century later. Such metal idols (often looted Christian or Iranian vessels) are known from Ob-Ugrian shrines.
p.tg: idol golden god shrine ostyaks demyan

p.h: The emperor: 'nearer to the dirty monkey than to man'
p.g: In his victory inscription the Qianlong emperor explains the Dzungars' revolt after his gifts by comparing them to beasts: closer to a filthy monkey than to man, and fiercer than bears and the Yu-ki. Amiot notes that he softened the monkey insult, and that the Yu-ki is a fabulous creature with a tiger's claws, a dragon's head and a fox's body.
p.q: Je savois que par la nature de leurs défauts, & de leurs vices, ils approchoient plus du sale Sapajou que de l'homme, dont ils ont cependant l'empreinte & dont ils portent l'auguste nom; mais, je l'avoue, je n'imaginois pas qu'ils pussent être plus féroces que les Ours, plus cruels & plus intraitables que les Yu-ki.
p.s: The Qianlong emperor (stone inscription), translated by Joseph-Marie Amiot
p.pe: Eleuths (Dzungars), described by the Qianlong emperor
p.t: I knew that by the nature of their faults and vices they were closer to the dirty monkey than to man, whose stamp they bear and whose august name they carry; but, I admit, I did not imagine they could be fiercer than bears, crueller and more untameable than the Yu-ki.
p.c: Imperial war propaganda, not description; Amiot says he toned down the original insult.

p.h: Russia is Gog and Magog
p.g: In a caravan leaving Bukhara, a Turkmen told Wolff that Russia would conquer the world, having built a fort in the sea near Khiva. A dervish added that the great mullahs of Samarkand said Russia was Gog and Magog, the destroying peoples of the end times.
p.q: A Turkomaun present said, "The Russians shall be the conquerors of the world. They have now built a strong castle almost in the midst of the sea, not far from Khiva. … A derveesh sitting among us made the following remark ; "The great mullahs of Samarcand assert that Russia is the Jaaj-Majooj, i. e. Gog and Magog
p.s: A Turkmen and a dervish, as reported by Joseph Wolff
p.c: A prophecy repeated in conversation, reflecting fear of Russian expansion.
p.tg: gog and magog russia prophecy dervishes

p.h: The rumour of the Lama's holy excrement
p.g: Stewart repeats a rumour, common in European books, that Tartar chiefs were given small portions of the Lama's excrement, kept it in gold boxes and mixed it into their food. On the same page he reports that Bogle 'strenuously insists' the Lama never gave such gifts, only little balls of consecrated flour, which credulous followers might then imagine to be something else.
p.q: It is even reported, that many of the Tartar chiefs receive certain presents, consisting of small portions of that, from him, which is ever regarded in all other persons as the most humiliating proof of human nature, and of being subject to its laws, and treasure it up with great reverence in gold boxes, to be mixed occasionally in their ragouts.
p.s: John Stewart (Philosophical Transactions, 1777)
p.pe: Tartar chiefs (Mongol and other Buddhist rulers)
p.c: Stewart labels it a report, and the eyewitness Bogle denied it.

p.h: Prester John is the Dalai Lama
p.g: Dividing 'Tartary' into six parts for his map, Strahlenberg makes the sixth Tibet and Tangut, 'where Dalai Lama, or Prester John, has his Residence'. The legendary Christian priest-king of the East has here become the Dalai Lama, head of the Buddhism of the Mongols and Kalmyks.
p.q: For the sixth Part, I have taken the Kingdoms of Thibet and Tanguth, where Dalai Lama, or Prester John, has his Residence, the Civil Government of which is entrusted to two Viceroys or Chans; but the Soldiers are a Sort of Kalmucks, call'd Coschuith, or Coschioth.
p.s: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (English translation, 1738)
p.tg: prester john dalai lama tibet maps

p.h: A hunting dog buried like a man, with its own little house
p.g: Brand watched the Voguls mourn a large hunting dog that had died suddenly. They lamented its virtues, buried it like a person with a pillow of wood under its head, and built a small wooden house six or seven feet high on four posts over its grave. He adds that this is said to be an age-old custom among them.
p.q: endlich bestätigten sie ihn gleich einen Menschen zur Erde, legten ihm ein darzu verfertigtes Holtz unter das Haupt, damit er sanft liegen möchte, und baueten nachmahls ein apartes Häuslein von Holtz, auff sein Grab, 6. biß 7. Fuß hoch, stehend auf vier Pfälen
p.s: Adam Brand (Neu-vermehrte Beschreibung, Lübeck 1734)
p.t: finally they laid him in the earth like a human being, put a piece of wood made for the purpose under his head so that he might lie softly, and afterwards built a separate little wooden house over his grave, six to seven feet high, standing on four posts

p.h: A goat that walked the rooftops from Balkh to Mazar
p.g: Mohan Lal records two local marvels. An old mud fort outside Balkh was said to grow taller at night (he wanted to check, but the caravan left). And the city had once been so vast that its roofs touched all the way to Mazar, so that a goat climbed onto a roof in Balkh and came down the next day in Mazar, some 20 kilometres away.
p.q: Without the city of Balk is an old mud fort, called Chihal Gazi, which, people say, in the night increases in its height. I wished to stop and verify the fact, but our caravan started at the very eve. … a goat climbed up one of the roofs in Balk, and descended next day at Mazar, whither his master followed him also.
p.s: Mohan Lal (1846 edition)
p.c: Local legends; Mohan Lal takes the goat story as proof of Balkh's former size, but did not test either tale.

p.h: A Mongol nun's prophecy of a war in heaven
p.g: Near the Great Wall Brand met Mongols or Tartars of the Dalai Lama's faith, who kept images in their houses with little pots of food and drink before them and set a white cock on the coffin at burials. Asked whom she worshipped, a Mongol nun telling her beads answered that it was the god whom 'our' God had thrust out of heaven, who would return and throw the Christians' God down.
p.q: Eine Mongalische Nonne, welche, mit einem Pater Noster in der Hand, continuirlich das Maul rührete, fragte man, wen sie anbetete, sie gab zur Antwort, den Gott, welcher von unsern Gott aus dem Himmel gestossen worden, und würde ihr Gott wieder im Himmel kommen, und wieder unsern Gott vom Himmel herunter werffen
p.s: Adam Brand (Neu-vermehrte Beschreibung, Lübeck 1734)
p.pl: Inner Mongolia (between the Nen River and the Great Wall)
p.pe: Mongols or 'Tartars' near the Great Wall
p.t: A Mongol nun, who with a rosary in her hand kept moving her lips continually, was asked whom she worshipped; she answered: the god who was thrust out of heaven by our God, and her god would come back into heaven and throw our God down from heaven again
p.c: A single conversation, probably through interpreters; the words may be garbled in translation.

p.h: Why Novgorod's crosses have no crescent
p.g: Cochrane was told that Novgorod was proud of the plain crosses on its steeples: they meant the Tartars had never entered the city. Cities re-conquered from the Tartars, he says, carry a crescent under the cross. This is a popular explanation that Russians told travellers; historians usually read the crescent at the foot of Orthodox crosses as an older Christian symbol, not a mark of Tatar rule.
p.q: The steeples of Novgorod present a monument of considerable pride in the estimation of its inhabitants. Their distinction is in the cross, at the top, standing alone, unaccompanied by the crescent, and this is an emblem intimating, that the Tartars, in all their invasions, never succeeded so far, as to enter the city.
p.s: John Dundas Cochrane (1824)
p.c: Local lore repeated as fact. Novgorod was indeed never taken by the Mongols, but the cross-and-crescent explanation is a legend.

p.h: The vegetable lamb: 'I have seen several'
p.g: On the salt steppe west of the Volga grows the 'Boranez', a fruit shaped like a lamb with feet, head and tail, covered in white down. Struys says the Tartars and Russians prize it and keep it in their houses, where he saw several, and that he had also seen one in Swammerdam's cabinet in Amsterdam. People in Astrakhan told him it grows on a stalk and dies when the grass around it is gone. This is the famous barometz legend, in real life probably a fern rhizome shaped to look like a lamb.
p.q: où croît le Boranez ou Bornitsch dont nous avons déjà parlé. Ce merveilleux fruit a la figure d'un agneau, avec les piés, la tête & la queue distinctement formés … Les Tartares & les Moscovites en font grand état, & la plupart le gardent avec soin dans leurs maisons où j'en ai vu plusieurs.
p.s: Jan Struys (French translation by Glanius, Amsterdam 1681)
p.t: where the Boranez or Bornitsch grows, of which we have already spoken. This marvellous fruit has the shape of a lamb, with the feet, head and tail distinctly formed … The Tartars and the Muscovites think highly of it, and most keep it carefully in their houses, where I have seen several.
p.c: He saw objects sold as barometz; how it grows is hearsay, and the whole idea is a legend.

p.h: Hairy wild people in Siberia
p.g: Riding with Edigü and Prince Chekre into 'Ibissibur' (this is one of the earliest uses of the name Siberia), Schiltberger heard of a mountain range that ends in a desert at the end of the earth, and of hairy wild people who eat grass. A captured wild man and woman were sent to Edigü. He also describes sled dogs as big as donkeys.
p.q: On the same mountain there are savages, who are not like other people, and they live there. They are covered all over the body with hair, except the hands and face, and run about like other wild beasts in the mountain, and also eat leaves and grass, and any thing they can find.
p.s: Johann Schiltberger (translated by J. Buchan Telfer, 1879)
p.pe: Peoples of Siberia under Edigü's campaign
p.c: The 'end of the earth' desert is what locals told him; the wild people may be his garbled view of forest peoples or a traveller's tale.
p.tg: siberia wild men marvel sled dogs edigu

p.h: A khan's descendant from Edinburgh University
p.g: In Simferopol an English gig drove into a courtyard and out stepped an old fellow-student of Alexander's from Edinburgh University: Sultan Katty Gherry Crim Gherry, of a branch of the Tatar khans of the Crimea, born in the Caucasus. On the next page Alexander adds that a missionary brought him to Britain, that he married a Miss Nelson of Edinburgh, and that he now had an imperial pension and estates on the south coast.
p.q: One day I was surprised to see an English gig drive into their court, with a mounted servant behind. A dark good-looking gentleman then alighted, and I recognised an old fellow-student at the University of Edinburgh, the Sultan Katty Gherry Crim Gherry. He was born in the Caucasus, of a branch of the Tartar Khans of the Crimea, was brought to Britain
p.s: James Edward Alexander (1830)
p.pe: Sultan Katty Gherry, of the Crimean khans' family (Giray)

p.h: A nation born of a princess and a wolf
p.g: Retelling a Chinese legend of the Uighurs, Deguignes says a Hun ruler shut his two beautiful daughters in a tower in the north so that heaven might marry them. An old wolf howled round the tower and made its den at the foot, and the younger sister, taking it for the god, went down to it. He adds that the Uighurs were said to imitate wolf howls in their songs, and that their tents stood on unusually high wheels, so the Chinese called them Kao-tche, 'high carts'.
p.q: Un vieux loup rodoit nuit & jour autour de la prison des Princesses Tartares, il observoit cette tour en faisant des heurlemens épouvantables; enfin il établit sa tanière au pied. La plus jeune persuadée que ce loup, qui examinoit depuis si long-tems la tour, ne pouvoit être que la divinité à laquelle son père l'avoit consacrée, encouragea sa sœur à descendre avec elle.
p.s: Joseph de Guignes, retelling a Chinese legend
p.t: An old wolf prowled night and day around the prison of the Tartar princesses; he watched the tower, howling frightfully, and finally made his den at its foot. The younger one, persuaded that this wolf, which had been watching the tower for so long, could only be the god to whom her father had dedicated her, urged her sister to go down with her.
p.c: Deguignes himself calls it the nation's 'fabulous origin'.
p.tg: wolf origin myth uighurs high carts

p.h: Feeding butter to a stone woman's mouth
p.g: On the Abakan steppe, crowded with ancient graves fenced with stone slabs, Pallas found carved standing stones which, like other stone images on the Yenisei steppes, were said to have been set up long before the time of the Kirgis. One, a tall bellied stone with a large open-mouthed woman's face, was called Kurtejak-tash, the 'woman stone'. Hunters heading out for sable prayed to it for luck and smeared fat or butter into its mouth.
p.q: Diese Wake ist unter den Nahmen Kurtejaktasch (Weiberstein) oder Ulu-Kurtejak (das grosse Weib) bey den heydnischen Tataren dieser Gegend bekannt, und wird sonderlich im Herbst, von den auf die Zobeljagd vorbey reisenden Heyden, fleißig um Glück angesprochen und mit etwas Fett oder Butter, welches die Anbeter in den ofnen Mund des Gesichts andächtig schmieren, gefuttert.
p.s: Peter Simon Pallas (Reise, first edition, St Petersburg 1771-1776)
p.pe: Heathen Tatars of the Abakan (Beltirs and other Khakas)
p.t: This stone is known among the heathen Tatars of this region by the name Kurtejak-tash (woman stone) or Ulu-Kurtejak (the great woman), and especially in autumn it is earnestly asked for luck by the heathens travelling past to the sable hunt, and fed with a little fat or butter, which the worshippers devoutly smear into the open mouth of the face.
p.tg: stone idols kurgans offerings khakas sable hunt

p.h: Subjects of five colours, Amazons and dog-heads
p.g: Listing the peoples conquered from Chinggis to Khubilai, the chronicle gives the 'five colours': blue Mongols, red Chinese, black Tibetans, yellow Sartagul (Central Asian Muslims) and white Solongos (Koreans). Then come four more peoples: Amazons, one other, people with an eye on the chest, and dog-headed people. Old wonder-lore sits beside a real map of the empire.
p.q: Die blauen Mongolen, über vierhunderttausend Häuser, die roten Chinesen, die schwarzen Tibeter, die gelben Sart'agwol, die weissen Solongwos … ferner vier weitere Völkerschaften: die T sug-te- Amazonen, die j/Yon-ru, die mit einem Auge auf der Brust und die mit Hundeköpfen.
p.s: Jigme Namkha (translated from the Tibetan into German by Georg Huth, 1896)
p.pe: Peoples subject to the Mongol khans
p.t: The blue Mongols, over four hundred thousand households; the red Chinese; the black Tibetans; the yellow Sartagul; the white Solongos... and four further peoples: the Tsug-te Amazons, the Yon-ru, those with one eye on the chest, and those with dogs' heads.
p.c: The marvellous peoples are traditional lore repeated by the author, not observation.
p.tg: dog-headed people amazons five colours subject peoples marvels

p.h: Elephant bones by the Volga: war elephants, not the Flood
p.g: A broken elephant tusk nearly a metre long had washed out of a river bank, and human bones and broken iron spearheads had been found nearby. Lepekhin sets aside the theories that the far north was once hot, that the Flood carried the beasts there, or that they were freaks of nature. He argues instead that Asian peoples trained elephants for war, that these animals were buried only a few hundred years ago, and that Tatar-style armies would never have bothered to saw off the tusks.
p.q: Daß aber die asiatischen Völker zum Theil Elephanten zum Gefecht und zur Schlacht abgerichtet haben, ist ja wohl, meines Erachtens, eine bekannte Sache. Und diesemnach ist meine Meynung, daß diese ausländischen Leichen nicht vor vielen tausend, sondern vor etlichen hundert Jahren nicht weit von der Wolga begraben worden sind. … Elephantenzähne abzusägen und mit fortzuschleppen, zumal wenn wir die Art bedenken, wie die Tatarn zu Felde zu ziehen pflegen.
p.s: Ivan Lepekhin (German translation, 1774)
p.t: That some of the Asiatic peoples trained elephants for fighting and battle is, in my opinion, surely a well-known fact. Accordingly my view is that these foreign corpses were buried not far from the Volga not many thousands but a few hundred years ago. … [another thing is] to saw off elephant tusks and drag them away, especially when we consider the way the Tatars are used to going to war.
p.c: He saw the tusk; the war-elephant explanation is his own guess. Such tusks are now known to be fossil mammoth ivory, and he himself mentions 'mammoth bones' from Siberia on the same page.

p.h: The mammoth: a giant beast that lives under the earth
p.g: Near Yeniseisk the envoys heard of a huge animal in the coldest north that burrowed underground and died if exposed to sun and air. Its white, ivory-like bones were dug from river mud and carved by Russians into cups and combs, and its flesh was eaten against fever. The foreign name was Ma-mien-tou-va (mamont), the Chinese called it kee-shoo (the 'hidden rat'). Staunton notes that John Bell heard the same tale and that frozen mammoth flesh had since been found.
p.q: In the very coldest parts of this northern country, a species of animal is found which burrows under the earth, and which dies if it is at all exposed at any time to the sun and air. Its bones are very white and shining, like ivory. … The Russians collect the bones of this animal, in order to make cups, saucers, combs
p.s: Tulishen (translated from the Chinese by George Thomas Staunton, 1821)
p.pe: Russians and Siberian natives (reported to the envoys)
p.c: Hearsay reported by the envoys; the belief that the animal lives underground is a folk explanation for frozen mammoth remains.

p.h: Scholars decide they are the peoples before Antichrist
p.g: After the Hungarian disaster, Thomas says, the whole world trembled. Even the emperor Frederick II was said to be thinking not of resistance but of a hiding place. Learned men searched old writings and concluded, above all from the prophecies attributed to Methodius, that these were the peoples who must come before Antichrist, and cities began fortifying themselves in case the Tartars marched on Rome.
p.q: Ipse etiam Fredericus Rom. Imperator non de resistendo, sed de latibulo dicitur cogitasse. Tunc litterati plerique viri veteres scrutantes scripturas, conjiciebant maxime ex dictis Methodii Martyris has fore illas gentes, quae praecedere debent antichristi adventum.
p.s: Thomas, archdeacon of Split, Historia Salonitana, in the first edition by Ivan Lučić (Lucius), Amsterdam 1666
p.pe: Tartars as seen by Latin scholars
p.t: Even Frederick, the Roman emperor, is said to have thought not of resisting but of a hiding place. Then many learned men, searching the old writings, conjectured, above all from the sayings of Methodius the Martyr, that these were those peoples who must come before the advent of Antichrist.
p.c: The claim about Frederick is gossip ('is said'); the Methodius prophecy is the Pseudo-Methodius apocalypse, which linked enclosed northern nations with the end of the world.

p.h: The Tartars crossed the 'impassable' torrid zone
p.g: East of Almaliq the legates reached wind-built 'mountains of sand' beyond which, Marignolli says, nobody before the Tartars believed there was habitable land. The Tartars crossed them into a vast plain that philosophers called the Torrid Zone and thought impassable; on the next page he adds that he crossed it twice himself. He is mixing a real desert crossing with the old scholarly theory of uninhabitable climate zones.
p.q: pervenimus ad Cyollos Kagon, id est, ad montes arene, quos faciunt venti, ultra quos ante Tartaros nullus putavit terram habitabilem, nec putabatur ultra aliquam terram esse. Tartari autem voluntate Dei mirabili industria transierunt, & fuerunt in campo maximo, ubi dicitur Torrida Zona, & inpertransibilis a Philosophis
p.s: Giovanni de' Marignolli (Latin text ed. Gelasius Dobner, 1768)
p.t: we came to the Cyollos Kagon, that is, to mountains of sand made by the winds, beyond which, before the Tartars, nobody thought there was habitable land, nor was it believed that any land lay beyond. But the Tartars, by God's will and with marvellous skill, crossed them and came into a vast plain, the place called the Torrid Zone, held by the philosophers to be impassable
p.c: The 'Torrid Zone' is a label from medieval theory, not a real description of a Central Asian desert.

p.h: A city buried overnight by a rain of sand and earth
p.g: East of Khotan Xuanzang heard of Ho-lo-lo-kia, a rich city that mistreated a holy man and was buried when 'it rained sand and earth' for a night. One man escaped by a tunnel. The town was now a great sand mound; kings who came to dig for its treasure were driven off by sudden winds and darkness. Beal's note points to other sand-buried towns reported by nineteenth-century travellers in the region.
p.q: The town of Ho-lo-lo-kia is now a great sand mound. The kings of the neighbouring countries and persons in power from distant spots have many times wished to excavate the mound and take away the precious things buried there; but as soon as they have arrived at the borders of the place, a furious wind has sprung up
p.s: Xuanzang and Bianji (translated by Samuel Beal, 1884)
p.c: A moral legend about punishment for disrespecting a Buddhist saint. It has nothing to do with Tartars; the region is the one 19th-century English writers called 'High Tartary'.

p.h: Stone towers, idols and Tibetan scrolls by the Caspian
p.g: In the same list the author repeats a report that General Bekovich, on his disastrous march to Khiva, found remains near the Caspian made up of four stone towers, stairs, idols and rolled-up 'Tangut' (Tibetan-script) writings. The same page also lists a ruined stone mosque on the Or and a tomb said to have been built by Khan Janibek. The Caspian report is second-hand, but it shows that ruins with idols and Tibetan writings in the steppe were already being reported in the 18th century.
p.q: Der General Bäkewitsch traf auf seinem unglücklichen Zuge nach Chiwa, nahe an der Kaspischen See Ueberbleibsel an, die in 4 steinernen Thürmen, Treppen, Götzenbildern, auch aufgerolleten tangutischen Schriften bestanden.
p.s: J. P. Falck, arranged and supplemented by J. G. Georgi (1785)
p.pl: Near the Caspian Sea (exact place not given)
p.pe: Unknown former inhabitants; report from Bekovich's Khiva expedition
p.t: General Bekovich, on his unfortunate march to Khiva, came upon remains near the Caspian Sea which consisted of 4 stone towers, stairs, idols and also rolled-up Tangut writings.
p.c: Hearsay about an expedition of 1717 that ended in massacre; no location or witness is given.

p.h: A wall against the Tartar tribes
p.g: Riding along a long raised bank near Gorgan, Fraser heard that the rich plain had once been shielded from the Tartar tribes by a mighty wall from the mountains to the sea. He dismissed it as a legend about 'fabulous kings'.
p.q: It is said that this rich tract was once separated from the desert beyond it, and protected from the incursions of the Tartar tribes by a wall of great strength, which ran from the mountains to the sea. I believe, however, this great work is attributed to some of the fabulous kings, and is probably fabulous itself.
p.s: James Baillie Fraser (footnote)
p.c: Fraser's doubt was misplaced: archaeologists have since traced a real brick barrier across this plain, the Great Wall of Gorgan, usually dated to the Sasanian period (5th to 6th century), long before any 'Tartars'.

p.h: Scholars who moved Atlantis to Spitsbergen
p.g: Pallas rejects the theory, pushed by the Augustinian friar Georgi, that Tibetan and Mongol Buddhism grew out of Nestorian Christianity or Manichaeism, calling it a heap of rubble glued together in a polemical spirit. He lumps it with other learned fantasies: the Chinese and Indians as an Egyptian colony, the Lapps as Israelites, pagan gods as biblical patriarchs, and the recent placing of Atlantis and the first seat of all learning as far north as Spitsbergen.
p.q: Mit dergleichen gelehrtem Schwall sind wohl eher die Chineser und Indianer zu einer ägyptischen Colonie, die Lappländer zu Israeliten, die Götzen des Heydenthums zu Patriarchen der Bibel gemacht, und noch neulich die Atlanten und mit ihnen, der erste Sitz aller Wissenschaften bis nach Spitzbergen verlegt worden
p.s: Peter Simon Pallas (Sammlungen historischer Nachrichten über die mongolischen Völkerschaften, part 2, 1801)
p.pe: Mongol and Tibetan Buddhists; European theorists
p.t: With such learned bombast the Chinese and Indians have before now been made into an Egyptian colony, the Lapps into Israelites, the idols of heathendom into patriarchs of the Bible, and only recently the Atlanteans, and with them the first seat of all learning, have been moved as far as Spitsbergen
p.c: Pallas does not name the Atlantis author; it fits J.-S. Bailly's northern Atlantis letters of 1779.

p.h: Melting a mountain of iron with seventy bellows
p.g: After a crushing defeat by the Tatars, the last two Mongol princes fled with their wives and herds into a valley ringed by mountains, Irgana-kon, reached only by a goat track. Four hundred years later their crowded descendants wanted out. A blacksmith noticed the mountain was thin and made of iron ore, so they piled wood and charcoal against it and melted a road through with seventy leather bellows.
p.q: a Farrier, who thought he had observ'd that the Mountain was not over thick in a certain Place, and also that it entirely consisted of Iron-Mine, propos'd to apply Bellows to it … they so effectually blew up by the help of 70 Leathern Bellows, that the Mountain at last coming to melt in this Place, left a Road large enough for the Passage of a loaded Camel
p.s: Abu'l Ghazi Bahadur Khan (English translation, 1730)
p.c: A famous Mongol origin legend (also in Rashid al-Din), not history.

p.h: Tatars who take the dam of Gog and Magog for a cobweb
p.g: As Hulagu closed on Baghdad, the last Abbasid caliph, told that the Mongol vanguard had crossed the Hamrin hills, asked how that could be. The answer, in Wassaf's ornate rhymed prose (rendered by Hammer in rhyme), paints the Tatars as a sea flood flying over peaks like eagles, for whom the legendary dam of Gog and Magog, Alexander's barrier against the peoples of the north, is no more than a cobweb. Hammer then describes how the Mongols ringed Baghdad with a hastily raised earthen rampart.
p.q: Das Heer der Tataren, die wie die Meeresfluthen einherfahren, überfliegt der Berge Gipfel wie der Adler Schaaren; da sie den Damm von Gog und Magog für Spinngeweb' ansehen, was soll auf des Hamrin's Höhen aus ihren Hufen wohl anders erstehen, als Staub, was soll aus dem Sturme, in dem sie daherfahren, wohl anders aufgehen, als Feuer und Raub
p.s: Wassaf (Persian court historian, early 14th century), translated by Hammer-Purgstall (1842)
p.pe: Hulagu's Mongol army ('the Tatars'); the caliph al-Musta'sim
p.t: The army of the Tatars, who come on like the floods of the sea, flies over the mountain tops like flocks of eagles; since they regard the dam of Gog and Magog as a cobweb, what else should rise from their hooves on the heights of Hamrin but dust, what else should come out of the storm in which they ride but fire and plunder
p.c: Literary rhetoric written decades later, not a record of what was said to the caliph.

p.h: Mammoths that burrow underground and die in the light
p.g: The Ides section reports mammoth tusks and bones thawing out of riverbanks, and a member of the embassy who found a head with half-rotten flesh. The Yakuts, Tungus and Ostyaks say the mammoth lives underground, making the earth rise and sink as it moves, and dies as soon as it sees daylight. The Russians of Siberia think it was an elephant-like beast buried by Noah's Flood.
p.q: Les Jakutes, Tungufes, & Ostiaques, prétendent qu'ils ne sortent jamais du sein de la terre, sous laquelle ils vont de côté & d'autre. Ils disent même qu'on voit souvent la terre s'élever & s'affaisser lors qu'ils sont en mouvement … Ils assurent, qu'ils meurent aussi tôt qu'ils découvrent la lumière
p.s: Evert Ysbrants Ides's route to China (1692-1695), summarized by the editors of the 1718 French edition of Le Brun and inserted in it
p.pe: Yakuts, Tungus and Ostyaks (and Siberian Russians)
p.t: The Yakuts, Tungus and Ostyaks claim that they never come out of the bosom of the earth, under which they go this way and that. They even say that one often sees the earth rise and sink when they are moving … They assure us that they die as soon as they see the light
p.c: Native belief and Russian flood theory reported by Ides; the bones and tusks themselves were real finds.

p.h: A plain without cities where the sun rises before a chop is cooked
p.g: Far to the north-west lies 'K'o-fu-ch'a', which Bretschneider identifies with the Kipchak steppe north of the Caspian. Yelü Chucai heard that it was endless plain, its people had no cities or towns, bred cattle and horses and made a drink from honey, and that summer nights were so short the sun rose again before a mutton chop could be cooked. Bretschneider shows the short-night detail was copied from a Tang-era account of a Siberian people.
p.q: To the north-west of Yin-du (Hindustan) is the realm of K'o fu-ch'a… The people there have no cities or towns. They breed much cattle and horses. They make a fermented beverage from honey. In that country the days (in summer) are long and the nights short. In little more than the time necessary to cook a mutton chop, the sun rises again.
p.s: Yelü Chucai's Si yu lu, in a Yuan-era abridgement (translated by E. Bretschneider, 1888)
p.pe: Kipchaks (the steppe later ruled by the Golden Horde)
p.c: Hearsay, partly borrowed from the Tang history; the Mongols did not conquer the Kipchak steppe until 1236.

p.h: A victory feast on top of the captured princes
p.g: After the Kalka, the Tatars crushed the captured Rus princes under boards and sat on top to feast, 'and so ended their lives'. Then they turned back from the Dnieper and vanished, and the chronicler confesses he does not know where they came from or where they went: 'God knows whence He brought them upon us, for our sins.'
p.q: а князи имъше издавиша, подъкладъше подъ дъскы, а сами верху сѣдоша обѣдати, и тако животъ ихъ концяша. … Татари же възвратишася отъ рѣкы Днѣпря, и не съвѣдаемъ откуду суть пришли, и кдѣ ся дѣша опять; Богъ вѣсть, отколѣ приде на насъ, за грѣхы наша.
p.s: Novgorod First Chronicle (PSRL vol. 3, 1841)
p.pe: Tatars (Mongols) and the defeated Rus princes
p.t: and the princes they seized and crushed, putting them under boards, and they themselves sat on top to dine, and so they ended their lives. … And the Tatars turned back from the Dnieper river, and we do not know whence they came nor where they have gone again; God knows whence He brought them upon us, for our sins.
p.c: Reported from survivors' accounts; not seen by a Novgorod writer.

p.h: The lost ancient nation of Lake Baikal: no trace
p.g: Turner had read a European theory, fashionable in the 1700s, that a lost ancient people near Lake Baikal had taught arts and sciences to India and Europe. He asked the Manchu-born chamberlain Soopoon Choomboo, who had travelled along the Baikal, about it. The answer: the area was thinly peopled and he knew of no monument showing remote antiquity. A striking early test of a 'lost civilisation of Tartary' idea.
p.q: My inquiries respected an ancient nation, supposed to have once inhabited the borders of the Baikal sea, in the interior of Tartary, and from which some persons conjecture, the learning, arts, and sciences of India, and even of Europe, to have been originally derived. If such a nation ever existed, the remembrance of it seems now to be buried in deepest oblivion.
p.s: Samuel Turner (1800)
p.c: The same page adds Soopoon Choomboo's answer: 'nor to his knowledge, was any monument existing, that bore marks of remote antiquity.' Turner's own view is only that the tradition, if real, is forgotten.

p.h: The khan's daughter who wrestled her suitors for horses
p.g: Kaidu Khan's daughter Aijaruc ('Bright Moon') refused to marry anyone who could not beat her. Each challenger staked horses, and she won more than 10,000. When a handsome prince staked 1,000 horses and her parents begged her to lose, she threw him on the palace floor anyway. She then rode to war with her father, snatching enemies from their ranks 'as deftly as a hawk'.
p.q: When both had taken post in the middle of the hall they grappled each other by the arms and wrestled this way and that, but for a long time neither could get the better of the other. At last, however, it so befel that the damsel threw him right valiantly on the palace pavement.
p.s: Marco Polo (translated by Henry Yule, 1871)
p.c: Polo was not present; Persian sources confirm a warrior daughter of Kaidu named Khutulun.

p.h: The rain stone of Yarkand
p.g: Among the curiosities of Yarkand, Izzet Ullah lists the 'Yedeh', a stone taken from the head of a cow or horse that can bring rain or snow. He admits he never saw it work, but says many people swore to it. Rain-stone magic (yada) was an old practice of Turkic and Mongol peoples. His closing line is a neat mix of belief and doubt, and Wilson's footnote praises his honesty.
p.q: The individuals who employ the stone are numerous; they are called Yedejis. The stone is to be smeared with the blood of some animal, and then thrown into water: a charm is read at the same time, upon which a strong wind springs up, and then rain and snow ensue… The truth of the story is known to God alone.
p.s: Mir Izzet Ullah (translated by H. H. Wilson)
p.c: Hearsay; the traveller says he had 'no opportunity of observing the fact'.

p.h: A Christian city seen in the sky above Tobolsk
p.g: Müller relays, somewhat apologetically, the omens that the Siberian chronicles say foretold the end of Tatar rule. The Tatars living around the site of later Tobolsk often saw a Christian city with churches and bell towers in the air and heard bells ringing. He says he tells it only to stay faithful to his source.
p.q: Wird man es mir wohl zu gute halten, wenn ich solche erzähle? Ich thue es aus keiner andern Ursache, als weil ich mich nicht gerne von meinem Originale entferne. Oft sollen die umher wohnenden Tataren über dem Orte, wo jetzt die Stadt Tobolsk stehet, eine Christliche Stadt mit Kirchen und Glockenthürmen in der Luft gesehen, und dabey auch ein Geläute von Glocken gehöret haben.
p.s: Gerhard Friedrich Müller (Sammlung Russischer Geschichte, vol. 6, 1761-1762), retelling the Siberian (Remezov) chronicle
p.t: Will I be forgiven for telling them? I do it for no other reason than that I do not like to depart from my original. The Tatars living round about are often said to have seen, above the place where the town of Tobolsk now stands, a Christian city with churches and bell towers in the air, and to have heard bells ringing too.

p.h: Prester John was really the Dalai Lama
p.g: Strahlenberg offers one example of how getting a name right can clear up history: the famous 'great priest John'. He says this priest, who sits between India and China in the land of Tangut, is the one Kalmyks and Mongols call Dalai Lama, with the added title 'Jegan', meaning holy. On the next page he claims the thirteenth-century friar envoys Carpini and Rubruck turned that title into the Christian name John, which is why the king of Portugal later sought Prester John in India and then in Abyssinia.
p.q: von dem sogenannten großen Priester Johann; dieser, welcher seinen Sitz zwischen Indien und China im Lande Tan-guht … hat, wird von allen Kalimucken, Mungalen und … Dalai Lama genannt … woraus nun klärlich zu ersehen, daß dieser Nahme sowol von den Indianern, als auch von den Kalmücken und Mungalen hergekommen
p.s: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (Vorbericht, Stockholm 1726)
p.pe: Kalmyks and Mongols; medieval European envoys
p.t: of the so-called great Priest John; he who has his seat between India and China in the land of Tangut … is called Dalai Lama by all Kalmyks, Mongols and … from which it is now clearly to be seen that this name came from the Indians as well as from the Kalmyks and Mongols

p.h: Gog and Magog are really Ung and Mungul
p.g: In Tenduc, which he says was once Prester John's capital, Polo meets the legend of Gog and Magog, the wild nations Alexander walled in. He offers a down-to-earth explanation: the local names Ung and Mungul, two peoples who lived there before the Tartar migration, had been misheard in the West as Gog and Magog. Yule's notes identify the Ung as the Ongut.
p.q: Here also is what we call the country of Gog and Magog ; they, however, call it Ung and Mungul, after the names of two races of people that existed in that Province before the migration of the Tartars. Ung was the title of the people of the country, and Mungul a name sometimes applied to the Tartars.
p.s: Marco Polo (translated by Henry Yule, 1871)
p.pl: Tenduc (Inner Mongolia, near the Yellow River bend)
p.c: Polo's 'Prester John' line here is King George of the Ongut, a Nestorian Christian prince.

p.h: Treasure hunters buried in the ruins, 1746
p.g: Thirty versts from the Utva river stood remains of masonry that the Kazakhs called Turalbash, or Charaba, 'brown horse's head'. When Cossacks tried to dig for treasure in them in 1746, four were buried alive, and 'since then they have been left in peace'. It is a small, real-life story of treasure hunting in steppe ruins.
p.q: Gegen Irtezkoe Vorpost (S. 176), 30 Werst vom Utwa sind Trümmer von Mauerwerk, die die Kirgisen Turalbasch, auch Charaba d. i. brauner Pferdekopf nennen. Als im Jahr 1746 Kasaken Schätze in denselben suchen wolten, wurden 4 verschüttet; seit dem haben sie Friede.
p.s: J. P. Falck, arranged and supplemented by J. G. Georgi (1785)
p.pe: Kirghiz-Kaisaks (who named the ruins) and Cossack treasure seekers
p.t: Near the Irtetskoe outpost (p. 176), 30 versts from the Utva, are remains of masonry which the Kirghiz call Turalbash, also Charaba, that is 'brown horse's head'. When in the year 1746 Cossacks wanted to search for treasure in them, 4 were buried; since then they have been left in peace.

p.h: Ruins blamed on the Mongols, and a Mongol hand on show
p.g: In his notes Francke records that popular tradition connected the many ruins at Mkhar-rdzong in Nubra with the Mongol general Galdan Tshewang, whose portrait head was kept at Diskit monastery in the hands of a guardian demon. Elsewhere in the book a missionary reports that at Phugtal monastery 'a dried human hand, which once was cut off a Mongol' was shown at a festival.
p.q: According to popular tradition the numerous ruins at Mkhar-rdzon in Nub-ra are connected with the Mongol general Dgah-ldan-tshe-dban, of whom a portrait head may be seen at the Bde-skyid monastery, where it is placed in the hands of the ogre Mgon-dkar.
p.s: A. H. Francke, translator's note (1926)

p.h: Holy relics sold among the Tatar tribes
p.g: Warren Hastings's briefing memorandum for Bogle passes on what he had been told about Tibetan Buddhism: each Tatar tribe had its own living Buddha (Kutuktu), all of whom deferred to the Dalai Lama, 'so that his excrements are sold as charms at a great price among all the Tatar tribes of this religion'. It is a startling piece of hearsay from a governor who had never been there.
p.q: Among the different Tatar tribes which are of this religion, there are persons called Ku-tchuck-tus, who are likewise esteemed living Fos. … it is even pretended that the Ku-tchuck-tus admit a superiority in the Dalai Lama, so that his excrements are sold as charms at a great price among all the Tatar tribes of this religion.
p.s: Warren Hastings (memorandum on Tibet, 1774)
p.c: Hearsay collected in Calcutta; Hastings himself hedges with 'it is even pretended'.

p.h: A Kalmyk idol that gave communion to the sick
p.g: Chappe brought back Kalmyk Buddhist idols from Tobolsk and had their meaning explained by Kalmyk envoys and later by a Kalmyk lama in St Petersburg. Of the copper figure Otschirbany he writes that the god was sent from heaven to fight demons who had stopped the sun and moon, and that a channel ran from its mouth to its anus so that lamas could drop a sacred pill through it into a sick person's mouth.
p.q: Ce Dieu est du troisieme ordre. Il fut envoyé du Ciel pour combattre de mauvais génies qui avoient arrêté le Soleil & la Lune. … La bouche de cette Divinité communique avec l'anus par un canal perpendiculaire. Les Lamas ou Prêtres en font usage pour donner la communion aux malades.
p.s: Jean Chappe d'Auteroche, from explanations given by Kalmyk envoys at Tobolsk
p.t: This god is of the third order. He was sent from heaven to fight evil spirits that had stopped the Sun and Moon. … The mouth of this divinity connects with the anus by a vertical channel. The lamas or priests use it to give communion to the sick.
p.c: Otschirbany is Vajrapani. Chappe owned and described the figure, but the ritual comes through interpreters and may be misunderstood.

p.h: Prester John: 'ten times more than the truth'
p.g: Rubruck traces the legend of Prester John to a Nestorian shepherd-lord of the Naimans who made himself king after the death of the Kara-Khitai ruler. The Nestorians called him King John and said ten times more about him than was true, as they make great rumours out of nothing. Rubruck crossed his pastures and found that nobody knew anything of him except a few Nestorians.
p.q: Mortuo Con cham, elevavit se ille nestorinus in regem et vocabant eum nestorini regem Johannem, et plus dicebant de ipso in decuplo quam veritas esset. Ita enim faciunt nestorini venientes de partibus illis: de nichilo enim faciunt magnos rumores … Sic ergo exivit magna fama de illo rege Johanne; et ego transivi per pascua ejus, nullus aliquid sciebat de eo nisi Nestoriani pauci.
p.s: William of Rubruck
p.t: When Con Khan died, that Nestorian raised himself up as king, and the Nestorians called him King John and said ten times more about him than the truth. For that is what Nestorians coming from those parts do: they make great rumours out of nothing … So the great fame of this King John went out; and when I crossed his pastures, nobody knew anything about him except a few Nestorians.

p.h: Reading Gibbon on Genghis Khan to an Uzbek holy man
p.g: Sheltering with a respected Uzbek pir (khaja) at Talikan, Moorcroft tried to translate into Persian the chapters of Gibbon's Decline and Fall about Genghis Khan and Timur. His host corrected the Persian style, was surprised a European knew so much about the 'Moguls', and admitted many facts were new to him. A European history of the Mongols thus travelled back to Central Asia.
p.q: Whilst under his protection, I attempted to render into Persian, for his use, the chapters of Gibbon which treat of Jangez Khan and Timur, in which the khaja took much interest, and corrected the style of the translation. He was much surprised that a European should have known so much of the history of the Moguls, and admitted that many of the facts were new to him
p.s: William Moorcroft (edited by H. H. Wilson, 1841)
p.tg: genghis khan timur gibbon memory history

p.h: Rocks that look like ruined buildings
p.g: A day before seeing the real ruins, Timkovsky camped by a granite ridge that from far off looked like a forest and close up looked like altars, a sarcophagus, a tower and 'the ruins of a house with a stone floor'. He calls it a 'lusus naturae', a freak of nature, and explains it as decomposed granite lying in slabs. On the following page his Mongol hosts add that the rock is full of loadstone that pulls at any gun brought near it.
p.q: At a distance it looks like a forest; but when seen near at hand, it presents an extraordinary lusus nature. These rocks resemble, now an immense altar, now a sarcophagus; here a tower, there the ruins of a house with a stone floor. The rock, a decomposed granite, lies in large masses from three to nine inches thick
p.s: George Timkowski (English translation, 1827)
p.c: The author himself judged these to be natural rock, not buildings.

p.h: Epic heroes die at the Kalka
p.g: The Nikon Chronicle adds names from Russian heroic poetry to the Kalka disaster: Aleksandr Popovich, his servant Torop, Dobrynia 'Golden Belt' and seventy great bogatyrs all fell to the Tatars. The same page tells how the captured princes were laid under planks while the Tatars sat on top to eat, crushing them. Older chronicles do not name these heroes; the compilers took them from oral epic.
p.q: убиша же на томъ бою: и Александра Поповичя, и слугу его Торопа, и Добрыню Рязаничя Златаго пояса, и седмьдесятъ великихъ и храбрыхъ богатырей, вси побіени быша гнѣвомъ Божіимъ за грѣхи наша отъ Татаръ.
p.s: Nikon Chronicle, PSRL vol. 10 (1885)
p.pe: Tatars (Mongols); Rus warriors including the epic heroes Aleksandr Popovich and Dobrynia
p.t: and in that battle they killed Aleksandr Popovich and his servant Torop, and Dobrynia Riazanich Golden Belt, and seventy great and brave bogatyrs; all were slain by the Tatars through the wrath of God for our sins.
p.c: The editors note that this sentence is found in only one manuscript (G). The heroes belong to epic song, not to 13th-century records.
