p.h: The owl that saved Genghis Khan
p.g: Unhorsed and alone after a lost skirmish, Genghis hid in a bush. As his enemies came to search it, an owl (the 'duc', eagle owl) landed on the bush, and they left, reasoning that no bird would sit where a man was hiding. Hayton says this is why every Tartar who can get an owl feather wears it on his head. Compare Riccoldo (W228), who tells a quite different owl story to explain the same feathers.
p.q: et sur ce un oisel, qui avoit non duc, vint e s'asist sur ce boisson … Les Tartars rendirent graces à Deu, e dès adonques orent en tante reverence cel oisel, qui est apellez duc, que chascun qui poet avoir de la plume de cel oisel la porte sur sa teste.
p.s: Hayton of Corycus, La Flor des estoires de la terre d'Orient (French text, 1307), ed. Ch. Kohler (1906)
p.t: and at that a bird called the duc (eagle owl) came and sat on the bush … The Tartars gave thanks to God, and from then on held that bird, called the duc, in such reverence that everyone who can get a feather of it wears it on his head.
p.c: A legend explaining a real custom (owl feathers worn on the head).

p.h: The translator: Irgana-kon is borrowed from Gog and Magog
p.g: The English translator is openly sceptical: he calls the origin of the Tatars 'fabulous', Oghuz Khan 'a mere Legend', and the bellows story 'a whimsical Invention'. In a footnote he suggests the enclosed-valley tale grew out of Arabic legends of Gog and Magog (Yajuj and Majuj) shut up behind the mountains of the far north.
p.q: Their melting their way out of the Mountains with seventy Bellows, is a whimsical Invention. … In all likelihood this Fiction of the Moguls being inclosed in the Mountain of Irgana Kon, took its Rise from one of the like kind, which we find in Arabik Authors relating to the People of Yajuj and Majuj, or Gog and Magog
p.s: The anonymous English translator's preface and footnote (1730), not Abu'l Ghazi
p.c: The Gog and Magog link is the translator's guess.

p.h: Yermak's body that bled for six weeks
p.g: Following the Remezov chronicle, whose author wanted Yermak made a saint, Müller tells how Tatars found the drowned Cossack leader by his armour. When a murza tried to strip it, blood ran from the corpse's mouth and nose as from a living man, so the Tatars laid the body naked on a scaffold and everyone who passed shot an arrow into it, and each time fresh blood flowed. Birds would not touch it, and after six weeks troubling dreams led the Tatars to bury him.
p.q: Alsobald lief dem Todten aus Mund und Nase häufiges Blut, nicht anders, als von einem lebendigen Menschen … Sie legten zu solchem Ende den Leichnam ganz entkleidet auf ein Gerüste, da denn ein jeder, der herzukam, oder vorüber gieng, einen Pfeil nach demselben abschoß, wovon jedes mahl frisches Blut aus der Wunde lief.
p.s: Gerhard Friedrich Müller (Sammlung Russischer Geschichte, vol. 6, 1761-1762), retelling the Siberian (Remezov) chronicle
p.t: At once much blood ran from the dead man's mouth and nose, just as from a living person … For this purpose they laid the body quite naked on a scaffold, and everyone who came up or passed by shot an arrow at it, and each time fresh blood ran from the wound.
p.c: A hagiographic chronicle story; Müller notes its author wished Yermak to be canonised.

p.h: A tower of 282 heads
p.g: Marching from Shamakhi towards the Kura, the embassy passed a circular 'pyramid' about fifty feet high with niches holding the heads of 282 Persian and Tartar chiefs of the Shamakhi rebellion, all beheaded in one morning on Nadir Shah's orders. The diarist notes that these Tartars had never accepted Persian rule, yet were punished as rebels.
p.q: …here is a circular pyramid of near 50 feet high; in which are niches filled with 282 human heads, of the late Persian and tartar chiefs of the Shamakie rebellion, who were all beheaded in one morning. These Tartars had not acknowledged subjection to Persia, and yet they were treated as rebels.
p.s: Anonymous journal of the Russian embassy to Persia of 1746, extract printed by Jonas Hanway (1753)
p.pl: Shirvan, between Shamakhi and the Kura River (Azerbaijan)

p.h: The 'plateau of Tatary' that exists only in their heads
p.g: Some 18th-century writers had argued that all Old World civilisation began on a high plateau in the middle of Tatary. Klaproth, discussing the Uighurs, says their little kingdom never counted for much and gives no support to that idea, and he says bluntly that the plateau exists only in the brains of those who believe in it.
p.q: L'hypothèse favorite de ceux qui veulent que toute la civilisation de l'ancien continent soit venue du plateau de la Tatarie, qui n'existe que dans leur cerveau, ne reçoit donc aucun appui de la part des Ouigour, dont le petit royaume ne s'est jamais élevé à une certaine importance politique
p.s: Julius Klaproth
p.pe: Uighurs (a Turkic people of the eastern Tian Shan)
p.t: The favourite hypothesis of those who would have all the civilisation of the Old World come from the plateau of Tatary, which exists only in their brains, therefore receives no support from the Uighurs, whose little kingdom never rose to any political importance
p.c: Klaproth is arguing against earlier scholars (notably Bailly); this is his judgement, not an observation.

p.h: Noah's Ark grounded in Tartary
p.g: In a chapter on Chinese origins Barrow argues that the 'heights of Tartary' are the highest land in the Old World, so the Ark probably first touched ground there rather than in Armenia, and that Tartars and Chinese share one origin. He suggests Noah's survivors may have followed the rivers down into China.
p.q: we may suppose that the ark, instead of resting in Armenia, first struck ground in that part of Tartary which is now inhabited by the Eleuths, as being the most elevated tract of country in the old world. From these heights large rivers flow towards every quarter of the horizon.
p.s: John Barrow
p.c: Pure speculation built on the biblical Flood and faulty geography.

p.h: Three heavenly maidens and a red fruit
p.g: The dynasty's origin legend: three heavenly maidens bathed in Lake Bulhuri below Bukuri mountain, east of the Changbai range. A magic magpie dropped a red fruit on the youngest one's clothes; she put it in her mouth, swallowed it and conceived a boy who could speak at birth. She named him Bukuri Yongshon, of the Aisin Gioro clan, and sent him downriver in a small boat to settle a land at war. The court presents this as sacred history.
p.q: 長白山之東有布庫哩山其下有池曰布勒瑚里相傳三天女浴于池有神鵲銜朱果置季女衣季女含口中忽已入腹遂有身尋産一男生而能言
p.s: Agui, Yu Minzhong and the Qianlong commission, Researches on Manchu Origins (Siku quanshu Wenyuange copy, Kanseki Repository transcription), quoting the dynasty's Record of Origins (Faxiang shiji)
p.t: East of the Changbai mountains is Bukuri mountain, and below it a lake called Bulhuri. It is handed down that three heavenly maidens bathed in the lake. A divine magpie, holding a red fruit in its beak, placed it on the youngest maiden's clothes. The youngest held it in her mouth; suddenly it went down into her belly and she conceived. Soon she bore a boy who could speak at birth.
p.c: A dynastic foundation legend, not history; the editors compare it to the miraculous births of the Shang and Zhou founders.

p.h: Twenty-seven days through ruined cities
p.g: After leaving the Khazar king, Sallam says, his party crossed a black, foul-smelling land, then travelled twenty (or twenty-seven) days among ruined cities. They were told these were the remains of cities overrun by Gog and Magog. Near the wall they found forts held by Arabic- and Persian-speaking Muslims with schools and mosques, who had never heard of the caliph.
p.q: nous passâmes, durant vingt (vingt-sept) jours, au milieu de villes en ruine. On nous apprit que c'étaient les restes des villes envahies autrefois et dévastées par les peuples de Gog et Magog. Nous arrivâmes enfin à des forteresses bâties dans le voisinage des montagnes … Nous y trouvâmes des personnes qui parlaient l'arabe et le persan. Ils sont musulmans, sachant lire le Koran
p.s: Sallam the Interpreter, as reported by Ibn Khurradadhbih (French translation by M. J. de Goeje, 1889)
p.pl: Central Asian steppe, north-east of the Khazars
p.pe: Peoples of the steppe; ruins blamed on Gog and Magog
p.t: we passed twenty (twenty-seven) days in the midst of ruined cities. We were told these were the remains of cities once invaded and laid waste by the peoples of Gog and Magog. At last we came to fortresses built near the mountains … There we found people who spoke Arabic and Persian. They are Muslims and can read the Koran
p.c: A ninth-century tale: the ruins are real or imagined, but the explanation (Gog and Magog) is what Sallam was told, not something he could check.

p.h: The golden old woman and the monstrous people beyond the Ob
p.g: Gerritsz explains that earlier knowledge of the road to the Ob came from a Russian itinerary published by Herberstein, into which 'innumerable fables' had been mixed: the Zolotaya Baba or golden old woman with her children, and monstrous people beyond the Ob. He offers Massa's newer information as a correction.
p.q: a travel from the Moscow to Colmogro, described by the Russians and thence on Petzora where the nations received the Christian faith in the year 1518, and further to the Ovy, and still a little further onward, in which innumerable fables have been mixed up of Slatababa, the golden old woman with her children, and the monstruous people beyond the Oby.
p.s: Hessel Gerritsz, preface to the 1612 Dutch tracts (English translation by F. J. Millard in the 1878 facsimile edition)

p.h: A roofless tomb, a walled-up tomb, a vine for a sinner
p.g: Kohl retells the stories behind several Khans' tombs: one left roofless so the dead ruler could look up at heaven, one walled up because its occupant felt unworthy of God's sunlight, and one with a vine planted over the head so that a Khan who bore little fruit in life might do better in death. Another Khan asked to be buried under the mosque eaves so rain could wash away his sins.
p.q: without a roof, because “he considered the Heavens so beautiful and sublime, that even from his grave he would wish to look towards the firmament, the abode of God.” Another had had his tomb entirely walled up, because, as the inscription ran, “he did not feel himself worthy to be shone on by the least ray of God's sun.”
p.s: J. G. Kohl (English abridged translation, 1844)
p.c: Kohl could not read the Arabic or Turkish inscriptions himself; these explanations were presumably given by guides and read like local tradition.

p.h: The storm cave of Oufbe
p.g: An old Tatar mullah of Semipalatinsk, who had travelled to Kulja, told the Kazan orientalist Kazim-Beg of a huge cave on the caravan road past Lake Alakol, called Oufbe in Tatar. It blew out storms lasting two days, strong enough to fling things into the lake; nobody dared go in, and only God knew how deep it was. Caravans waited a week for the winds to pass.
p.q: est une grande caverne souterraine; elle porte le nom tatar d'Oufbé. Quelquefois, et principalement en hiver, elle produit des tempêtes violentes qui durent pendant deux jours. L'entrée de cette caverne ressemble à celle d'un vaste caveau, et personne n'ose y entrer, ni même y regarder de bien près. Sa profondeur est inconnue à tout le monde, à l'exception de Dieu (Allah).
p.s: Mullah Sayfulla Kazi of Semipalatinsk, reported in a letter by Mirza Kazem-Beg, translated by Alexander von Humboldt
p.t: there is a great underground cave; it bears the Tatar name Oufbe. Sometimes, and chiefly in winter, it produces violent storms that last for two days. The entrance of this cave looks like a vast vault, and no one dares to enter it or even look at it closely. Its depth is unknown to everyone except God (Allah).
p.c: Third-hand: Humboldt prints Kazem-Beg's English letter in French, and Kazem-Beg himself only guessed that fire had once come out of the cave. The pass is known for violent winds.

p.h: The Sugar Lake and the khan's clever wife
p.g: Beside the ruined 'queen's house' at Tsarev lies a lake the Tatars call the Sugar Lake, and Gmelin retells their story. A khan (his name is cut off in the scan) was persuaded to put aside his beautiful low-born wife; she outwitted him by carrying him, drunk after a feast, into her own chamber, so he sent her to live in a house by this lake. Knowing he loved falconry, she threw sugar into the lake every day to draw swans and geese, so the khan came daily to hunt and rest with her until death. Gmelin notes drily that the lake really is sweeter than other waters, which may be how the tale began.
p.q: so warf dieselbe alle Tage eine große Menge Zucker in den angeführten bey dem Haus befindlichen See, und lockte dadurch eine große Anzahl von Schwanen und Gänsen herbey, … daß er bey dem See täglich erschien, nach geendigter Jagd bey der Königin ausruhte … Es ist würklich an dem, daß ermeldeter See ein süßeres Waßer bey sich führet, als andere Flüße
p.s: Samuel Gottlieb Gmelin, retelling a Tatar story
p.pe: Tatars (a tale about a khan of 'Great Tartary')
p.t: so every day she threw a great quantity of sugar into the lake by the house, and so drew a great number of swans and geese, … so that he appeared daily at the lake and rested with the queen after the hunt … It is indeed true that this lake has sweeter water than other rivers
p.c: A local Tatar legend, told as such.
p.tg: legend khan queen falconry sugar lake

p.h: Amazons near the Kalmyks, and an Amazon's dress in the palace
p.g: In Georgia Chardin asked about the Amazons of classical legend. He met no one who had been to their country, but many told stories, and in the prince's palace he was shown a large woman's garment of coarse wool said to have belonged to an Amazon killed near Kakheti. The Georgian prince's son told him a numerous unknown people lived five days north, always at war with 'the Tartars, which they call Calmac'.
p.q: I confess, I never saw any Person in Georgia who had been in the Country of the Amazons; but I have heard many of 'em tell Stories of those People. And they shew'd me in the Prince's Palace, a large Female habit of a course Woollen Stuff
p.s: Jean Chardin (English translation, London, 1691)
p.pe: Kalmyks (as the Georgians called them) and a legendary people beyond
p.c: Chardin reports the stories but, on the next page, rejects the classical details as Greek fables.

p.h: Jordanus on the 'Great Tartar' of China
p.g: The Dominican bishop Jordanus, who never went to China, repeats what 'trustworthy people' told him of the Great Tartar: very rich, just and generous, with paper money and monasteries like Europe's. Some subjects keep their dead unburied at home for up to ten years, serving them food as if alive, and great lords are buried with a horse and one or two favourite servants alive.
p.q: De Magno Tartaro, quod audivi à fide dignis narro … Ibi, mortuos suos non comburunt; non etiam sepeliunt, aliquotiens per decem annos … sed tenent eos in domibus, et ministrant sibi cibaria, sicut si esset vivus. Magni domini, cùm moriuntur, sepeliuntur cum equo uno, et cum uno vel duobus suis servitoribus vivis sibi magis dilectis.
p.s: Jordanus Catalani of Severac (Mirabilia descripta, c. 1330), in the 1839 edition
p.pe: Mongol emperor of China and his subjects
p.t: Of the Great Tartar I tell what I heard from trustworthy people … There they do not burn their dead; nor do they bury them, sometimes for ten years … but they keep them in their houses and serve them food as if they were alive. Great lords, when they die, are buried with one horse and with one or two of their favourite servants alive.
p.c: Explicit hearsay: Jordanus served in India and never reached China.

p.h: Trial by goat and sieve among the pagan Tatars
p.g: Hammer's first appendix translates the Ottoman geography Menazir ul-awalim, which here copies al-Qazwini's Athar al-bilad (1275). The Tatars are described as a hard, bloodthirsty Turkic people who worship the sun; their coming is counted among the Prophet's foretold wonders, with a saying about broad-faced, small-eyed 'Turks' who will tie their horses to the pillars of the mosques. A woman once held captive tells how, when her captor fell ill, his kin suspected her of poisoning him, set her on a goat and had a sorceress swing a sieve over her while they stood round with drawn swords; when the goat bleated she was freed. The Ottoman author adds that these pagan Tatars differ from the Crimean and Nogai Tatars, long since Muslims.
p.q: Ich war eine Zeitlang unter den Tataren gefangen, als der, so mich gefangen genommen, krank ward. … Eines Tages stellten sie eine grosse Versammlung an, brachten eine Ziege, und setzten mich darauf. Eine Zauberinn kam, mit einem Siebe in der Hand, schwang dasselbe und sprach einige Worte … Während diess geschah, meckerte die Ziege unter mir. Sie sagten, es ist nicht, wie wir geglaubet haben, und liessen mich los.
p.s: A captive woman quoted in al-Qazwini's Athar al-bilad, as excerpted in the Ottoman Menazir ul-awalim; German translation by Hammer-Purgstall (appendix 1)
p.pe: Pagan Tatars before the Mongol conquests, as seen by Muslim writers
p.t: I was for a time a captive among the Tatars, when the man who had taken me prisoner fell ill. … One day they held a great assembly, brought a goat and set me on it. A sorceress came with a sieve in her hand, swung it and spoke some words … While this was happening, the goat bleated under me. They said: it is not as we believed, and let me go.
p.c: A single anecdote passed through two compilers, framed by hostile religious prophecy; not a description of Golden Horde practice.
p.tg: divination sorceress sieve goat prophecy qazwini

p.h: Prester John's kingdom 'still in being'
p.g: Avril takes up the medieval legend of Prester John, the Christian king of the East. Following Marco Polo, he places John's kingdom in Tenduc or Tangut, between China and Mughal India, and a page earlier concludes that the Dalai Lama must be the real 'Prester John', a line of Christian rulers turned idolaters.
p.q: For the Kingdom of Tenduc, or as others read it, Tanchut, this Kingdom, I say, where Marcus Paulus places Preste-John, is still in being, if we may believe those who have travell'd through it, and lies between China and the Empire of the Great Mogul.
p.s: Philippe Avril (English translation, 1693)
p.pe: Tartars of Tangut; the Dalai Lama
p.c: A legend Avril tries to fit to the facts; he never went there.
p.tg: prester john legend dalai lama tangut marco polo

p.h: Were the Tartars the Lost Ten Tribes?
p.g: Chevalier repeats a learned theory that 'Tartar' was a corruption of 'Tatares', supposedly a Syriac word for 'remnant', making the Tartars the remnant of the Ten Tribes of Israel carried off by the Assyrians. He presents it as what 'some say', not as his own view.
p.q: There are some who say that the name of Tartar is improper and corrupted, and that they ought to be called Tatares or Totares, A word which in the Syriack Language signifies a Remnant, supposing that these people are the remnant of the Ten Tribes which Salmanazar and his predecessors led away captive into Assyria
p.s: Pierre Chevalier (translated by Edward Brown, 1672)
p.c: A scholarly speculation of the period, reported secondhand.

p.h: Gog and Magog shut behind a rock at the end of the world
p.g: Bergeron retells what French chroniclers such as Joinville and Nangis had heard from envoys: the Tartars said that at the northern end of the earth a rock no one could pass shut in the peoples Gog and Magog, whom Bergeron equates with the Mongal of other writers and the Moal the Tartars call themselves, destined to come with Antichrist at the end of the world. Behind the rock lay the sandy desert where the Tartars lived as tributary herders until Chinggis roused them.
p.q: estoient enclos les peuples appellez Goths & Magoths (qui est le Gog & Magog de l'Escriture, & le Mongal des autres Escriuains, & le Moal des Tartares mesmes). Que ces gens-là deuoient venir à la fin du monde auec l'Antechrist.
p.s: Pierre Bergeron (Traicté des Tartares, 1634), paraphrasing Joinville, Nangis and other French chroniclers
p.pe: Tartars (Mongols), as imagined by medieval French chroniclers
p.t: the peoples called Goths and Magoths were shut in (who are the Gog and Magog of Scripture, the Mongal of other writers and the Moal of the Tartars themselves). And that these people were to come at the end of the world with Antichrist.
p.c: Secondhand legend; the chroniclers' 'Tartar origin story' is already filtered through biblical expectation.
p.tg: gog and magog antichrist legend origin

p.h: A Turkish prince speared in a dream for raiding a monastery
p.g: The New Monastery at Balkh was so rich that rulers coveted it. A son of the Turkish Yabghu khan (named on the previous page) led his whole horde to plunder it and camped nearby. That night he dreamed that the guardian god Vaisravana drove a long halberd through his chest; he woke in pain, sent for the monks to beg forgiveness, and died before the messenger returned.
p.q: 其部落率其戎旅奄襲伽藍欲圖珍寳去此不逺屯軍野次其夜夢見毗沙門天曰汝有何力敢壊伽藍因以長㦸貫徹胷背可汗驚寤便苦心痛
p.s: Xuanzang and Bianji, book 1 (Chinese text, Siku quanshu copy)
p.pe: Western Turks (son of the Yabghu khan)
p.t: [He gathered] his tribes and led his troops to fall on the monastery by surprise, meaning to seize its treasures. He camped in the open not far from here. That night he dreamed he saw the god Vaisravana, who said: 'What power have you, that you dare to destroy this monastery?' and drove a long halberd through him from chest to back. The khan woke in terror, with a pain in his heart.
p.c: A monastery's protective legend, told to discourage raiders.

p.h: The town of Katak, buried by a rain of sand
p.g: A holy man warns the town of Katak of God's wrath and leaves. The muezzin goes back for a last call to prayer, sees sand falling like dry snow, and finds the town buried up to the minaret, from which he jumps to escape. Mirza Haidar adds that winds sometimes uncover the minaret or a house where everything is in order but the owner is white bones. The editor notes that sand does not fall like snow but that dunes do bury towns.
p.q: So he again ascended and, looking round, discovered that it was raining sand, and to such a degree that the whole town was covered ; after a little while he noticed that the ground was rising, and at last only a part of the minaret was left free.
p.s: Mirza Haidar Dughlat, retelling a story from Maulana Khwaja Ahmad (translated by E. Denison Ross, 1895)
p.pe: Muslim townspeople of Katak in the Tarim basin
p.c: A pious legend passed down in one family; the editor's note compares it with real sand-buried ruins seen by Forsyth, Bellew and Przhevalsky.
p.tg: buried city sand legend minaret katak

p.h: The emperor's corpse relayed so no one finds the grave
p.g: When the emperor dies, Jordanus heard, men carry the body with great treasure to a certain spot, drop it and run 'as if the devil were after them'; others then snatch it up and do the same, relay after relay, so that the burial place can never be found and the treasure never stolen. His death is kept secret until a successor is quietly enthroned. Secret Mongol royal burials are real; the relay detail is hearsay.
p.q: Cùm imperator moritur, portatur cum maximo thesauro, à quibusdam hominibus, usque ad certum locum, ubi deponunt corpus, et fugiunt quàm possunt, sicut si diabolus insequeretur eos; et sunt alii parati qui immediatè corpus rapiunt, et simili modo faciunt usque ad alium locum; … et hoc faciunt ne locus possit inveniri
p.s: Jordanus Catalani of Séverac, O.P. (Latin text, ed. Coquebert de Montbret, Recueil de voyages IV, Paris 1839)
p.t: When the emperor dies he is carried with a very great treasure by certain men to a certain place, where they set down the body and flee as fast as they can, as if the devil were chasing them; and others are ready who at once snatch up the body and do the same as far as another place; … and they do this so that the place cannot be found
p.c: Hearsay; compare Carpini and Marco Polo on the secret cemetery of the khans.
p.n: OCR normalized against the page image.
p.tg: secret burial treasure khan funeral legend

p.h: Sacred rats that gnawed a Xiongnu army's harness
p.g: West of Khotan stood mounds made by rats 'as big as hedgehogs', with gold and silver fur. Long ago, the story went, a Xiongnu army camped there; the king of Khotan prayed to the rats, and in the morning the raiders found every strap, bowstring and fastening gnawed through. Khotan built the rats a temple, and travellers still got down from their carts to bow as they passed.
p.q: The Hiung-nu, hearing their approach, were overcome by fear. They hastened to harness their horses and equip their chariots, but they found that the leather of their armour, and their horses' gear, and their bow strings, and all the fastenings of their clothes, had been gnawed by the rats.
p.s: Xuanzang and Bianji (translated by Samuel Beal, 1884)
p.c: Xuanzang introduces it as 'the common story' he heard. Beal notes a parallel in Herodotus (mice gnawing an Assyrian army's bowstrings).

p.h: Mongols descended from the Asuras
p.g: Among the opening legends of the Tibetan history, Das lists one that gives each great people a different origin: the Indians from the gods, the Chinese from the naga demigods, and the Mongolians from the asuras, the demons who fought the gods. It sits beside the story of the Tibetans' descent from a monkey.
p.q: The origin of the people of Aryavartta (India) from the gods, that of the Chinese from the Naga demi-gods, and that of the Mongolians from the Asura (demons who fought with the gods)
p.s: Sarat Chandra Das, English analytical contents to his edition of Sumpa Khenpo's Tibetan text (Calcutta, 1908)
p.c: A summary line by the editor; Sumpa reports it as a traditional legend.

p.h: Melons that burst open with a lamb inside
p.g: Odoric reports the 'vegetable lamb': melons on the 'Caspean Mountains' that ripen and split to reveal a little lamb. He admits he did not see it and heard it from others. Yule's note traces the later 'Tartar lamb' or borametz legend, which Scaliger placed among the Tartars of the Zavolha horde, and identifies the likely source as a woolly fern root.
p.q: Another passing marvellous thing may be related, which however I saw not myself, but heard from trustworthy persons. For 'tis said that in a certain great kingdom called Cadeli there be mountains called the Caspean Mountains, on which are said to grow certain very large melons. And when these be ripe, they burst, and a little beast is found inside like a small lamb
p.s: Friar Odoric of Pordenone (translated by Henry Yule, 1866)
p.c: Hearsay, and Odoric says so himself. Yule identifies Cadeli with the Volga (Athil) country.

p.h: A shining Christian city seen in the sky over the Tatar capital
p.g: The chronicle claims that the Tatar khans, princes and Muslim clergy saw, year after year, a glowing Christian city with churches and ringing bells hovering in the air over the spot where Tobolsk cathedral later stood. It is a foretelling legend written to show that God had given the land to the Russians, not an eyewitness report.
p.q: При сихъ во вся лѣта видѣнія царь и князи, агуны, муллы и абызы и протчіе бусурманы на томъ мѣстѣ, идѣже нынѣ градъ Тоболескъ и соборная церковь до колоколни, видѣшася христіанскій со свѣтомъ градъ въ воздухѣ, и церкви и звонъ велій, яко ими дивитися и ужасно недоумѣя, что будетъ се.
p.s: Kungur (Remezov) chronicle, article 18 (1880 printed text)
p.pe: Siberian Tatars (Muslim clergy and nobles of Sibir)
p.t: In their time, every year, the tsar and the princes, akhuns, mullahs, abyzes and the other Muslims saw visions: on the place where the town of Tobolsk and the cathedral church up to its bell tower now stand, a Christian city appeared in the air with light, with churches and a great ringing, so that they marvelled and were terrified, not knowing what it would be.
p.c: A pious prophecy legend composed after the conquest; the same page adds a pillar of fire and gold and silver sparks on the town site.
p.tg: vision phantom city tobolsk prophecy bells

p.h: 'Of that fruit I have eaten': the lamb that grows in a gourd
p.g: Mandeville improves on Odoric's melon-lamb: in Caldilhe gourds are cut open to reveal a little beast of flesh, bone and blood, and he claims to have eaten it. He then swaps marvels with his hosts, telling them of the barnacle trees of Britain whose fruit turns into birds. The next page places the enclosed peoples of Gog and Magog in the Caspian mountains of the same region.
p.q: And there groweth a manner of fruit, as though it were gourds. And when they be ripe, men cut them a-two, and men find within a little beast, in flesh, in bone, and blood, as though it were a little lamb without wool. And men eat both the fruit and the beast. And that is a great marvel. Of that fruit I have eaten
p.s: 'Sir John Mandeville' (Cotton manuscript, modern spelling ed. A. W. Pollard, 1900)
p.c: Odoric only heard the story; Mandeville turns it into a personal tasting. The editor's index tentatively places Caldilhe in Korea, but the tale is the Volga 'Tartar lamb' legend.

p.h: Claws of a giant bird, or a rhinoceros?
p.g: Summarising the explorer Hedenstrom, Wrangel says one of the Lyakhov Islands seemed to be made of mammoth bones, which hunters had carried off by the boatload for eighty years. Along the Arctic shore lay skulls of two unknown beasts, one found with what looked like three-foot claws of a giant bird. The Yukaghirs used these 'claws' to strengthen their bows and told marvellous tales about the bird. A footnote says Dr Kyber believed they came from a kind of rhinoceros.
p.q: Near these last-named skulls something like the claw of an enormous bird is generally found. These claws are often three English feet long … The Jukahiri, who make use of these horny claws, to give increased force to their bows, maintain that the head and claws have both belonged to an enormous bird, respecting which they relate a number of marvellous stories.
p.s: Ferdinand von Wrangel (English translation by Mrs Sabine, 1840), summarising Hedenstrom's journal
p.c: Not about Tartars. The 'claws' are almost certainly the horns of the extinct woolly rhinoceros, as Kyber suspected; the giant bird is Yukaghir legend.

p.h: A pillar built of horse skulls
p.g: On a conical hill above the Akhtuba, Kalmyks stationed at the military posts had built a circular column entirely of horse skulls and jawbones, with a low wall and ditch decorated with more bones and a huge horse head on top pointing east. The bones came from an epidemic that had killed the post's horses and those of the wintering Kirghiz.
p.q: …the Kalmuks who were stationed here at the military posts have erected a singular monument. It is a circular column, raised on the very summit of the hill, and constructed entirely of the skulls and jaw-bones of horses, closely adapted to one another:
p.s: Peter Simon Pallas (English translation, 1812 edition)
p.pe: Kalmyks of the Russian frontier posts

p.h: The town the locals said had sunk into the earth
p.g: At Uvek the ground sometimes caved in over deep stone cellars. The local people took these cellars for 'sunken stone buildings' and believed the whole town had sunk into the earth when the ground broke open, with many other tales Lepekhin thought too odd to repeat. He dismisses this as the chatter of the common people and prefers his own explanation: a Tatar town destroyed by an enemy, whose buried cellars remained.
p.q: Das gemeine Volk glaubt, er sey in die Erde durch einen Durchbruch derselben versunken, weil man zuweilen Stellen findet wo die Erde sich in die darunter liegenden tiefen steinernen Keller hineingestürzt hat und durchgebrochen ist, welche Keller sie für versunkene steinerne Gebäude halten; diesem fügen sie noch viele andere Mährgen und ein Gewäsche bey, welches zu wunderlich ist, als daß man es anführen könnte.
p.s: Ivan Lepekhin (German translation, 1774)
p.pe: Russian peasants of the Saratov district, about the old Tatar site
p.t: The common people believe it sank into the earth when the ground broke open, because one sometimes finds places where the earth has fallen into deep stone cellars lying beneath and broken through, and these cellars they take for sunken stone buildings. To this they add many other little tales and chatter, too strange to be repeated.
p.c: Folk belief reported and rejected by Lepekhin; he saw the collapsed cellars himself.

p.h: Nomads who asked to be fired on
p.g: Back in Paris Chappe heard from the Chevalier de Saint-Pierre that a large band of Tartars once approached a Russian fort on the Siberian lines. Warned that they would be fired on unless they withdrew, they held a council and sent word asking the commander to fire. After the first cannonade killed several of them they held another council and asked again, and only left after the third.
p.q: Un gros détachement de ces Tartares s'approcha, il y a quelques années, des lignes de Sibérie; le Commandant d'un des Forts Russes les ayant apperçus, & ignorant l'intention de ces Tartares en troupe, leur fit savoir qu'il feroit faire feu sur eux, s'ils ne se retiroient. Ces Tartares s'assemblent, & après avoir tenu conseil, ils envoient prier le Commandant d'ordonner qu'on fit feu; on le fit.
p.s: Jean Chappe d'Auteroche, retelling a story from the Chevalier de Saint-Pierre
p.t: A large detachment of these Tartars approached the Siberian lines a few years ago; the commander of one of the Russian forts saw them and, not knowing what this band of Tartars intended, let them know he would open fire on them if they did not withdraw. The Tartars gathered, held a council, and sent to ask the commander to order the firing; it was done.
p.c: A second-hand anecdote told in Paris, used by Chappe to argue that some nomads did not know firearms; nothing confirms it.

p.h: Timur's pyramid of skulls, as the Turkmens told it
p.g: Snowed in at a desert camp, Wolff listened to Turkmens talk of Alexander and Timur as if they had lived yesterday. One told how Timur punished the Khan of Khwarazm by building a pyramid of human skulls cemented with clay at Urgench, sparing only dervishes, scholars and poets.
p.q: It is remarkable to hear these Turkomauns speak of the exploits of Alexander and Timur, exactly as if of modern occurrence. … He made a pyramid at Organtsh entirely of skulls of men, cemented with clay. He spared the lives of none, except those of holy derveeshes, of the learned, and of poets, around whose houses he placed Karawl, i. e. guards.
p.s: A Turkmen in the Merv desert, as reported by Joseph Wolff
p.pe: Turkmens of the Merv desert; Timur (Tamerlane)
p.c: Oral tradition. Timur's skull towers are recorded elsewhere (Wolff also mentions one at Sabzevar), but this telling is folk memory.
p.tg: timur skulls oral tradition turkmen urgench

p.h: Prester John unmasked as a steppe king, and his letter as a forgery
p.g: Pétis identifies the famous Prester John of Asia with Ong Khan, king of the Keraits and Genghis Khan's early patron, and summarises the boastful letter in Prester John's name, which claimed seventy vassal kings and rule over Gog and Magog. He then declares the letter a forgery spread by Nestorian Christians. Elsewhere (n126) he notes that the Great Wall of China was called by Arabs the Bank of Gog and Magog.
p.q: But 'tis not difficult to discover that this Letter is a Counterfeit, and that it was not writ by Ounghcan. The Nestorians who in that Country were very numerous, having established themselves there in the Year 757. by the means of the Missionaries of Moussoul and Basra, were the Authors of this Letter
p.s: François Pétis de la Croix (English translation, 1722)
p.c: The identification of Prester John with Ong Khan goes back to Marco Polo; the claim that Nestorians forged the letter is Pétis's own theory.

p.h: The rope trick at a Mongol governor's feast
p.g: At a banquet given by the emir Qurtay at El Khansa (Hangzhou), the Khan's jugglers performed. A ball on a strap was thrown up out of sight; a boy climbed the strap and vanished; the master followed with a knife and threw down the boy's limbs, then put them together and the boy stood up. Ibn Battuta says he was so shaken he had palpitations. The Muslim judge beside him swore it was all illusion.
p.q: he then threw the hand of the boy upon the ground, then his foot ; then his other hand, then his other foot ; then his body, then his head. He then came down, panting for breath, and his clothes stained with blood. … The juggler then took the limbs of the boy and applied them one to another
p.s: Ibn Battuta (translated by Samuel Lee, 1829)
p.c: He says he witnessed it; a judge present called it trickery. Some scholars doubt how much of the China section is first-hand.

p.h: Gog and Magog, a span and a half tall
p.g: Sallam asked the guards at the gate whether they had ever seen one of Gog and Magog. They said they had once glimpsed several on top of the mountain before a violent wind blew them back, and at that distance they looked no more than a span and a half tall. On the same page he describes the wall's striped look, yellow copper and black iron in alternate layers.
p.q: Nous demandâmes aux gardiens de la porte s'ils avaient jamais vu un individu de la race de Gog et Magog; ils nous racontèrent qu'ils en avaient aperçu, un jour, plusieurs au-dessus de la montagne, mais qu'un vent impétueux les avait rejetés de leur côté. Vus à cette distance, leur taille ne paraissait pas dépasser un empan et demi.
p.s: Sallam the Interpreter, as reported by Ibn Khurradadhbih (French translation by M. J. de Goeje, 1889)
p.t: We asked the guards of the gate whether they had ever seen one of the race of Gog and Magog; they told us that one day they had glimpsed several on top of the mountain, but a violent wind had thrown them back to their own side. Seen at that distance, they seemed no taller than a span and a half.
p.c: Hearsay from guards, told by Sallam; de Goeje's footnote discusses which side of the wall the wind blew them to.

p.h: Governors licensed the looting of tombs
p.g: Before the tsars took an interest, Strahlenberg says, the governors of Tara, Tomsk, Krasnoyarsk and other towns let townsmen go out in caravans to rob the steppe graves in return for a tenth of the gold and silver. The looters smashed the finds and shared the pieces out by weight. He owned only a broken fragment of a bell-metal mirror to show for it.
p.q: …the Governours of the Cities of Tara, Tomskoi, Crasnoyahr, … used to give Leave to the Inhabitants, to go in voluntary Caravans, to these Tombs, in Order to ransack them, on Condition that … the Governour should have an Allowance, generally the Tenths. These Caravans, … used, … to knock to Pieces these choice Antiquities, and give to each Person his Share, by Weight.
p.s: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (English translation, 1738)

p.h: The sky-stone that makes cold, rain and snow
p.g: Rowing up the Irtysh, Yermak's men came to the little town of Tashatkan, where, they were told, a stone had fallen from the sky, dark red in colour, and from it at times came cold, rain and snow. Yermak and his men marvelled at 'God's work'. Weather stones (the 'yada tash' of Turkic and Mongol lore) were believed to bring rain and snow.
p.q: И погребоша къ Ташатканскому городку; и въ томъ городкѣ спалъ камень съ небеси … видомъ багровъ, и отъ него де временемъ восходитъ стужа, дождь и снѣгъ. И о семъ Ермакъ съ товарыщи дивился Божію дѣянію.
p.s: Kungur (Brief Siberian) Chronicle, Remezov tradition, 1880 edition
p.t: And they rowed to the little town of Tashatkan; and in that town a stone fell from the sky … dark red in appearance, and from it, they say, at times there arises cold, rain and snow. And at this Yermak and his comrades marvelled at God's doing.
p.c: Hearsay reported with 'de' ('they say'); the size of the stone is missing in the manuscript.

p.h: A Tibetan lama loots the Song tombs and builds a pyramid of bones
p.g: Under Khubilai a Tibetan lama in favour with the Mongols dug up the tombs of the Song emperors near Shaoxing, reportedly finding much gold and jewels, and piled the bones with those of oxen and horses into a pyramid. The outraged local officials jailed him, but Mongol lords and court lamas got Khubilai to free him and return most of his treasure, which, Gaubil says, the Chinese never forgave.
p.q: Sa passion pour l'or & l'argent le porta jusqu'à déterrer les corps morts des Empereurs, & des Grands dont le tombeau étoit près de Chaohing. Il y trouva, dit-on, beaucoup d'or, d'argent, & de bijoux. De ces ossemens mêlés avec des os de bœuf, & de chevaux il fit une pyramide.
p.s: Antoine Gaubil, translating the Chinese annals
p.pe: Mongols (Yuan court of Khubilai); a Tibetan lama; Chinese
p.t: His passion for gold and silver drove him to dig up the dead bodies of the Emperors and great men whose tombs were near Shaoxing. He found there, it is said, much gold, silver and jewels. From these bones, mixed with the bones of oxen and horses, he made a pyramid.
p.c: The Chinese histories were hostile to the lamas and to this episode; 'dit-on' marks the treasure as report.

p.h: 360 giant bronze gods, one for each day, carried off as trophies
p.g: Brought before the Tartar king, Pinto describes a square courtyard lined with four rows of bronze statues of men 'like savages' with maces and crowns, gilded, 27 palms high, with frizzy hair 'like Kaffirs'. The Tartars told them these were the 360 gods who made the days of the year, taken from a great temple in a Chinese city 'to triumph over them' and show the world he had captured China's gods.
p.q: no qual estauão quatro fileyras de estatuas de bronzo em figura de homens a modo de saluagens com maças, & coroas do mesmo, porem tudo cozido em ouro, os quais idolos, ou gigantes, ou o que quer q eraõ, tinhão daltura vinte & sete palmos, & seys de largo nos peytos … & pregũtando nòs aos Tartaros pela significação daquellas figuras, nos disseraõ que eraõ os trezẽtos & sessenta deoses
p.s: Fernão Mendes Pinto (Peregrinaçam, Lisbon 1614)
p.t: in which there were four rows of bronze statues in the form of men like savages, with maces and crowns of the same, but all gilded, which idols, or giants, or whatever they were, were twenty-seven palms high and six wide at the chest ... and when we asked the Tartars the meaning of those figures, they told us they were the three hundred and sixty gods
p.c: Pinto's Tartar episodes are widely regarded as fictional or built from hearsay; treat as claimed travel.
