p.h: Rumour: the Tartars will pile up a mountain to overtop the walls
p.g: With the Tartars on the coast, Thomas says the people of Split started 'empty rumours'. Some said the Tartars were building huge siege machines to throw the towns down; others that they were heaping up earth and stones like a mountain, so they could stand higher than the cities and take them easily. Thomas himself calls these rumours vain and baseless: a record of fear, not of what happened.
p.q: Coeperunt autem vanos agitare rumores, confingentes opiniones vanas, & inanes. Dicebant alii quod ingentes machinas, & plurima instrumenta bellica Tartari fabricarent, quibus Civitates has deiicere conabantur; asserebant alii, quod ad montis instar terrae, ac lapidum congeriem acervabant, & sic Civitatibus supereminentes, facile eas esse capturos.
p.s: Thomas, archdeacon of Split, Historia Salonitana, in the first edition by Ivan Lučić (Lucius), Amsterdam 1666
p.pe: Tartars as imagined by frightened citizens
p.t: They began to spread empty rumours, inventing vain and idle opinions. Some said that the Tartars were building huge machines and many instruments of war with which they were trying to throw down these cities; others asserted that they were heaping up a pile of earth and stones like a mountain, and so, rising above the cities, would easily capture them.
p.c: Thomas reports these as rumours he did not believe.

p.h: Bones of those who hid from a Tartar invader
p.g: In the cave monastery at Kiev, after oil-weeping skulls and a supposed relic of the Holy Innocents, the monks showed Alexander walled-up cells, fitted with glass panes, holding the bones of a thousand priests and townspeople. They were said to have hidden from a Tartar invader and been suffocated in their refuge.
p.q: In cells which were built up, with a thick piece of glass in the wall, were the bones of one thousand of the unfortunate priests and people of Kiev, who thought to conceal themselves from a Tartar invader, but who were inhumanly suffocated in their sanctuary.
p.s: James Edward Alexander (1830)
p.c: He saw the bones; the story of how they died is the monks' tradition, told alongside other relics he plainly doubted.

p.h: Inscribed Cuman tombstones in a Moravian church? The editor doubts it
p.g: Kuun quotes the Czech Jesuit Bohuslav Balbin, who said that near Ivancice and the Oslavany convent there was a church whose floor was paved almost entirely with Cuman tombs and stones inscribed in their letters, 'as I saw myself'. Kuun says plainly that he hardly believes it. It is a good example of a striking claim reported and then doubted by the editor himself.
p.q: «Superest hodieque aliqua barbarorum memoria non procul Evanczicio et Oslovanensi Coenobio, insigne templum Christianorum, in quo plurima Cumanorum sepulchra et saxa litteris illorum incisa spectantur, quibus saxis totum fere Templi solum stratum est, ut ipse vidi.» Ceterum hanc Bohuslavi narrationem ego quidem vix veram esse putaverim.
p.s: Geza Kuun, Latin introduction to his edition of the Codex Cumanicus (Budapest 1880), quoting Bohuslav Balbin, Epitome historica rerum Bohemicarum (Prague 1677)
p.t: 'There survives even today some memory of the barbarians not far from Ivancice and the Oslavany convent: a notable Christian church in which very many tombs of the Cumans and stones carved with their letters are to be seen, with which stones almost the whole floor of the church is paved, as I saw myself.' For my part I would hardly think this story of Bohuslav's true.
p.c: Balbin claims to have seen the stones; Kuun doubts it, and no such Cuman inscriptions are known.
p.n: Checked against the page image.

p.h: A total eclipse on the Kerulun
p.g: At noon on 23 May 1221, on the south bank of the Kerulun, the sun went dark enough for the stars to show. Bretschneider notes that the astronomer Alexander Wylie calculated a solar eclipse on exactly that day and that Chinese astronomical annals record it on the same date, 'a stamp of authenticity to the whole narrative'. In Samarkand that winter a local astronomer told Changchun it had reached six-tenths there, and the sage concluded that the same eclipse looks different from place to place (p.79).
p.q: On the 1st of the fifth month (May 23), at noon, an eclipse of the sun happened, while we were on the southern bank of the river. It was so dark that the stars could be seen, but soon it brightened up again.
p.s: Li Zhichang, disciple of Changchun, in the Si yu ki (translated by E. Bretschneider, 1888)

p.h: The 'Tartars' Road' over Mount Vlaško
p.g: Writing four centuries later, the Trogir historian Giovanni Lucio (Ivan Lučić) explains why King Béla did not trust the island next to Trogir: the Hungarians knew that Tartars swam their horses across huge rivers. He then records a local tradition that the Tartars, leaving, rode past in the king's sight along the slope of Mount Vlaško, and that the road there had been called 'the Tartars' road' ever since, just as a nearby rock is still called the King's Rock.
p.q: sapendo gl'Ongari, che li Tartari erano soliti passare con Caualli à nuoto grossissimi fiumi, dubitassero, che passassero anco nell'Isola Bua … i quali nell'andar via passarono à vista sua sopra la costa del monte Vlasco, hauendo lasciato con tal occasione il nome alla strada, che d'indi in qua vien detta strada de Tartari
p.s: Giovanni Lucio (Ivan Lučić), Memorie istoriche di Tragurio ora detto Traù (Venice, 1674)
p.pe: Mongol army of Kadan (in local tradition)
p.t: the Hungarians, knowing that the Tartars were accustomed to cross very large rivers by swimming with their horses, feared that they would cross to the island of Bua as well … who, as they went away, passed in his sight along the slope of Mount Vlasko, having on that occasion left their name to the road, which from then on has been called the Tartars' road
p.c: A place-name tradition recorded in 1674, not a medieval report.

p.h: The khan's statue in Moscow
p.g: Olearius retells the great Crimean raid of 1521: the khan besieged Moscow and forced the Grand Duke to sign himself a tributary. To prove it, the story goes, the khan set up a statue of himself in Moscow before which the Grand Duke had to bow to the ground each time he paid tribute; when the charter was later recovered, the Muscovites smashed the statue.
p.q: Mendligeri, to make it appear he was Sovereign Lord of Moscou, caused a Statue of his to be erected in the heart of the City, and would needs oblige the Great Duke, to express his subjection, to smite the ground with his head, before that Statue, as often as he paid Tribute
p.s: Adam Olearius (English translation by John Davies, 1669)
p.c: History retold from older books a century after the event; the khan's name is garbled and the statue detail is not confirmed.

p.h: Dog-headed men and people who live on smells
p.g: Benedict the Pole's short report lists the peoples beside the friars' route: Mordvins, Bashkirs, and then the Cynocephali with dogs' heads and the Parossites who cannot chew and live on the smell of food. He also notes the rich city of Ornarum taken by the Tartars with floods of water. Rockhill's note traces the monsters to Pliny and Solinus.
p.q: then the Cynocephales, who have dogs' heads ; and then the Parocitae, who have a small narrow mouth, who can masticate nothing, but who live on liquids and sustain themselves on the odours of meats and fruits.
p.s: Benedict the Pole (translated by W. W. Rockhill, 1900)
p.pe: Peoples on the northern edge of the Tartar lands
p.c: Book-learned legend placed on the map, not something Benedict saw.

p.h: The cathedral for Kazan and the blinded architect
p.g: St Basil's Cathedral on Red Square was built to celebrate Ivan the Terrible's capture of Kazan, the Tatar capital, in 1552. Haxthausen compares it to a rainbow-coloured dragon and repeats the tale that Ivan had the architect blinded so he could never build anything finer. He clearly marks it as hearsay ('is said to').
p.q: Ivan Vasilievitch ordered it to be erected in 1554 by an Italian, to commemorate the conquest of Kazan. After it was completed, he is said to have asked the architect whether he would undertake to make a plan for a still more singular building ; and when the latter in his vanity answered in the affirmative, he ordered his eyes to be put out
p.s: August von Haxthausen (translated by Robert Farie, 1856)
p.pe: Ivan IV; the conquered Kazan Tatars
p.c: Russian tradition names the builders as the Russian masters Barma and Postnik, not an Italian, and the blinding story is a legend with no contemporary evidence.
p.tg: st basil's kazan conquest legend ivan the terrible

p.h: Victims' blood smeared on faces and beards
p.g: The Aimaqs are quiet under their chiefs, Elphinstone says, but savage in war. He reports throwing prisoners off cliffs and shooting them with arrows, and one occasion, told him by a man who was there, when they drank their victims' blood. A footnote (garbled) compares this to the Mongols' treatment of prisoners.
p.q: I have authentic accounts of their throwing their prisoners from precipices and shooting them to death with arrows; and on an occasion at which a … with whom I have conversed assisted, they actually drank the warm blood of their victims, and rubbed it over their faces and beards.
p.s: Mountstuart Elphinstone (1815)
p.c: An atrocity story from a single informant, the kind of tale told about enemies; Elphinstone could not check it.

p.h: Russian treasure hunters in 'Tartarian tombs'
p.g: In a long footnote on tomb treasures, Clarke suggests that Turkish beliefs about gold hidden in ancient ruins may come from real finds in tombs. He adds that the Russians had found 'immense treasure' in 'Tartarian tombs', referring readers to his earlier book on the Tomb of Alexander (1805). The graves he means are the steppe kurgans, not necessarily Tatar at all.
p.q: The immense treasure found by the Russians in Tartarian tombs has been alluded to by the author, upon a former occasion.
p.s: Edward Daniel Clarke (footnote, 1816)
p.c: 'Tartarian tombs' is a loose label for any ancient burial mound on the steppe; the footnote does not say who was buried in them.

p.h: Moravian legends: bakers' 'hands, feet and ears' and Tartar arrows in the fields
p.g: Hormayr collects Moravian memories of the invasion: Stramberk, which alone held out, where bakers every Pentecost bake pastry 'hands, feet and ears' because the Mongols cut these from the dead and sent them to their khan in sacks; a field where tiny horseshoes, swords and very long foreign arrows are dug up; and the legend that Jaroslav of Sternberg killed a Mongol prince at Olomouc. These are local traditions, not medieval evidence.
p.q: Stramberg im Preraner-Kreise ist der Ort, der sich der Mongolen allein erwehrte, zu dessen ewigem Gedächtnisse der Bäcker alljährlich um Pfingsten, dem Tage der Erlösung, Hände, Füsse und Ohren bäckt, weil die Mongolen diese den Erschlagenen und wohl auch vielen Lebenden abzuschneiden
p.s: Joseph von Hormayr, editor's narrative (1842)
p.t: Stramberk in the Prerov district is the place that alone fended off the Mongols; in its eternal memory the baker every year at Pentecost, the day of deliverance, bakes hands, feet and ears, because the Mongols were wont to cut these off the slain, and probably many of the living
p.c: Local folklore reported by a nineteenth-century editor; the Mongol victory at Olomouc and Sternberg's slaying of a khan are later legends.

p.h: Gog and Magog on the Onon River
p.g: An anonymous description of the Mongols printed next in Weber sets out their lands, from Lake Khövsgöl east to the sand desert, to the Argun, and north-west to the rivers Onon and Sikoi, a country which, it says, has been said since ancient times to be inhabited by Gog and Magog. The same description goes on to the lamas, the Dalai Lama and whether he could be Prester John.
p.q: ferner biß an das Land Argun, und von dort wiederum Nord-west biß an den Fluß Onon und Sikoi, welches wie man von Alters hersaget, von Gog und Magog bewohnet wird.
p.s: Anonymous description of the Mongols, printed in Weber
p.t: further to the land of Argun, and from there again north-west to the rivers Onon and Sikoi, which, as has been said from ancient times, is inhabited by Gog and Magog.
p.tg: gog and magog onon mongolia legend

p.h: Yermak's armour: too heavy to swim in
p.g: In the arsenal at Tobolsk, which smelled more like a stable, Holman was shown the portrait and armour of the Cossack conqueror Yermak. He handled the chain shirt and found it so heavy that he understood why Yermak sank for good when, in his last battle, he stepped short of 'the Tartar king's galley'. He adds that he cannot say whether the story is fable or history.
p.q: the portrait and armour of Yermack; the former a miserable daub; the latter consisting chiefly of a chain shirt, so heavy that one cannot wonder at his going irretrievably to the bottom, when, in his last battle, he stepped short of the Tartar king's galley, and fell into water. Whether the history of this banditti leader be fabulous or not, it is at least interesting
p.s: James Holman (1825)
p.c: Holman handled the armour but could not judge the portrait; he calls it a daub on others' word. Whether the armour was really Yermak's is not tested.

p.h: The Great Khan sunk by enemy swimmers
p.g: Hayton's account of the death of the Great Khan Mongke: besieging an island in the sea of Cathay, he was sunk when the clever local people sent swimmers under his ship to bore holes in its hull until it filled and he drowned. The Kohler edition notes that a French manuscript garbled the Latin word for sponge-divers into 'spiongeorges'.
p.q: entra par mer au roiaume de Cathaï, e come il assegast une isle, laquele il voloit prendre par mer, la gent de cele terre, qui sont molt engignous, manderent homes noeors, e ceaus entrerent desouz le vaissel où Mango Can estoit
p.s: Hayton of Corycus, La Flor des estoires de la terre d'Orient (French text, 1307), ed. Ch. Kohler (1906)
p.t: he went by sea into the kingdom of Cathay, and as he was besieging an island which he wanted to take by sea, the people of that land, who are very ingenious, sent swimmers, and they went under the ship in which Mango Can was
p.c: Not true as told: Mongke died in 1259 during a land siege in Sichuan, reportedly of illness or a wound.

p.h: A Russian hut on the old Oxus nobody dares touch
p.g: The Turkmens told Muraviev that at the mouth of the dry river bed stood a hut built in the Russian style that no one would pull down out of superstitious fear, and whose builder nobody knew. Muraviev guessed it dated from Prince Bekovich's expedition sent by Peter the Great a century earlier.
p.q: Kiat informed me that the mouth of this old river bed, although choked with sand, is still distinguishable on the Caspian, and that by it there stands a hut (isba) constructed on the Russian plan. No one knows who the builder of this was, but the neighbouring Turcomans are restrained from demolishing it by superstitious dread.
p.s: Nikolai Muraviev (translated by W. S. A. Lockhart, 1871)
p.c: Muraviev did not see the hut; the link to Bekovich is his guess.
p.tg: uzboy oxus hut peter the great superstition

p.h: A stone that 'burns like a candle' in Witsen's Tartary book
p.g: Among the rocks of the district Schrenk lists a black, combustible shale soaked with bitumen from the Ukhta, known locally as Domanik, and in a footnote he notes that the naphtha springs there were already known to Witsen. He translates the passage from the first edition of Witsen's 'Noord en Oost Tartarye' (Amsterdam 1692): a shallow in the river drives a black oil to the surface, and a stone found there burns like a candle with a black light. Schrenk calls it the oldest report of the Domanik, a real oil-bearing rock, and goes on to later Russian accounts of an old timber enclosure built over the oil spring.
p.q: der Fluss Oegta [Uhta] ist eine Tagereise vom Petschorastrom entfernt; an diesem Flusse … findet sich darin eine Untiefe (drooghte die daer in is), die eine Fettigkeit aufs Wasser treibt, welche schwarze Naphta ist; welcher Stein dort auch gefunden wird, und brennt wie eine Kerze, ein schwarzes Licht von sich gebend.
p.s: Nicolaes Witsen (Noord en Oost Tartarye, 1692), quoted in German translation in a footnote by Alexander Gustav von Schrenk
p.t: the river Oegta [Ukhta] is a day's journey from the Pechora; on this river … there is a shallow in it (drooghte die daer in is) which drives a fattiness onto the water, which is black naphtha; which stone is also found there, and burns like a candle, giving off a black light.
p.c: The 'black light' is Witsen's wording, and his source for it is not given here. Schrenk confirms that the shale exists and burns, but not Witsen's exact description.
p.tg: witsen naphtha oil shale pechora tartary label

p.h: The officer boiled alive by the Tartar women
p.g: After Abaqa's army turned tail before the Mamluks in Syria, Riccoldo says, a great Tartar baron was caught plotting revolt. When the khan wanted to execute him, the Tartar ladies asked for him instead, boiled him alive and fed him in tiny pieces to the whole army as a warning.
p.q: obstiterunt domine et mulieres Tartarorum, petentes eum sibi dari. Quo accepto coxerunt eum viuum, et dederunt eum comedere incisum per partes minimas toti exercitui in exemplum aliorum.
p.s: Riccoldo of Monte Croce, Liber peregrinationis, ed. J. C. M. Laurent (Leipzig, 1873)
p.t: the ladies and women of the Tartars opposed it, asking that he be given to them. When he was handed over they cooked him alive and gave him, cut into the smallest pieces, to the whole army to eat, as an example to others.
p.c: A lurid atrocity story Riccoldo did not witness; treat as rumour.

p.h: Mice that wander 'like the Tatars'
p.g: Describing Kamchatka's root voles, Steller says the strangest thing about them is that they roam like Tatars, leaving the whole peninsula in great herds at certain times and staying away for years. He adds that they store food in cleaned larders, and that in spring dead mice are found with aconite root in their mouths, as if they had ended their lives in famine. The comparison shows 'Tatar' had become a byword for any wandering horde.
p.q: Das Seltsamste bey denen kamtschatzkischen Mäusen ist, daß sie nach Art derer Tataren herum wandern, und sich alle auf einmal heerweise zu gewissen Zeiten aus ganz Kamtschatka retiriren, einige Jahre wegbleiben
p.s: Georg Wilhelm Steller (ed. J. B. Scherer, 1774)
p.t: The strangest thing about the Kamchatka mice is that they wander about in the manner of the Tatars, and all at once, in whole herds, withdraw at certain times from all of Kamchatka and stay away for some years
p.c: The vole migrations are real; the idea that mice kill themselves with aconite is Steller's (or local) interpretation.

p.h: A carter's boast exposes a Tartar plot
p.g: Alexander heard from a civilian that in 1828 the Crimean Tatars were ready to revolt, stirred up, he guessed, by the Turks. A Karaite Jewish merchant of Bakhchysarai grew suspicious when his Tatar carter refused well-paid work, followed him home and overheard him telling his mother to wait until the Russians lost at Anapa. The man was arrested and confessed to a plot, spies were set to work and the leaders punished.
p.q: Russians are defeated before Anapa, and you'll see that we will be masters of the Crimea again. I have cast an eye at the Karaémee's house and garden; his tribe, as well as the Muscovites, will ere long not possess a foot of the country." On this the Tartar was taken up, and he confessed that there was a plot on foot to rise against the Russians
p.s: Words attributed to a Crimean Tatar carter, in a story Alexander heard from a civilian (1830)
p.c: Secondhand anecdote from the Russian side; the 'confession' may have been forced. On the previous page Alexander says he himself saw no cause for Tatar complaint.

p.h: The end-of-time peoples of Pseudo-Methodius
p.g: Straight after naming the Tatars, the chronicler quotes the prophecy he thinks explains them: peoples driven into the desert by Gideon would come out at the end of time and conquer everything from the east to the Euphrates and from the Tigris to the Black Sea, except Ethiopia. He hedges at once: 'God alone knows who they are.' This is the same book legend that western writers linked to Gog and Magog.
p.q: тако бо Меѳодій рече: яко къ скончанью временъ явитися тѣмъ, яже загна Гедеонъ, и поплѣнять всю землю отъ встока до Ефранта и отъ Тигръ до Понетьскаго моря, кромѣ Еѳіопья.
p.s: Laurentian Chronicle, citing the Revelation of Pseudo-Methodius, PSRL vol. 1 (1846)
p.pe: Tatars (Mongols), read as an apocalyptic nation
p.t: for thus Methodius said: that toward the end of time those whom Gideon drove out will appear, and they will capture all the land from the east to the Euphrates, and from the Tigris to the Pontic Sea, except Ethiopia.
p.c: A prophecy the chronicler read in a book, offered as one guess among several.

p.h: Timur's archers could not hit the giant Buddhas
p.g: At Bamiyan, Mohan Lal repeats the local story that Timur, returning from India, ordered his best archers to shoot down the colossal statues, but that not one arrow struck them. He had just recounted that Hindus credited the statues to the five Pandava brothers of the Mahabharata; Muslims linked them with the pre-Islamic idols Lat and Manat.
p.q: Being tempted by his religion, he ordered his expert archers to discharge their arrows against the images, which he wished to level to the ground ; but none of the arrows struck them, the cause of which I know not.
p.s: Mohan Lal (1846 edition)
p.c: Tradition, not history; the statues were in fact Buddhist, carved around the sixth century AD.

p.h: A khan's dome for a beloved Christian wife
p.g: From her window Craven saw a domed building and was told a khan built it as the tomb of a Christian wife he loved so much he could not be consoled, placing it where he could always see it. It is the story later attached to the Dilara Bikeç mausoleum. A footnote adds ruined baths and summer houses near the town; she went into one round bath lined with white marble, with niches for bathers.
p.q: I saw from the windows a kind of dome which raised my curiosity, and I am told it is a monument built to the memory of a Christian wife, which the Khan loved so tenderly that he was inconsolable for her loss
p.s: Elizabeth Craven (letters published London, 1789)
p.c: A romantic local story told to her; the source does not name the khan or the wife.

p.h: A golden tree with jewel fruit inside a tent
p.g: At a feast given by Timur's chief wife, the envoys were shown a tent containing a golden oak as tall as a man, with a trunk as thick as a leg, fruit of rubies, emeralds, turquoises, sapphires and pearls, and enamelled golden birds pecking at it. It echoes the silver tree Rubruck saw at Karakorum (W043), and Rockhill's note to Rubruck mentions Clavijo's tree.
p.q: there was a golden tree, made to resemble an oak ; with the trunk as big as a man's leg, from which many branches spread out in all directions, with leaves like those of an oak ; and it was as high as a man … The fruit of this tree consisted of rubies, emeralds, turquoises, sapphires, and wonderfully large pearls
p.s: Ruy González de Clavijo (translated by Clements R. Markham, 1859)
p.pe: Timur's chief wife Cano (Saray Mulk Khanum) and her court
p.tg: golden tree jewels tent court marvel

p.h: Cut in half for stealing a pail of milk
p.g: A Tartar ambassador returning from Cathay lodged in Barbaro's house at Tana. His servant told 'wonders' of Chinese justice: a man who drank a widow's milk in the market was seized and cut in two on the spot. Barbaro passes it on as the ambassador's report, not something he saw.
p.q: being on a daye in Madian, which signifieth the markett place, they did see a woman carieng a payle of mylke on her heade, to whom one came that tooke it from her : and beginneng to drynke, she beganne to crye out … Wherevpon, he was incontinently taken, and with a swearde cutt in sonder by the myddest
p.s: Giosafat Barbaro, reporting a Tartar ambassador's servants (Tudor translation by William Thomas)
p.pe: Chinese of Cathay, as described by a Tartar ambassador's servants
p.c: A traveller's tale told at second hand about Ming China.

p.h: A giant's grave and a stone table on the Don
p.g: On the upper Don the book lists a 'Volotova mogila', a giant's grave (volot is the old Russian word for a giant), at the mouth of the Mecha, and further down the 'Don beseda' (Don meeting-place), 'a stone table and stone vessels'. Nearby were the Tatar fords into Rus. These folk names for kurgans and rocks sit side by side with military route data.
p.q: а устьѣ рѣки Мечи съ вышія страны Волотова могила. … А ниже устья Сосны, на Дону, Донская бесѣда, каменной столъ и каменныя суды.
p.s: Book of the Great Map, first edition 'Drevniaia rossiiskaia idrografiia' (1773)
p.pe: Unnamed (folk landmarks on the Tatar frontier)
p.t: and at the mouth of the river Mecha, on the upper side, is the Giant's Grave. … And below the mouth of the Sosna, on the Don, is the Don Meeting-place, a stone table and stone vessels.
p.c: The 1838 edition reads 'Bolotova' (marsh) where the 1773 edition reads 'Volotova' (giant's).
p.tg: giant's grave kurgan stone table folklore don

p.h: The wonder-working magicians of Tartar times
p.g: Discussing Chinese divination, Semedo says some are said to keep familiar spirits, but he never saw any. In the time of the Tartar, he adds, there were many deeply sunk in such arts, and according to Marco Polo they worked marvels; today nothing of the kind is clearly known. He is sceptical and leans on Marco Polo for the Mongol period.
p.q: Dizese, que algunos tienen Familiares, i q̃ los consultan. Destos no vi. Antiguamente en tiempo del Tartaro huvo muchos, i muy empantanados en esto: i, segun Marco Veneto, hazian maravillas. Oy no sè que aya cosa alguna destas con claridad.
p.s: Álvaro Semedo, S.J. (Spanish edition by Manuel de Faria e Sousa, Madrid 1642)
p.pe: Mongol (Yuan) era magicians, as recalled by Semedo
p.t: It is said that some have familiar spirits and consult them. Of these I saw none. Anciently, in the time of the Tartar, there were many, and very deeply sunk in this; and, according to Marco Polo, they worked marvels. Today I do not know that there is any such thing clearly.
p.c: Second hand from Marco Polo; Semedo says he saw none.
p.n: OCR normalized against the page image; long s normalized, abbreviation marks (q̃, õ, ẽ) kept as printed.
p.tg: sorcery familiar spirits marco polo yuan divination

p.h: Goblins of the Altai
p.g: As the party headed for the Altai, one of Chen-hai's servants said these mountains were notorious for goblins and that one had pulled him by the hair, and Chen-hai added that a Naiman khan passing through had been bewitched and forced to offer the goblin a sacrifice. Changchun said nothing. Crossing the desert beyond, the escort rubbed blood on their horses' heads against goblins, and the sage smiled that goblins flee from a good man (p.64); earlier the diarist had seen traces of sacrifices to mountain spirits on a peak, and many grave mounds below (p.58).
p.q: One of the servants of Chen-hai reported that these mountains had a bad fame for their goblins, and that once a goblin pulled him by the hair. Chen-hai narrated further, that once it occurred also to the Khan of the Naiman … to be charmed by a goblin, and that he was obliged to offer a sacrifice to him. The master did not make any remark on these tales.
p.s: Li Zhichang, disciple of Changchun, in the Si yu ki (translated by E. Bretschneider, 1888)
p.c: Hearsay told to the diarist, reported without comment, as his master received it.

p.h: Mass weddings by lot 'toward Tartary'
p.g: Mendoza passes on a story that in the provinces toward Tartary, and in Tartary itself, governors set an age by which men and women must either enter religion or marry. At the appointed time all who are to marry gather in a designated city, where twelve elders record their names and wealth; if there are more men than women, they draw lots, and the surplus wait until next year. He introduces it with 'they say'.
p.q: Dizen que en las Prouincias hazia la Tartaria, y en la mesma Tartaria, se acostumbra vna cierta manera de casar muy estraña, y es que los Virreyes, o Gouernadores tienen señalado tiempo, assi a los hombres como a las mugeres paraque hasta llegar a tal edad tengan obligacion, o de meterse en Religion, o de casarse.
p.s: Juan González de Mendoza (Historia del gran Reyno de la China, Rome 1585)
p.pe: Peoples of the northern provinces and 'Tartary itself'
p.t: They say that in the provinces toward Tartary, and in Tartary itself, a certain very strange manner of marrying is customary, which is that the viceroys or governors have set a time for both men and women, so that on reaching a certain age they are obliged either to enter religion or to marry.
p.c: Hearsay introduced with 'they say'; the story echoes older European tales (such as Herodotus's Babylonian bride market) and has no clear Asian source.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image; long s normalized.

p.h: The 'Golden Hill' of Kerch
p.g: In the Kerch museum of ancient Greek finds, Jesse reports a Tatar tradition that centuries earlier about forty poods (some 1,440 pounds) of gold had been taken from one of the nearby burial mounds, which they therefore called the Golden Hill. He calls the story 'no doubt fabulous'.
p.q: The Tartars have a tradition, that upwards of forty pouds, nearly one thousand four hundred and forty pounds English, of this metal, in ornaments and coin, were, several hundred years ago, taken from one of the tumuli in the neighbourhood; and they call it in consequence the Golden Hill. This is, no doubt, fabulous
p.s: Captain William Jesse
p.c: The mounds were ancient Greek and Bosporan burials, not Tatar; the tradition is about finding treasure, not building.

p.h: Amazons beyond Samarkand, subject to Timur
p.g: Clavijo repeats what he heard at Samarkand: fifteen days toward China lived a land of women who met men once a year, kept their daughters and sent their sons to the fathers. He adds that they were Greek Christians, once subjects of the emperor of Cathay, now of Timur, and descended from the Amazons of Troy. A classic legend attached to a real direction on the map.
p.q: These women are subject to Timour Beg ; they used to be under the emperor of Cathay, and they are Christians of the Greek Church. They are of the lineage of the Amazons who were at Troy, when it was destroyed by the Greeks.
p.s: Ruy González de Clavijo (translated by Clements R. Markham, 1859)
p.pe: A women's nation said to live toward China
p.c: Hearsay of a classical legend; no one in the party went there.

p.h: An editor moves Almaliq and Sarai to Japan
p.g: Faced with unfamiliar names, the Prague editor Gelasius Dobner trusted a Franciscan martyrology that placed the martyrs 'in Japan' and concluded that Almaliq and Sarai were Japanese islands, Sarai being 'Sayrock Xymo' (probably Kyushu, which Jesuit writers called 'Saicoku' or 'Ximo'). In fact Almaliq lay in the Ili valley of Central Asia and Sarai on the lower Volga. By the eighteenth century the geography of the medieval Tartar empires had become hazy even for scholars.
p.q: Et cum Martyrologium S. Francisci Seraphici dicat eos passos in Japonia, verosimillime Armalec una ex insulis fuit Japonie, quemadmodum mox supra nominata Saray verosimillime est hodierna insula Sayrock Xymo una inter tres precipuas Japonie insulas in Oceano orientali.
p.s: Gelasius Dobner, editor (footnote, 1768)
p.pe: Editor's note on the Tartar cities of Almaliq and Sarai
p.t: And since the Martyrology of Saint Francis says they suffered in Japan, Almaliq was most probably one of the islands of Japan, just as Sarai, named just above, is most probably the present-day island of Sayrock Xymo, one of the three chief islands of Japan in the eastern Ocean.
p.c: The editor's error, not Marignolli's.

p.h: Solomon's rock at Osh
p.g: From informants Meyendorff heard of Takht-i-Suleiman, the rock above Osh, where tradition said Solomon had sacrificed a camel and a stone still showed the blood. Sick people lay on a flat stone there hoping to be cured. He treats the story as superstition and notes that reports of ruins there were disputed.
p.q: Tradition states that Solomon sacrificed a camel on this spot; where the blood is shewn on a stone still perfectly red. It is, however, particularly frequented by people suffering rheumatic or other pain ; who are said to be cured by extending themselves on a flat stone near the building.
p.s: Georg von Meyendorff (translated by William Monteith, 1840)
p.c: A local legend reported at second hand.

p.h: A wall up a cliff no Tartar horse could climb
p.g: Careri found the Wall one of the greatest and 'most senseless' works ever made. What made him laugh was seeing it carried to the top of a precipitous mountain where 'the Tartar cavalry' could never have climbed; and if the Chinese thought raiders could scramble up the cliffs, it was foolish to think so low a wall would stop them. A rare eyewitness who was unimpressed.
p.q: Ma quel, che affatto mi sembrò da ridere, fu a vedere il muro tratto ancor fino alle cime d'un'altissimo, e straripevol monte, ove appena vi sarebbero appiccati i picchi: non che montar vi potesse la cavalleria Tartara per entrar nel paese.
p.s: Giovanni Francesco Gemelli Careri (Giro del Mondo, part IV, Naples 1700)
p.t: But what struck me as altogether laughable was to see the wall carried even to the peaks of a very high and precipitous mountain, where hardly even woodpeckers could cling, let alone the Tartar cavalry climb up to enter the country.
p.c: His own opinion of the defensive logic.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image; long s normalized.

p.h: Greek soldiers' descendants in 'Chinese Tartary'
p.g: Listing people who claimed descent from Alexander the Great, Burnes adds that Tungan soldiers from western China garrisoning Yarkand claimed descent from Alexander's soldiers. He notes the claimants in the Oxus hills were Tajiks, who lived there 'before it was overrun by Toorkee or Tartar tribes', and doubts the claims against the historical record.
p.q: the soldiers of the Toonganee tribe, who are sent from the western provinces of Chinese Tartary, and garrison Yarkund and the neighbouring cities, claim also a Grecian origin. They, however, seek, with greater modesty, a descent from the soldiers of Alexander's army
p.s: Alexander Burnes (1834)
p.c: Reported claims that Burnes himself questions.

p.h: A khan who 'received the edict kneeling'
p.g: Tulishen writes that Ayuki Khan knelt to receive the Chinese emperor's letter and turned north to wish him well. The translator Staunton adds a sharp footnote: it is very unlikely that an independent prince would humble himself so in his own court; the Chinese claim to rule the whole world simply required every letter from the emperor to be described as received on bended knee.
p.q: Nothing certainly can be more improbable than that an independent prince, in the midst of his own court, should have voluntarily subjected himself to such a humiliation; … but it seems that the assumed attribute of universal sovereignty, which occasions every communication from the Emperor of China to claim the authority of an Edict, also requires that such an edict should be supposed to have been received
p.s: George Thomas Staunton (translator's footnote)
p.c: The translator doubts the author's official version of events.

p.h: Du Halde's 'lying miracle' of the earthquake
p.g: Davis praises the Jesuit astronomer Adam Schall, who kept his post after the Tartars took the empire, but he mocks Du Halde for padding the story with miracles. He quotes Du Halde's claim that when the regents tried to confirm Schall's death sentence, an earthquake scattered them every time, until a general pardon was granted. Davis calls this one of the 'lying miracles' with which Du Halde 'has not blushed to disfigure his work'.
p.q: this sentence was carried to the Princes of the blood and to the regent for confirmation; but, as often as they attempted to read it, a dreadful earth quake dispersed the assembly. The consternation was so great, that they granted a general pardon;
p.s: Jean-Baptiste Du Halde, quoted (and rejected) by John Francis Davis
p.pe: Manchu regents and the Jesuit Adam Schall
p.c: Davis quotes it only to dismiss it. (A real earthquake did strike Beijing in 1665 during Schall's trial.)
p.tg: jesuits adam schall miracle earthquake du halde

p.h: A shaman's night séance and a demon on the roof
p.g: Rubruck describes how Mongol diviners answered the Khan's questions: meat is laid in the middle of the house at night, the shaman mutters charms, beats a drum on the ground, raves and is tied up, and the 'devil' comes in the dark to eat and give answers. He then repeats a story from the goldsmith Guillaume about a hidden Hungarian who heard the demon shrieking on the roof, unable to enter because a Christian was present.
p.q: celuy qui fait l'inuocation commence à murmurer ses charmes, & tenant vn tabourin en la main, le frappe fort contre terre, & se demene & agite en sorte qu'il deuient comme hors de soy, & commence à resver, puis il se fait lier bien serré; lors le diable vient durant l'obscurité de la nuict, & luy donne à manger de ces chairs
p.s: William of Rubruck (French translation by Pierre Bergeron, 1634)
p.t: the one who performs the invocation begins to mutter his charms and, holding a drum in his hand, beats it hard against the ground, and throws himself about so that he becomes as if beside himself and begins to rave; then he has himself bound tight; then the devil comes in the darkness of the night and gives him some of the meat to eat
p.c: Rubruck did not attend such a séance; the roof-demon story comes secondhand from Master Guillaume, and he frames it all as devil-worship.

p.h: A steppe king lost in the snow, saved by a saint
p.g: In his note on the legend of Prester John, Ritter traces its roots to a real report: a letter to the Nestorian patriarch in Baghdad saying that the king of the Kerait, lost while hunting in snowy mountains, was rescued by a saint who demanded he believe in Christ. The king then asked visiting Christian merchants about baptism, and asked how to keep the fasts when his people ate only meat and milk; the patriarch allowed milk. Ritter thinks this tale, found in Syriac and Arabic authors (via Bar Hebraeus and Assemani), was one seed of the later fantasy of a Christian priest-king in Asia.
p.q: der König des Volks der Cherit (i.e. Kerait) der im Innern der Turkländer gegen Nord-Osten wohne, habe sich auf der Jagd im wilden Schnee-Gebirge so verirrt gehabt, daß nur ein Sanctus seinen Weg ihn habe zurückführen und retten können. Dieser sey ihm erschienen mit den Worten: „Willst du an Jesum Christum glauben, so helfe ich dir aus der Noth.“
p.s: Carl Ritter (paraphrasing a letter reported by Bar Hebraeus and other Syriac authors)
p.pe: Kerait (a steppe people Ritter counts among the eastern Turks and 'Tartari')
p.t: the king of the people of the Cherit (that is, Kerait), who lived in the interior of the Turk lands toward the north-east, had lost his way so badly while hunting in the wild snow mountains that only a saint could lead him back and save him. The saint appeared to him with the words: 'If you will believe in Jesus Christ, I will help you out of your distress.'
p.c: Ritter trusts the date (1007) because Syriac and Arabic authors agree, but the miracle comes from the convert's own reported letter.
p.tg: prester john kerait nestorians miracle mare's milk

p.h: Turning over corpses for buried flour
p.g: After the Tartars stormed the island refuge where he had sheltered, Roger lived as a fugitive in the woods. Hunger drove him to creep back onto the island at night and turn over the bodies of the dead in search of buried flour and meat. He hid in caves, dug holes or crept into hollow trees, while (he says on the next page) the Tartars combed the thickets like dogs hunting hares and boars.
p.q: Ita quod necessitate famis et sitis me acrius perurgente de nocte compellebar intrare insulam, et corpora euertere mortuorum, ut sepultam farinam et carnes ad esum mihi, vel aliud comestibile inuenirem … Oportebat me inuenire cauernas, vel foveas facere, vel arbores quaerere perforatas in quas me possem recipere
p.s: Master Roger (Rogerius), Carmen miserabile, in the 1885 Budapest edition (Chronica minora)
p.pl: Hungary (a fortified island in the Körös region)
p.t: So, with hunger and thirst pressing me hard, I was forced at night to go onto the island and turn over the bodies of the dead, to find buried flour and meat to eat, or anything else edible … I had to find caves, or dig pits, or look for hollow trees in which I could hide

p.h: A horse stuffed with straw and worshipped
p.g: Barbaro says the northern lands of Zagatai and Moxia were inhabited by Tartars who were mostly idolaters, then describes a Moxii rite: a horse staked down and shot with arrows, eaten, its hide stuffed with straw and propped up as if alive. On the next page he says it was set on a scaffold in a tree and worshipped, with furs hung as offerings, and that other idolater Tartars worship images carried on their carts.
p.q: At a certein tyme of the yere they vse to take a horse : which they laie alonge on the plaine. … Than they stufe the hyde so full of strawe, that it seemeth hole again ; and in every of his legges putt a pece of woodde ; and so sett him afoote againe, as though he were on lyve.
p.s: Giosafat Barbaro (Tudor translation by William Thomas, c. 1550)
p.pe: The Moxii (Moksha Mordvins), grouped by Barbaro with northern 'idolater' Tartars
p.c: The Moksha are a Finnic people, not Tatars; Barbaro says he 'learned' this, not that he saw it.

p.h: 'Lama' means a cross, and the Manchus wear crosses
p.g: To support his idea that the peoples of Tartary were once Christian, Avril claims that 'lama' means 'cross' in the Tartar language, and that the Manchus who conquered China in 1644 always wore crosses they called lamas. It is a striking example of a missionary reading his hopes into reports.
p.q: he bears the Name of Lama, which in the Tartar Language signifies a Cross: And the Bogdoi who conquer'd China in 1644, and who are subject to the Dalae in all matters of Religion, wear always Crosses about 'em, which they call Lama's also
p.s: Philippe Avril (English translation, 1693)
p.c: 'Lama' is a Tibetan word for a teacher, not a cross; this is Avril's mistaken inference.

p.h: Prester John was a mishearing
p.g: Like Strahlenberg before him, Fischer explains the legend of Prester John as a European mistake: the first Europeans in Tibet and Mongolia misheard a title, their fancy shaped it into 'Prêtre Jean' or 'Juan', and so it spread through the world. They forgot that Tibetans and Mongols spoke neither French, Italian nor Portuguese, and were pleased to find what they hoped for; later came strange etymologies and fables of an Indian 'Johannes Presbyter'.
p.q: der name Pretre Jean oder Juan, ist von den erstern Europäern, die dorthin gekommen, unrecht gehöret, hernach von ihrer fantasei übel gebildet, und so weiter in die welt geschikket worden. Diesen guten leuten fiele nicht ein, daß die Tibetaner und Mogolen, unter denen sie sich befanden, weder französisch, noch italiänisch noch portugiesisch verstunden
p.s: Johann Eberhard Fischer (Sibirische Geschichte, introduction, 1768)
p.pe: Tibetans and Mongols; medieval European travellers
p.t: the name Prêtre Jean or Juan was wrongly heard by the first Europeans who came there, then badly shaped by their fancy, and so sent out into the world. It did not occur to these good people that the Tibetans and Mongols among whom they found themselves understood neither French, nor Italian, nor Portuguese
p.c: Fischer's explanation, following Strahlenberg; not a proven derivation.

p.h: The bride inside the Red Rock
p.g: Webster records a legend 'implicitly believed by the Tartars': a girl forced to marry against her will prayed to Allah to bury her alive inside the red rock of Keesil-tash, and at every full moon at midnight the rock opens and she walks out in her bridal clothes. The next page adds a Tatar's dry joke about why a Russian count failed to see her.
p.q: She besought Allah to hide her from the world, and to bury her alive in the centre of the Keesil-tash. This prayer was granted, and she was snatched away by an invisible hand. She is said to inhabit the rock, but at every full moon, at midnight, the rock, as it is declared, opens, and the lady walks forth in her
p.s: James Webster
p.c: Local legend as told to Webster; the sentence ends 'bridal garments' on the next page.

p.h: A man with four heads and twenty-four arms
p.g: On the walls behind the idols at Ablai-kit were paintings that baffled Gmelin. He says he has not the patience to describe them and refers the curious to alchemical pictures, as equally absurd. His examples: figures with several heads and many arms, one trampling a man's head, and a many-headed man embracing a woman.
p.q: Man siehet z. E. einen Mann mit 4 Köpfen und 24 Armen, einen andern mit 2 Köpfen und 8 Armen. Der erstere tritt mit einem seiner rechten Füße einem Menschen auf den Kopf und hat noch zween andere Menschen zu seinen Füßen liegen.
p.s: Johann Georg Gmelin (German original, Göttingen, 1751)
p.t: One sees, for example, a man with 4 heads and 24 arms, another with 2 heads and 8 arms. The first treads with one of his right feet on a man's head and has two more men lying at his feet.
p.c: Gmelin does not identify the figures; they match the many-armed deities of Tibetan Buddhist art. He knew them only from his men's report and the pieces they brought back.

p.h: The captain bound in raw cowhide
p.g: During the 1771 flight the Kalmyks captured a detachment under Captain Dudin, and, Bergmann says, Ubashi had the officer's head and hands bound in strips of fresh cowhide, which tightened as they dried. Bergmann heard this from one of Dudin's own Cossacks, a Persian by birth, who later escaped from Kalmyk and then Kazakh captivity and saw his officer two months after his capture, still bound and awaiting death. What became of Dudin was never known.
p.q: Einer seiner Kosaken, ein gebohrner Perser, … aus dessen eigenem Munde ich diesen Zug von Grausamkeit erfahren habe: sah seinen Rittmeister zwey Monate nach der Gefangenschaft wieder, mit den Streifen von Kuhhaut um Kopf und Hände, in dem schrecklichsten Zustande, alle Augenblicke seinen Tod erwartend, der ihn zu fliehen schien.
p.s: Benjamin Bergmann, from an eyewitness Cossack
p.pl: Kalmyk steppe, east of the Volga
p.pe: Torghut Kalmyks and a captured Russian officer
p.t: One of his Cossacks, a Persian by birth, from whose own mouth I learned of this act of cruelty, saw his captain again two months after his capture, with the strips of cowhide round his head and hands, in the most terrible state, expecting death at every moment, though death seemed to flee him.
p.c: A single informant's account of wartime cruelty, told decades later.

p.h: A sung city with walls of wood, stone and iron
p.g: Georgi wrote down a heroic tale the Tungus sang, whose hero names he judged to be Mongol. It begins with a prince living in a city with a triple wall, the outer of wood, the middle of stone and the inner of iron, yet dwelling in a yurt with a steel post for his horse. Later his daughter, turned into an eagle, finds a silver yurt with a golden roof on a hill with silver grass and lakes of milk. It shows how steppe epics imagined walled cities alongside tents.
p.q: In einem Reiche war der Fürst Dolodai, welcher 2000. Knechte hatte, und in einer Stadt mit einer dreyfachen Mauer, die äussere hölzern, die mittlere steinern und die innere eisern, wohnten. An der Thüre seiner Jurte stand eine Säule von Stahl, an welche er sein Prachtpferd band.
p.s: A Tungus sung tale, as written down by Georgi
p.pe: Tungus (Evenki) singers of a tale with Mongol heroes
p.t: In a kingdom lived Prince Dolodai, who had 2000 servants, and they lived in a city with a triple wall, the outer of wood, the middle of stone and the inner of iron. At the door of his yurt stood a pillar of steel, to which he tied his splendid horse.
p.c: A folk epic, not a description of a real place; Georgi thought the Tungus had taken it from the Mongols.
p.tg: epic legend city walls iron yurt

p.h: A Chaghatai prince makes wind and rain
p.g: In India, Babur notes calmly that the Chaghatai prince Tokhta Bugha Sultan 'performed some of his enchantments' in his boat, and a high wind rose and it began to rain. This is the steppe weather magic with a rain-stone (yada) that Erskine's introduction calls wholly of Tartar origin and traces to a legendary stone given by Noah to Japhet.
p.q: I sent for the Sultans into the boat ; Tokhteh Bugha Sultan performed some of his enchantments. A high wind having risen, it began to rain.
p.s: Babur (translated by John Leyden and William Erskine, 1826)
p.pe: Chaghatai Mongol princes in Babur's army
p.c: Babur records the rain following the rite without comment; the link to the rain-stone is Erskine's (introduction, p. xlvii, n58).
p.tg: rain magic yada stone sorcery weather

p.h: A unicorn's horn on the coast of Tartaria
p.g: Arguing for a sea route to China round the north of Asia, Jenkinson pointed to a unicorn's horn found on the 'coast of Tartaria', which he thought must have floated there from the east. Sir Humphrey Gilbert, reporting the debate, scoffs that the 'barbarous Tartarians' might not know a unicorn's horn at all, and that such a horn would not float. The editors note the many forms of the unicorn legend across Asia.
p.q: His second reason is, that there was an Vnicornes horne … found vpon the coast of Tartaria, which could not come (sayd … he) thither by any other meanes then with the tides
p.s: Sir Humphrey Gilbert, reporting Anthony Jenkinson's argument (ed. Morgan and Coote, 1886)
p.pe: 'Barbarous Tartarians' of the northern coast of Asia
p.c: Nobody here saw the horn; it may have been a walrus or narwhal tusk, but the source does not say.
p.n: OCR normalized; printed margin notes omitted.
p.tg: unicorn northeast passage arctic tartaria marvel

p.h: A rescued Tatar slave in a Venetian wine cellar
p.g: In a Rialto wine cellar Barbaro found two chained men who looked like Tartars, runaway slaves of the Catalans recaptured by the vintner. He had them freed by the magistrates and took them home. One turned out to be a servant of the khan's customs officer at Tana, who recognised Barbaro's Tana name, Jusuph, and fell to the ground.
p.q: I asked him what was his name. He answered, Chebechzi, which signifieth a bulter of meale. And whan I had well behelde him, I saied vnto him, doest thou knowe me ? He answered, no. But, as soone as I mentioned Tana and Jusuph (for so they called me there), he fell to thearthe, and wolde haue kissed my feete : saieng vnto me, thou hast saved my lief twies
p.s: Giosafat Barbaro (Tudor translation by William Thomas, c. 1550)

p.h: A high lama who ages with the moon
p.g: Bell reports what Mongols told him about their chief lama, the Kutuchtu at Urga. On the previous page he describes how a boy successor is 'found' by making him pick out his predecessor's belongings. Here he adds the popular belief that the Kutuchtu had lived fourteen generations and grew young and old again with each month.
p.q: The Mongalls relate, that their Kutuchtu has now lived fourteen generations, and renews his age every moon; for, at the new moon, he appears like a youth; when she is full, like a full-grown man; but, when near the change, he is an old man with grey hairs.
p.s: John Bell (Travels, 1763)
p.c: Popular belief reported second hand; Bell himself thinks it ridiculous.

p.h: The runaway slave who hid in Sarai for ten years
p.g: To show how vast Sarai was, Ibn Arabshah tells a story: a slave ran away from one of the city's notables, opened a shop in an out-of-the-way street and made his living there for about ten years, and in all that time his master never came across him or saw him.
p.q: حكي ان رجلا من اعيانها هرب له رقيق في مكان منحي عن الطريق وفتح له حانوتا يتسبب فيه ويحصل له قوتا واستمر ذلك الحين نحوا من عشر سنين لم يصادفه فيه مولاه ولا اجتمع به ولا رآه وذلك لعظمها وكثرة اممها
p.s: Ahmad ibn Arabshah (Arabic text, print catalogued 1842)
p.t: It is told that a slave of one of its notables ran away to a spot off the main road, opened a shop there, traded in it and earned his living; this went on for about ten years, and his master never came upon him there, nor met him, nor saw him, because of the city's size and the multitude of its peoples.
p.c: A 'they say' anecdote, told to make a point about size, not a checked fact.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of this print is garbled); vowel marks and the asterisk dividers of the rhymed prose omitted.

p.h: Gog and Magog beyond the mountains, fires in the night
p.g: This page is not by Nieuhof but from Athanasius Kircher's China Illustrata, bound into Ogilby's English volume. Kircher quotes an Arabic geographer on the cities of Gog and Magog beyond an unclimbable snowy mountain: people who climb it rarely return, and those who do report many fires at night. Kircher then fits this to the Great Cham's empire and Prester John.
p.q: On the other side of the Mountain are many Cities of Jagog and Magog. And it often happened, that the Inhabitants of this Region, out of a certain curiosity, ascend some part of it … but many never return … some that have return'd safe, relate, that in the Region on the other side of the Mountain in the night season, are many fires
p.s: an Arabic geographer as quoted by Athanasius Kircher (appendix in Ogilby's 1669 volume, not by Nieuhof)
p.pl: Central Asia (placed by Kircher near Cathay and Tangut)
p.pe: Gog and Magog, identified with the Great Cham's realm
p.c: Not part of Nieuhof's text; a learned legend passed through several books.
p.tg: gog and magog kircher legend prester john

p.h: A martyr's prophecy against the Tartars of Sarai
p.g: Marignolli names the Franciscans killed at Almaliq the year before he arrived and credits one of them, Pascal the Spaniard, with visions and prophecies: that the Tartars of Sarai on the Volga would be destroyed by a flood, that Almaliq would perish, and that the ruler would be killed three days after the martyrdom. He presents the dead friars as holy martyrs 'shining with miracles'.
p.q: frater Paschalis Hyspanus, qui fuit Propheta, & vidit celum apertum, & predixit sibi, & Sociis suis martirium, & Thartaros de Saray destruendos diluvio, Armalec perituram, propter ipsorum martirium, Imperatorem illum tercio die occidendum post ipsorum martirium
p.s: Giovanni de' Marignolli (Latin text ed. Gelasius Dobner, 1768)
p.pe: Tartars of Sarai (Golden Horde) and of Almaliq (Chagatai khanate)
p.t: Brother Pascal the Spaniard, who was a prophet, saw heaven opened and foretold martyrdom for himself and his companions, and that the Tartars of Sarai would be destroyed by a flood, that Almaliq would perish because of their martyrdom, and that that emperor would be killed on the third day after their martyrdom
p.c: Pious report: Marignolli arrived after the killings and repeats what the local friars remembered.

p.h: A shaman who seemed to fly
p.g: Riccoldo says the Tartars honour above all men certain 'boxitae' (bakhshis), priests of idols from India, wise and grave, who practise magic with the help of demons, show many marvels and foretell the future. One of their leaders was said to fly, but, Riccoldo reports, it was found that he only walked just above the ground without touching it and sat on nothing solid.
p.q: Nam et vnus maior inter eos dicebatur volare, sed secundum veritatem repertum est, quod non volauit, sed ambulabat iuxta terram et eam non tangebat, et quando videbatur sedere, nulla re solida sustentabatur.
p.s: Riccoldo of Monte Croce, Liber peregrinationis, ed. J. C. M. Laurent (Leipzig, 1864)
p.pe: Tartars and their 'baxitae' (Buddhist or shamanic priests)
p.t: For one of the greater among them was said to fly, but according to the truth it was found that he did not fly, but walked close to the ground without touching it, and when he seemed to sit he was held up by nothing solid.
p.c: Hearsay about a wonder, which Riccoldo half-debunks (not flying) and half-repeats (levitating).

p.h: Painted giants who guard the passes of Tartary
p.g: Describing officials' houses in Canton, Cruz notes huge gates painted with two giants holding staves. He saw four such figures in a temple, said to be portraits from life of men the king keeps to guard the weakest passes of Tartary, big-limbed and twelve or thirteen palms tall. What he saw were painted door gods; the frontier story is what he was told.
p.q: tẽ na frõtaria hũas portas muy grandes como portas de hũa cidade, com dous gigantes pintados cõ hũs bastões nas mãos: eu vi quatro em hũ pagode (que he tẽplo de idolos) tirados polo natural dalgũs q̃ dizẽ ter el Rey q̃ lhe guardã os passos
p.s: Gaspar da Cruz, O.P. (Tractado, Évora 1569)
p.pe: Door-guardian figures in Canton, said to portray the king's frontier guards
p.t: on the front they have some very large doors, like the gates of a city, with two giants painted on them holding staves in their hands. I saw four in a pagoda (which is a temple of idols), portrayed from life of some whom they say the King keeps to guard for him the passes [that are weakest in Tartary; they are very big-limbed, perhaps twelve or thirteen palms tall].
p.c: He saw paintings; the story that they depict real giant frontier guards is hearsay.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of this blackletter print is garbled); long s normalized, the Tironian sign for 'and' given as 'e', a few contractions (de, per, pro, terra) expanded, other abbreviation marks kept as printed; the sentence ends on the next page (n44): 'mais fracos da Tartaria, sam muy mẽbrudos, poderã ser de doze ou treze palmos dalto', given in brackets in the translation.
p.tg: giants door gods canton frontier guards paintings

p.h: A Ming emperor hanged with a bowstring
p.g: Martini says the Hongguang emperor, first ruler of the Southern Ming at Nanjing, was betrayed to the Tartars after less than a year on the throne, sent to Peking, and publicly hanged on the town walls with a bowstring, 'which kind of death the Tartars esteem most noble'.
p.q: This unfortunate Prince being thus betrayed before he had reigned full one year, was sent to Peking, and there upon the Town Walls was hanged publickly in a Bow string, which kind of death the Tartars esteem most noble.
p.s: Martino Martini (English translation, London 1654)
p.pe: Manchu Tartars and the Ming claimant Hongguang
p.c: Reported from a distance; other sources give different details of his death, which came in 1646.

p.h: A Kalmyk khan said to eat only from gold
p.g: Avril reports that the chief khan of the Kalmyks claimed descent from Tamerlane, forced Russians and Uzbeks to pay him tribute, dressed always in white and ate only from gold plate. On the next page he checks the rumour: a French officer in Moscow who had been in this khan's tent near Astrakhan, with 100,000 Tartars, confirmed his splendour but never saw gold or silver plate.
p.q: He is very Potent, and therefore forces the Muscovites and the Yousbecks to pay him a certain Tribute, or else he would be continually Harrassing their Countries. 'Tis also reported that he is very Magnificent, that he goes always clad in White, and never eats but serv'd in Gold Plate.
p.s: Philippe Avril (English translation, 1693)
p.c: Rumour, partly contradicted by the eyewitness Avril cites.

p.h: The mooncake massacre of 1368
p.g: Huc tells the Chinese tradition behind the Moon festival: in about 1368 the Chinese rose against the Mongol dynasty, passing the signal in letters hidden in the festival cakes, and killed the Mongol soldiers billeted in their homes. When the priests told this to a Mongol family, the old man wept and said a day of vengeance would come. The massacre story is a legend, not established history.
p.q: The signal was given by a letter concealed in the cakes which, as we have stated, are on that day, mutually interchanged throughout the country. The massacre was effected, and the Tartar army dispersed in the houses of the Chinese, utterly annihilated. This catastrophe put an end to the Mongol domination
p.s: Évariste Huc (translated by William Hazlitt, 1852)
p.c: A Chinese folk tradition that Huc repeats as history.

p.h: Headless statues and skull cups
p.g: Heikel found that all the carved stone figures at the first two monuments had lost their heads. He explains this by old Mongolian customs: enemies' heads were carried off as trophies, chiefs' skulls were made into drinking cups (the Irkutsk museum held one), and stones set round a grave stood for enemies killed. So attackers would naturally knock the heads off figures that stood for Turks. His explanation is a guess drawn from old accounts, not something he saw happen.
p.q: Celles-là comme toutes les autres statues trouvées auprès de ce 1er monument et du 2e, n'ont pas de tête, ce qui n'a rien d'étonnant pour ceux qui connaissent les anciennes moeurs des peuples de la Mongolie, chez lesquels on avait coutume d'emporter à de longues distances les têtes des ennemis en guise de trophées. On façonnait même en coupes les crânes des chefs tués à la guerre.
p.s: Axel Heikel, Inscriptions de l'Orkhon (Helsingfors 1892)
p.t: These, like all the other statues found near the first and second monuments, have no heads, which is not surprising to those who know the ancient customs of the peoples of Mongolia, among whom it was the practice to carry enemies' heads long distances as trophies. The skulls of chiefs killed in war were even made into cups.
p.c: The missing heads are observed; the explanation is Heikel's own guess from written sources.
p.n: Checked against the page image.

p.h: Rumour: the emperor himself called in the Mongols
p.g: Hormayr notes that German enthusiasm for the crusade against the Mongols was weakened by a slander spread by papal partisans: that Emperor Frederick II, who liked the company of Arabs, Jews and heretics, had himself summoned the Mongols. He also repeats the chronicle story of an old Englishman, expelled from the crusader army, captured serving the Tartars as interpreter and guide.
p.q: die von den Päpstlichen überall ausgestreute Verläumdung: der mit Arabern, Juden und Ketzern am liebsten verkehrende, ruchlose Kaiser Friedrich selber, habe die Mongolen herbeigerufen.
p.s: Joseph von Hormayr, editor's narrative (1842)
p.t: the slander spread everywhere by the papal party: that the wicked Emperor Frederick himself, who liked best to keep company with Arabs, Jews and heretics, had called in the Mongols.
p.c: Hormayr reports the rumour as propaganda; there is no evidence Frederick invited the Mongols.

p.h: Aley the shaman, father of twelve sons
p.g: The Yakut founding story continues with Aley, a runaway from the Buryats who became Omogai's overseer and was thought to have supernatural powers. He declared himself a shaman, prophesied that Omogai's daughter would bear no children, and chose the chief's adopted girl instead. After Omogai's death most of the tribe followed Aley, who is said to have had twelve sons; the eldest founded a named tribe.
p.q: He observed, that all his tribe esteemed Aley to adoration; for they supposed him to possess supernatural powers, and attributed his continual good fortune and success to the immediate influence of spirits. … Aley now avowed himself a Shaman, and assumed the powers of divination.
p.s: Martin Sauer (1802), relating Yakut tradition
p.c: Oral legend, not history.

p.h: Queen Suyumbike, the rain-making enchantress
p.g: During the siege, the Russian soldiers in the trenches suffered from constant heavy rain, and everyone blamed the magic of the Tatar queen Sumbyeka (Suyumbike), 'celebrated as an enchantress', and the city's sorcerers. Inside Kazan, people hid in cellars and caves dug in the courtyards, and the defenders shot at their own captured kinsmen tied to the Russian palisades rather than surrender.
p.q: The Russian warriors who were stationed in the trenches without tents, suffered much from the constant heavy rains; and this annoyance was universally ascribed to the arts of the Tatar queen Sumbyeka, who was celebrated as an enchantress, and to the subordinate kolduni, or sorcerers of the city.
p.s: Adolph Erman (translated by W. D. Cooley, 1848), following the Russian chronicles
p.c: A belief of the besiegers recorded in the chronicles. Historically, Suyumbike had already been sent to Moscow before the final siege.

p.h: A city driven out by tarantulas
p.g: A story said the people of the 'city' at Madzhary had been driven away by swarms of great tarantulas, which is why the stream is called Byvalla, from the Tartar 'by' (tarantula) and 'valla' (bad). Pallas says there is no basis for it: despite searching diligently, he never found a single tarantula there.
p.q: There is no foundation for believing what is related of this supposed city, that its inhabitants have been expelled by great numbers of the large tarantula, or Phalangium araneodes, from which traditionary account the rivulet Byvalla has received its name; By, being the Tartar word for the tarantula, and valla, signifying bad or evil.
p.s: Peter Simon Pallas (English translation, 1812 edition)
p.pe: local tradition about the Madzhary ruins

p.h: The evil eye that eats a man's liver
p.g: In a footnote Elphinstone records an Afghan belief that some Hazaras have a power of 'fascination': reading the damaged scan, they can eat out the liver of anyone they stare at. He calls it a fable, common in India and Persia and pinned on various tribes. It is a good example of a travelling rumour attached to a people seen as outsiders.
p.q: who … the liver of any person on whom they fix their eyes. This fable is very common in India and Persia, and is attributed to various tribes.
p.s: Mountstuart Elphinstone (footnote, 1815)
p.c: The words describing the power itself are badly garbled in the scan; the gloss gives the most likely reading.

p.h: Stone statues of legendary lovers that received offerings
p.g: On the Ayagoz river, Levshin writes, stood a pointed building carefully built of smooth stone slabs, containing three stone statues. The Kazakhs said two of them showed the lovers famous in their tales (Bayan and Kozy-Korpesh, heroes of a Kazakh epic) and the third their servant, and believers brought them offerings. A building credited not to vanished giants but to a local love story.
p.q: Въ немъ три каменныя статуи, изъ коихъ двѣ, по словамъ Киргизъ Казаковъ, изображаютъ прославляемыхъ въ сказкахъ любовниковъ … а третья ихъ служанку. Вѣрующіе въ подлинность сихъ изображеній приносятъ имъ жертвы.
p.s: Aleksei Levshin (1832)
p.t: In it are three stone statues, of which two, according to the Kirghiz-Kazakhs, depict the lovers celebrated in their tales … and the third their servant. Those who believe in the authenticity of these images bring them offerings.
p.c: The description of the building itself (pointed, of smooth stone slabs) is at the foot of the previous page, n212. The lovers' names are omitted here because the OCR garbles them.

p.h: 800,000 captives and old men given to boys
p.g: After the 1521 raid the Crimean khan is said to have driven off more than 800,000 prisoners, selling many to the Turks at Kaffa. Herberstein repeats the lurid claim that old captives, worth little at market, were handed to Tartar youths for practice in killing. He flags the numbers himself ('scarcely be considered credible', 'they say').
p.q: But he took with him from Moscow so great a multitude of prisoners as would scarcely be considered credible ; they say that the number exceeded eight hundred thousand, part of whom he sold in Kaffa to the Turks, and part he slew.
p.s: Sigismund von Herberstein (translated by R. H. Major, 1851-52)
p.c: The figure is a rumour and far larger than is plausible; the slave trade through Kaffa itself is well documented.

p.h: Why can't there be another Heliopolis, in Tartary?
p.g: In his preface the author answers readers who doubted his story. Many cities share a name, he argues (two Frankforts, two Lyons, two Chalons), so why deny that besides Heliopolis in Egypt there could be the one he describes in Tartary? He also compares his doubters to those who laughed at the idea of the Antipodes before Columbus.
p.q: Why must it be deny'd, but that besides Heliopolis in Egypt, there may be that other of which I have given the Relation in Tartary.
p.s: 'Heliogenes de L'Epy', preface (English translation, 1689)
p.c: The protest of truth is a standard device of imaginary voyages.

p.h: A Kalmyk ruler who searched for the legendary valley of Ergene Kon
p.g: Discussing Abulghazi's legend that the ancestors of the Mongols lived shut in the valley of Ergene Kon until a whole mountain was melted to let them out, Müller adds a curious report he had been assured of: the Zunghar ruler Galdan Tseren, having heard the story from Bukharans, searched for such a valley as a refuge for his treasure and family, and was said to have found one somewhere in his lands.
p.q: Es ist merkwürdig, daß, wie man mich versichert, der Calmückische Beherrscher Galdanzerin nach langem Suchen eine dergleichen Ebene zwischen dem Gebürge, wie Irgene-Kon von Abulgasi beschrieben ist … innerhalb den Gränzen seines Gebiets, man weiß nur nicht wo, soll gefunden haben
p.s: Gerhard Friedrich Müller (Sammlung Russischer Geschichte, vol. 6, 1761-1762)
p.t: It is remarkable that, as I am assured, the Kalmyk ruler Galdan Tseren after long searching is said to have found such a plain among the mountains, as Ergene Kon is described by Abulghazi … within the borders of his territory, only no one knows where

p.h: Dining with the last khan of the Great Horde
p.g: Herberstein says the Crimean khans came from the old 'Savolha' royal line and fought its last king, Sheikh Ahmed. Defeated, the khan fled to Lithuania, was held in the island castle of Trakai, and there Herberstein met him at dinner. He writes that this ended the line of the Great Horde kings, heirs of the Golden Horde.
p.q: was apprehended in the attempt and taken back to the castle of Troky, four miles from Vilna, where I saw him and dined with him. This was the termination of the reign of the kings of Savolha, and together with them ended the race of the kings of Astrachan, who derived their origin from the same royal line.
p.s: Sigismund von Herberstein (translated by R. H. Major, 1851-52)
p.pe: Sheikh Ahmed (Scheachmet), khan of the Great Horde (Savolha)
p.c: His claim that the Astrakhan line ended here is contradicted a few pages later, where a king of Astrakhan regains his throne.

p.h: The Hill of the White Stallion and the Khan's Well
p.g: Describing a caravan road from Chorny Yar on the Volga to Madshar, day by day, Güldenstädt passes on the names of its waymarks. One big hill was called Kok Aigir, ‘White Stallion’, because a Tatar khan, overjoyed at the birth of a son, had a white stallion slaughtered there. The next stage reached the Khan's Well, covered by a great stone pierced with holes through which water was drawn, and ringed by stone statues like those he had seen between Mozdok and Cherkassk. He gives this as a route report, not as a journey of his own.
p.q: Am 9ten Tage kommt man zeitig an einen großen Hügel, genannt tatar. Kok Aigir d. i. Schimmel-Hengst, zum Andenken der Begebenheit, da ein tatarischer Chan aus Freude über die Geburt eines Sohnes hieselbst ein Schimmel-Hengst schlachten ließ … Chan Schokrak d. i. Chansbrunnen, der mit einem großen Stein bedekt ist, in den verschiedene Löcher gehauen, durch die das Wasser heraufgezogen wird.
p.s: Johann Anton Güldenstädt (ed. P. S. Pallas, 1791)
p.pl: Steppe between the Volga and the Kuma
p.t: On the 9th day one arrives early at a large hill, called in Tatar Kok Aigir, that is, White Stallion, in memory of the event when a Tatar khan, for joy at the birth of a son, had a white stallion slaughtered here … Chan Schokrak, that is, the Khan's Well, which is covered with a large stone in which various holes are cut, through which the water is drawn up.
p.c: A place-name story passed on by informants; no khan or date is named.

p.h: A Tatar cart turned to stone
p.g: Near the same wells the Kalmyks told Zwick they had once cleared an old well and found a Tatar cart (arba) turned to stone, and he heard of similar finds in the Kuma marshes. He did not see it himself, and offers a sober explanation: salty soil hardens wood, as the Volga fishermen knew from their salting tubs.
p.q: In an old well in this neighbourhood, which the Calmucs cleared out some years ago, they are said to have found a Tartar arba in a state of petrifaction. Similar cases, as we were elsewhere told, have been found in the Kuma Morass. That the saltness of the soil may have contributed to the preservation of the wood is the more probable
p.s: Heinrich August Zwick (English edition, 1831)
p.c: Hearsay; Zwick reports it and explains it but did not see the cart.

p.h: The newly married bride's horn with a bell
p.g: Cheremis brides, the book says, wear a horn a yard long planted in the middle of the forehead, with a silk tassel and a little bell whose sound reminds the bride that she has just changed her state. The same paragraph then repeats a lurid slander about fathers and their daughters, likened to a tale told of Ceylon.
p.q: les nouvelles mariées ajoûtent un ornement qui leur est tout particulier: c'est une corne longue d'une aune qu'elles se plantent au milieu du front; au bout de laquelle il y a une houpe de soie, & au milieu de cette houpe une clochette, dont le bruit sert à faire souvenir la mariée qu'elle a depuis peu changé d'état.
p.s: Jan Struys (French translation by Glanius, Amsterdam 1681)
p.t: newly married women add an ornament all their own: a horn a yard long, which they plant in the middle of the forehead; at its end is a silk tassel, and in the middle of this tassel a little bell, whose sound serves to remind the bride that she has lately changed her state.
p.c: Probably taken from Olearius. The horned bridal headdress is plausible; the slander that follows is not evidence of anything.

p.h: An Uzbek map of the world
p.g: The Khivan minister showed Abbott a world map by an Uzbek scholar that put Italy north of England and Russia south of China. Abbott, tongue in cheek, decided not to argue.
p.q: A map of the world, the production of a profound Oozbeg philosopher, was then produced ; I begged a clue to this singular chart, and was rather surprised to find, that Italy lay north of England ; and Russia south of China.
p.s: James Abbott
p.c: Abbott is being sarcastic about the map.

p.h: Barrels of gold, some of them fake
p.g: Perry repeats the story of why Prince Vasily Golitsyn's army turned back from the Crimea in 1689: the Tatars brought him barrels of gold ducats, 'amongst which, as 'tis said, there were many Counters', and he made peace in the field. On the page before, he reports that the Crimean khan would inherit the Ottoman throne if the sultan's male line failed.
p.q: …being tempted by a great Sum of Ducats of Gold, which they brought to him in Barrels (amongst which, as 'tis said, there were many Counters) he concluded Conditions of Peace in the Field, and withdrew his Army.
p.s: Captain John Perry (The State of Russia, 1716)
p.c: Court rumour, marked as such by Perry ('as 'tis said').

p.h: Were the Mohicans Tatars?
p.g: On a trip to America Wolff thought he saw signs that Native Americans were of 'Tatar race': a shared word for 'great', a fondness for the number nine, and a custom of playing a mournful flute outside a sweetheart's tent like the Turkmens. It is a striking example of how far the Tatar idea could stretch.
p.q: Many of their customs, besides words in their language, and their physiognomy, rather seem to me to betray a Tatar race. Thus, for instance, they have the word kelaun, great, which is also used in the same sense at Bokhara. They have nine as a favourite number, which the Tatars also have.
p.s: Joseph Wolff
p.pe: Mohican people of North America, compared with Tatars and Turkmens
p.c: Wolff's own speculation from a few coincidences.
p.tg: native americans tatar race speculation number nine

p.h: The wind that turned the catapult stones back
p.g: When Kuremsa's Tatars attacked the unfortified town of Lutsk in a winter flood, the townsmen cut the bridge. Kuremsa set up siege engines, but, says the chronicler, God, St John and St Nicholas worked a miracle: the wind blew the stones back onto the Tatars, and then the sling of the engine broke. The Tatars went back to their camp in the steppe.
p.q: Богъ же чюдо створи, и святый Иванъ, и святый Никола, вѣтру же таку бывшу, яко порокомъ вергшу вѣтръ же обращаше камень на нѣ, пакы же мечющимъ на нѣ крѣпко изломися, Божіею силою, пракъ ихъ, и не успѣвше ничтоже вратишася во станы своя, рекше въ поле.
p.s: Hypatian Chronicle, PSRL vol. 2 (1843)
p.t: But God worked a miracle, and St John and St Nicholas: there was such a wind that when the engine threw, the wind turned the stone back upon them; and again, as they hurled hard, by the power of God their sling broke, and having achieved nothing they went back to their camps, that is, to the steppe.
p.c: Told as a miracle; the wind may have been real, the saints' part is the chronicler's reading.

p.h: A Tartar emperor in Asia who keeps Christian rites
p.g: The same informant adds that the 'Cham', emperor of the Tartars in Asia, lives not far from the Circassians and still keeps many Christian rites because his people were once converted. This is an echo of the medieval Prester John and Christian khan legends, repeated as current news.
p.q: Adiecit autem, Cham, Tartarorum in Asia Imperatorem, non procul ab ea gente abesse, qui multum adhuc rituum Christianorum retineat, cũ olim ad fidem nostram accesserint.
p.s: Antonio Possevino, S.J. (Moscovia, Vilnius 1586), reporting an unnamed informant 'N.'
p.pe: 'Cham, emperor of the Tartars in Asia'
p.t: He added, moreover, that the Cham, Emperor of the Tartars in Asia, is not far from that people, and still keeps much of the Christian rites, since they once came over to our faith.
p.c: Rumour with no named ruler or place; by 1580 no Christian 'Cham' ruled near the Caucasus.
