p.h: Fireproof cloth from a Tatar prince
p.g: The traveller reports a quarrel between two Tatar princes of the Kazan region, father and son, which almost came to battle over a woman until Prince Golitsyn, governor of Kazan and Astrakhan, made peace. In thanks the Tatar prince gave Golitsyn a large piece of cloth that would not burn, said to be still made in Cathay between China and Bukhara. The traveller, who had himself once brought asbestos stone from Cyprus, received a piece.
p.q: worauf der Tartarische Prinz diesem Scheids-Mann unter andern Sachen ein grosses Stück unverbrennlichen Leinwands schenket, wovon der Herr Poppe und ich wiederum von diesem etwas bekommen. Er sagte mir, daß es zu Katai, zwischen China und Bucharen, noch würklich gemacht würde.
p.s: Journal of an unnamed painter-traveller (evidently Cornelis de Bruyn, 1703) printed in Weber, Das veränderte Russland
p.t: whereupon the Tartar prince gave this arbitrator, among other things, a large piece of incombustible linen, of which Mr Poppe and I in turn received some from him. He told me that it was still actually made in Cathay, between China and Bukhara.
p.c: Cited from the 1744 reissue, which reprints the 1721 text page for page with clearer OCR.

p.h: The rumour that Wolff had been to Tartarus
p.g: Wolff found a rumour running through Bukhara that he knew 72 languages and 72 religions, had spoken with 72 nations, and had even visited the 'land of darkness', which he glosses as Tartarus. The word play between Tartary and Tartarus here comes from Wolff's own gloss.
p.q: A report was spread abroad, I found, throughout the whole country of Bokhara, that Mullah Joseph Wolff, the grand derveesh from England, was acquainted with seventy-two languages, with seventy-two religions, and had conversed with seventy-two nations of the earth. That, further, I had been in Sulmistaun, i. e. the ' land of darkness," Tartarus
p.s: Joseph Wolff
p.c: Gossip about Wolff himself; the 'Tartarus' gloss is his.

p.h: The vegetable lamb was really cotton
p.g: Watching Bukharan cotton being sold at the Nizhny Novgorod fair, Erman explains the old story of the Baranets, a plant that grew a living lamb, told near the Caspian and repeated by Herberstein in the 1500s. He was sure it came from an embellished description of the cotton plant, and he quotes Herberstein's Latin, including Herberstein's remark that nothing is impossible for the Creator.
p.q: It appears to me quite certain that the story of the zoophytic plant, called Baranez, or lamb-plant, (formed as a diminutive, from Baran, a sheep,) originated in some embellished account of the cotton plant. Herberstein relates it at full length and unchanged, just as he had heard it
p.s: Adolph Erman (translated by W. D. Cooley, 1848)
p.pe: Bukharan traders; Russian and European writers
p.c: Erman's cotton theory is one explanation among several; others point to a fern (Cibotium barometz) whose woolly rhizome was sold as the 'Tartarian lamb'.

p.h: A Tatar khan's statue in Moscow before which the Tsar must bow
p.g: Struys retells the Tatar raid that took Moscow and made the Grand Prince pay tribute. The elder of two Tatar brothers, 'Mendliguerits', had a statue of himself set up in Moscow before which the Tsar would have to prostrate himself whenever he sent the tribute. The story, told from older books, is about the 1521 raid of the Crimean khan Mehmed Giray and his brother Sahib Giray of Kazan.
p.q: Des deux Chefs Tartares qui étoient frères, l'aîné nommé Mendliguerits, avant que de quitter Moskou, s'y fit dresser une statuë devant laquelle l'Empereur seroit obligé de se prosterner
p.s: Jan Struys (French translation by Glanius, Amsterdam 1681)
p.pe: Kazan and Crimean Tatars (the khan Mehmed Giray)
p.t: Of the two Tartar chiefs, who were brothers, the elder, named Mendliguerits, before leaving Moscow, had a statue of himself set up there, before which the Emperor would be obliged to prostrate himself
p.c: Book history, not observation; the details, including the statue, come from older written accounts and cannot be checked here.

p.h: Eyes that could bore through brass: a captive poet's Tatars
p.g: Elias quotes the Persian poet Amir Khusrau of Delhi, who had been a prisoner of Mongol raiders and describes them with hatred: narrow piercing eyes, faces set on necks, noses spreading from cheek to cheek. Elias warns that the poet was 'burning with dread and resentment' and omits 'offensive details'. On a later page Elias notes that Khusrau calls the same people Tatars, Turks and Moghuls.
p.q: There were more than a thousand Tatar infidels and warriors of other tribes, riding on camels, great commanders in battle, all with steel-like bodies clothed in cotton ; with faces like fire, with caps of sheepskin, with heads shorn. Their eyes were so narrow and piercing that they might have bored a hole in a brazen vessel
p.s: Amir Khusrau, quoted in Ney Elias's introduction (1895)
p.c: Hostile caricature by a former captive, quoted in translation by the editor.

p.g: Right after the Magog passage, Cruz cites a treatise on the Antichrist by one Pedraza, who says these Scythians live beyond the Caspian, are a huge multitude, and will come to help the Antichrist at the end of time. Cruz offers it as support for his own view. It is the old Gog and Magog end-of-the-world legend, repeated from a book.

p.h: Priest John and the Tartar princes
p.g: Zwick's historical introduction repeats the medieval story of Prester John: a certain Master Philip told Pope Alexander III of marvels in Tartary and of the Christian priest-king there, and the Pope sent a letter east in 1177. Zwick is summarising older histories, not reporting anything he saw.
p.q: The first intelligence of the Tartarian Princes at Karakorum, was brought to Alexander the Third, by one "Master Philip," … who professed to have travelled in Tartary, and added many marvels of the might and dominion of Priest John, the head of the church at that place.
p.s: Heinrich August Zwick (historical introduction, English edition, 1831)
p.c: Second-hand history. Karakorum was not founded until the 1220s, so placing Priest John there in 1177 is Zwick's anachronism.

p.h: Villagers told to hide their women from 'Tartar' brutes
p.g: An imperial edict ordered villagers along the route to stay at work and women to keep out of the foreigners' sight. A Chinese general explained why: an earlier party of Tartars from 'barbarous tribes' passing through had assaulted village women, and all foreigners were suspected of the same.
p.q: A party of Tartars belonging to some barbarous tribes, passing through the country on a similar occasion to the present, violated the women of the villages on the route; and as all foreigners are alike despised by the Chinese, we, until known, were suspected of equal brutality.
p.s: Henry Ellis, reporting General Wang
p.c: Hearsay from an official; the tribe, date and place are not given.

p.h: Horse skulls against witchcraft
p.g: Tatars and Bulgarian settlers alike stuck a horse's skull up near their houses to ward off witchcraft. Holderness links it, on hearsay, to the ancient Taurians, said to have used human skulls. On the same page a hired Tatar driver refuses to start a journey on a Tuesday, an unlucky day.
p.q: It is a very common custom in the Crimea, with the Tatars as well as the Bulgarian settlers, to stick up a horse's skull near their houses, in order to preserve them from witchcraft.
p.s: Mary Holderness
p.c: The Taurian comparison is secondhand ('I am told').

p.h: Cave spirits that steal Tatar calves
p.g: The Tatars who guided Lepekhin to the warm caves near Tabynsk would not go near the entrance, let alone inside. They told him that spirits lived in the caves and often dragged calves and small livestock down the holes, and many swore they had seen the spirits, in human shape, hauling Tatar cattle inside. Lepekhin blames 'old wives' chatter' and goes in anyway.
p.q: Die Tatarn getrauten sich nicht nahe an die Höle zu treten, … und erzählten uns unbegreifliche Fabeln, von den in diesen Hölen wohnenden Geistern, welche außer der Furcht ihnen auch Schaden zufügten, indem sie nicht selten Kälber und anderes kleines Vieh in die hineinführenden Löcher zögen; sie versicherten uns viele von ihnen wären Augenzeugen davon gewesen, wie die Geister in Menschengestalt der Tatarn Vieh hineingeschleppt hätten.
p.s: Ivan Lepekhin (German translation, 1775)
p.pe: Tatars of the village of Kurmanaevo near Tabynsk
p.t: The Tatars did not dare go near the cave, … and told us incredible fables about the spirits living in these caves, which besides frightening them also did them harm, often dragging calves and other small livestock into the holes that lead inside; they assured us that many of them had been eyewitnesses of how the spirits, in human shape, had hauled the Tatars' cattle in.
p.c: Local belief reported by a sceptical outsider.

p.h: Milk that makes you drunk: a German chemist scoffs
p.g: Lepekhin describes how the baptized Kalmyks distil fermented mare's milk into a spirit, with two kettles joined by a tube sealed with clay, and says he saw it more than once, as Professor Gmelin had reported. Foreign chemists called this a fable. His German translator adds a footnote quoting the chemist Caspar Neumann, who had never seen a Kalmyk or Tatar: Neumann found it hard to believe that the 'Tartars' could achieve such a thing and thought the recipe (with millet and barley added) looked 'truly Tartarish'. The translator uses the quotation to show how prejudice misled even a careful scientist.
p.q: daß dergleichen seltene Begebenheit von den Tartarn zuwege gebracht würde, als welche, meines Wissens, wohl wenig oder keine physikalisch-chymische Erfindungen der Welt dargethan, auch wohl nicht leicht darthun werden; … da ich denn nicht läugnen kann, daß mir im ersten Anblick die Ingredientien wahrhaftig recht tartarisch vorkamen
p.s: Caspar Neumann, German chemist, quoted in a footnote by Lepekhin's German translator (1774)
p.pe: Baptized Kalmyks, and 'Tartars' in general as imagined by a German chemist
p.w: September 1768 (Neumann writing earlier in the century)
p.t: that such a rare thing should be brought about by the Tartars, who, as far as I know, have shown the world few or no physical or chemical discoveries and are hardly likely to; … whereupon I cannot deny that at first sight the ingredients struck me as truly Tartarish
p.c: The sneer is Neumann's, quoted in order to refute it; Lepekhin himself vouches for the milk spirit from what he saw.
p.tg: kumiss distilling prejudice milk spirit tartarish

p.h: Flags that frighten away hobgoblins
p.g: At the corner of almost every Tartar house flew a long flag printed with 'Om mani padme hum' and topped with a tuft of black yak hair. Gerard reports that these flags and the stone piles on the roofs were believed to scare off ghosts and evil spirits.
p.q: The Durchuts and Lapchas are considered efficacious in frightening away ghosts, hobgoblins, and evil spirits, which are universally believed in.
p.s: Alexander Gerard (ed. George Lloyd, 1841)

p.h: The white elephant with thirty-three heads
p.g: Summarising Kalmyk Buddhist books, the authors describe the world-mountain and its guardian elephant, two leagues long and white as snow, with thirty-three red heads, six trunks each spouting fountains, and a young virgin on every star above them. They note, in a footnote, similar marvels in medieval European cosmography. This is religious myth they report, not something anyone claimed to see.
p.q: where dwells an elephant two leagues long, white as snow, and named Gasar Sakitschin Koven (protector of the earth). This fabulous animal has thirty-three red heads, each furnished with six trunks, whence spout forth as many fountains, all surmounted with six stars.
p.s: Xavier Hommaire de Hell (English translation, 1847)
p.c: A second-hand summary of Kalmyk religious books; the authors do not name the text they used.

p.h: Mammoth from 'Behemoth'
p.g: Strahlenberg argues that the word 'mammoth' comes from the Behemoth of the Book of Job, brought into Tartary by Arabs who found the bones of huge beasts and called them 'Mehemot'. He says the Tartars call the animal 'Khir', and cites an exiled Russian priest who said the old Siberian form was 'Memoth'. He admits he could not find out what kind of animal the bones came from.
p.q: And these Arabs coming into Tartary, and finding there the Relicks of some monstrous great Beasts, not certain of what Kind they might be, they called these Teeth Mehemot, which afterwards became a Proper Name, among the Tartars; and, by the Russians, is corruptly pronounced Mammoth.
p.s: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (English translation, 1738)
p.c: His Behemoth etymology is speculation and is not accepted today.

p.h: A living Buddha whose face follows the moon
p.g: Timkovsky reports what the Khalkhas believed about their koutouktou (Jebtsundamba Khutughtu), the reincarnating high lama of Urga: that he had already lived through sixteen generations and that his face aged and grew young again with the moon. He presents it as their belief, not his.
p.q: The Kalkas affirm, that their koutouktou has already seen sixteen generations, and that his physiognomy changes with the phases of the moon. At new moon, he has the appearance of a youth; at the full, of a man in the prime of life; and appears quite old in the last quarter.
p.s: George Timkowski (English translation, 1827)
p.c: A popular belief reported secondhand.

p.h: Gog and Magog from a khan's name?
p.g: Strahlenberg criticises the French editor of Abulghazi for suggesting that the biblical names Gog and Magog came from a khan called Budenür-Mogack, an idea also found in Pétis de la Croix. He insists that the Tatar original text, under an Arabic name, shows something quite different. It shows how European scholars tried to fit the peoples of Tartary into biblical prophecy.
p.q: item pag. 148 praesumiret, der Nahme Gog & Magog entstehe von einem Könige oder Chan, der Budenür-Mogack geheissen, (welches, wo mir recht ist, La Croix in seinen Remarquen auch anführet) da doch der Tatarsche Grund-Text unter einem Arabischen Nahmen solches ganz anders beweiset.
p.s: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (Vorbericht, Stockholm 1726)
p.t: likewise on p. 148 he presumes that the name Gog and Magog comes from a king or khan called Budenür-Mogack (which, if I am right, La Croix also cites in his remarks), whereas the Tatar original text, under an Arabic name, proves it quite otherwise.

p.h: A people from 'unknown lands' whose reason for coming no one knows
p.g: Duke Otto of Bavaria, writing from Straubing on 11 April 1241, two days after Liegnitz, warns the bishop of Augsburg of a barbarous people 'of infinite multitude, coming from distant and unknown parts', whose reason for coming nobody knows except that they persecute and kill Christians. He reports Cracow's land destroyed, the duke of Poland defeated, and the Tartars at the borders of Bohemia in three armies, and fears for all Germany.
p.q: quedam gens barbara Tartarorum crudelis nimium, multitudinis infinite, de longinquis et ignotis partibus adveniens, cujus causam adventus aliam ignoramus, nisi quod christianos universos impie prosequantur et occidant.
p.s: Duke Otto II of Bavaria, letter to Bishop Siboto of Augsburg, Straubing, 11 April 1241 (printed by Hormayr, 1842)
p.t: a certain barbarous people of the Tartars, exceedingly cruel, of infinite multitude, coming from distant and unknown parts, the cause of whose coming we do not know, except that they wickedly pursue and kill all Christians.

p.h: 'A Tartarean law' and the image of 'some Tartar'
p.g: At Nanchang, local graduates petitioned to have the Jesuits expelled. In Trigault's Latin their complaint says the foreigners had moved from cramped lodgings to grand houses, preached a 'tartarea' law, and handed out pictures of 'some Tartar or Saracen' they called God come down from heaven. The word play is Latin: tartareus means hellish, from Tartarus, while 'tartarus' here also means a barbarian foreigner. It is Trigault's rendering, not the petition's own Chinese wording.
p.q: Eos ipsos primum in angustis sedibus habitasse, nunc vero alias capaces atque magnificas coemisse, legem ab iisdem tartaream praedicari, rude vulgus in fraudem induci … eos certas imagines distribuere, nescio cuius tartari aut Saraceni, quem dicebant esse Deum, qui ad mortales instruendos liberandosque e caelo venerat
p.s: Chinese petitioners at Nanchang, as rendered in Latin by Nicolas Trigault (1615)
p.pe: Chinese scholars accusing the Jesuits; 'Tartar' as an insult
p.t: that these same men at first lived in cramped lodgings, but have now bought others, roomy and magnificent; that they preach a Tartarean law and lead the ignorant crowd into deception … that they hand out certain images of some Tartar or Saracen, whom they said was God, who had come down from heaven to teach and set free mankind
p.c: A hostile petition summarised in Latin by the Jesuits' own historian.

p.h: Was the yurt copied from a bird's nest?
p.g: Bergmann offers his own 'hypothesis' about how the Mongol peoples invented the felt tent. Living in treeless country, they could neither dig caves nor build huts of branches, so perhaps one of them copied the hanging, bag-shaped nest that the penduline tit weaves from plant wool. Because a house cannot hang from a branch, the Mongols set it on the ground and put the door at the bottom. He presents this frankly as a guess.
p.q: Dieser merkwürdige Vogel bereitet aus einer Art von Wolle, einen länglichen Sack, den er so geschickt an Zweige befestigt, daß weder Wind noch Wetter im Stande sind, seine schwebende Wohnung zu beschädigen. Diese Methode, dünkt mich, benutzten die Voreltern der Kalmüken, um sich nach dem Beispiele des Remes Hütten einzurichten, die sie in der Folge immer mehr zu vervollkommnen und mit Holzwerk immer besser zu stützen suchten.
p.s: Benjamin Bergmann
p.pl: Kalmyk steppe west of the lower Volga (Kalmykia)
p.pe: Ancestors of the Kalmyks and Mongols (Bergmann's theory)
p.t: This remarkable bird makes from a kind of wool an oblong bag, which it fastens to twigs so skilfully that neither wind nor weather can damage its hanging home. This method, I fancy, the forefathers of the Kalmyks used, to make huts for themselves after the example of the remez [penduline tit], which they afterwards tried to perfect more and more and to support ever better with woodwork.
p.c: Bergmann's own speculation, not a Kalmyk tradition.

p.h: A town swallowed by the earth for its wickedness
p.g: Next to the ruined castle of Uvek, the Russians told the English, there had stood a town they called Sodom, which God had swallowed into the earth with part of the castle because of its people's wickedness. It is a local legend attached to real ruins, and the narrator clearly labels it as Russian report.
p.q: adioyning to the same was a towne called by Russes Sodom. This towne & part of the castle (by report of the Russes) was swallowed into the earth by the iustice of God, for the wickednesse of the people that inhabited the same.
p.s: Christopher Burrough's reports, in Hakluyt (ed. Morgan and Coote, 1886)
p.pe: Russians' legend about a ruined Volga town
p.c: Legend reported by Russian boatmen, not observed.

p.h: Stone men by the salt spring
p.g: By a stream in the Manych steppe, opposite the salt that the people of Azov gathered, the book marks 'stone men, idols'. These are the carved stone statues ('kamennye baby') that stood on steppe kurgans, set up by earlier nomads such as the Polovtsy. The clerks give no builder, only the landmark.
p.q: А по правой сторонѣ по тому истоку люди каменные болваны, противъ той соли, что емлютъ Азовцы.
p.s: Book of the Great Map (1627), ed. Yazykov (1838)
p.pe: Unnamed makers of steppe stone statues
p.t: And along the right side of that stream are stone people, idols, opposite the salt that the Azov people take.
p.c: The identification with kurgan stelae is the usual scholarly reading; the book does not describe them.

p.h: Tatars collect money to 'free' a charming Greek lady
p.g: After mocking whirling dervishes, Maria offers a story to the Tatars' credit: a Greek-born countess, married to a Russian general, so charmed the Tatars of Eupatoria with her Turkish that they took her for a Muslim woman held captive by Christians and secretly raised money to buy her freedom.
p.q: so charmed the honest Tartars with the graces of her person, and conversation in the Turkish language, that they, ignorant of her rank and quality, conceived an idea of her being a fair daughter of Mahomet, held in Christian bondage by the right of war, and secretly opened a subscription among themselves to purchase her liberty
p.s: Maria Guthrie (letter, translated by Matthew Guthrie, 1802)
p.c: An anecdote about another traveller, not something she witnessed.

p.h: The Tartar and the princess of Ghulghula
p.g: Mohan Lal tells the legend of Shahr-i Ghulghula, the ruined fortress city by Bamiyan, said to have been built by an unbeliever before Muhammad's time. A Tartar from Badakhshan besieged it in vain until the ruler's daughter, in love with him, wrote telling him to cut off the water. He took the fort, married her, and then killed her for betraying her father.
p.q: A Tartar, native of Badakhshan, resolved to invade it, and laid siege to it. When he found great difficulty in subduing it, and was on the point of dismissing his camp, he fortunately received a letter, with the following contents, from the beautiful daughter of the Kafar, who had fallen in love with the Tartar
p.s: Mohan Lal (1846 edition)
p.c: A folk tale; in history Shahr-i Ghulghula was destroyed by Genghis Khan's army in 1221.

p.h: Lands ruined by the raids of Gog and Magog
p.g: Describing the far north, al-Umari says the eastern end is a region peopled by Gog and Magog within the Barrier (the wall). He reports that the Rus lands and the land of the Ankariyya (Hungarians) are inhabited, but that the land of Sisaban was once flourishing and populated and fell to ruin long ago because Gog and Magog raided it.
p.q: فأوله من جهة الشرق قطعة معمورة بيأجوج ومأجوج ، فيما هو داخل السد … قالوا : فأما الروسية ، فعامرة آهلة . وكذلك الأنكرية . وأما بلاد سيسبان ، فقد كانت عامرة آهلة مسكونة ، ثم خربت من قديم ، لإغارات يأجوج ومأجوج عليهم
p.s: al-Umari (Arabic text ed. Ahmad Zaki Pasha, Cairo 1924)
p.pl: Far north-east of the seventh clime
p.t: Its beginning on the eastern side is a stretch peopled by Gog and Magog, within the Barrier … They say: as for the Rus lands, they are flourishing and inhabited, and so are those of the Ankariyya; but the land of Sisaban was once flourishing, populated and settled, then fell to ruin long ago because of the raids of Gog and Magog upon them.
p.c: 'They say': copied lore, of the same family as Sallam's ruined cities.

p.h: Hungary after the Tartars: church towers the only signposts
p.g: Hormayr's own nineteenth-century retelling of what King Bela found on his return: church towers the only guides, grass growing in the streets, whole days' journeys without a living soul, thousands of unburied corpses, wolves snatching children, and human flesh sold openly. It is vivid but it is Hormayr's rhetoric, built on chronicles like Master Roger's, not an eyewitness text.
p.q: waren Kirchthürme die einzigen Wegweiser, Gras und Gesträuch auf Strassen und Gassen, ganze Tagereisen weit keine menschliche Seele, aber viele tausende, unbegrabene, halb verwesete, grässlich verstümmelte Leichen
p.s: Joseph von Hormayr, editor's narrative (1842)
p.t: church towers were the only signposts, grass and brush on roads and lanes, whole days' journeys without a human soul, but many thousands of unburied, half-rotted, horribly mutilated corpses
p.c: Editorial narrative written six centuries later; the famine cannibalism detail comes from medieval chronicles and is repeated without a source.

p.h: Twenty-four thousand scholars killed: a story at fourth hand
p.g: The editor Ibn Juzayy inserts a report passed down a chain of four people: a scholar from Iraq, met at Mecca, said that 24,000 learned men died in the Tartar war in Iraq and that he and his nephew were the only scholars who escaped. It is a vivid example of how atrocity figures travelled by word of mouth, and the text is careful to show the chain.
p.q: that in the war with the Tartars in Irak not fewer than four and twenty thousand learned men perished ; and that himself, and that man, pointing to his brother's son, were the only learned men who had escaped.
p.s: Ibn Juzayy, the editor, citing a chain of informants (translated by Samuel Lee, 1829)
p.c: Fourth-hand report added by the editor, not by Ibn Battuta; the number cannot be checked.

p.h: The Kalmyk 'Kaaba' and Alexander's wall
p.g: Evliya records what Kalmyks told him about a domed shrine they call their Kaaba, far to the east beyond a sea of ice. He adds his own learned gloss: Alexander built the Wall of Gog and Magog from every kind of metal, the mountains the Kalmyks call the Yildirak Dag, then built this dome with ancient sages and hid his treasures in it. On a following page Kalmyk elders say their ancestors died from a deafening noise behind the metal mountains.
p.q: سد اسکندر داغلرن جمیع معادنلردن بنا ایدوب قوم قالمغك ( یلدراق داغ ) دیدکلری سد یأجوجدر بعده اسکندر بونلرك کعبه دیدکلری قبه‌یی بنا ایدوب
p.s: Evliya Celebi (Ottoman text, Istanbul 1928, vol. 7)
p.pl: Beyond the Kalmyk steppe (unspecified, far east)
p.t: [Alexander] built the Barrier of Alexander, the mountains, out of every kind of metal; it is the Barrier of Gog, which the Kalmyk people call the 'Yildirak Dag' [the glittering mountain]; afterwards Alexander built the dome which they call their Kaaba.
p.c: Evliya's modern editor adds a long note calling the story an invention; it mixes Kalmyk (Buddhist) pilgrimage tales with Islamic Alexander legend.

p.h: Broken ribs cured by drinking gruel
p.g: Reuilly watched a Tatar remedy: a servant of Atai Myrza who broke two ribs falling from his horse was made to drink water-gruel until his belly swelled, under threat of the bastinado, so the ribs would push back into place. Reuilly will not vouch for the cure but admits the man was better by the time he left.
p.q: A domestic of Atai Myrza having fallen from his horse, and had two of his ribs broken, his master made him drink water gruel till his belly was prodigiously inflated; and when he refused to take more, he was threatened with the bastinado and drenched with the gruel… his master assuring me that the ribs would get into their places spontaneously.
p.s: Jean Reuilly (English translation, 1807)

p.h: A 'magician' who dug up a jewel and won the Ilkhan's trust
p.g: In a footnote from the Syriac chronicler Bar Hebraeus, d'Ohsson tells of Abd al-Rahman, a slave's son who escaped the sack of Baghdad, worked as a carpenter in Mosul, and then claimed spirits had taught him magic. Taken to the Mongol ruler Abaqa, he asked to be brought to the treasure castle of Tala, paced the ground, pointed to a spot, and there a ring with a precious stone was dug up. From then on he was believed to command demons, and under Ahmad he ran the whole kingdom.
p.q: il se mit à mesurer le sol de côté et d'autre; puis il indiqua un endroit où l'on devait creuser, et se tint lui-même à quelque distance. En creusant on trouva un anneau, où il y avait une pierre d'un grand prix; on le porta à Abaca. Ce fait ayant confirmé les paroles du prétendu magicien, on ajouta foi à tout ce qu'il disait
p.s: Constantin d'Ohsson, summarising Bar Hebraeus (footnote)
p.pe: Mongols of the Ilkhanate (Abaqa and Ahmad Tegüder)
p.t: he began to measure the ground this way and that; then he pointed to a spot where they should dig, and himself stood some distance away. Digging, they found a ring set with a stone of great value; it was taken to Abaqa. This having confirmed the words of the so-called magician, everything he said was believed
p.c: A hostile anecdote from a Christian chronicler about a Muslim favourite; d'Ohsson calls him a 'so-called' magician.

p.h: A jar of old Tartar coins falls out of a cliff
p.g: Resting under red gravel cliffs on the Volga near Astrakhan, Cook was told by his colonel that merchants picnicking there had seen part of the cliff collapse, releasing an earthen jar full of old Tartar coins in gold and silver. The colonel said he had seen some of them.
p.q: when they were taking their dinner, part of the cliff fell down, and with it, an earthen jar full of old Tartar coin, some of which he had seen, both gold and silver.
p.s: John Cook, reporting a Russian colonel (published 1770)
p.c: Second-hand; the coins are not described further.

p.h: 'Away with those new devils and their thundering puffs'
p.g: Horsey claims he persuaded Ivan IV to arm captured Scottish mercenaries and send them against the Crimean Tartars. Twelve hundred Scots with guns, he boasts, did better than 12,000 Russian archers, and the Tartars, unused to firearms, fled crying out against the 'new devils'.
p.q: Twelve hundred of them did better service against the Tartor then 12 thowsand Russes, with their shortte bowe and arowes. The Crim, not knowinge then the use of peece and pistolls, stroken dead of their horses with shott they sawe not, cried : " Awaye with those new divells that com with their thunderinge puffs ;"
p.s: Sir Jerome Horsey (memoir; ed. E. A. Bond, 1856)
p.c: A boastful anecdote; the Crimean khanate had firearms and Ottoman gunners by this time.

p.h: Horses stabled in the emperors' palaces
p.g: On the Grand Canal Staunton notes that the Chinese still looked on Tartars in general as barbarians. As proof they told a four-hundred-year-old story about the Mongol capture of Beijing: the conquerors lived in tents and put their horses in the imperial palaces.
p.q: they repeat the story, popular amongst them for four centuries, that when the Mongol Tartars seized first upon Pekin, they erected tents for their own accommodation, while they put their horses in the palaces of the Chinese emperors.
p.s: George Leonard Staunton
p.pe: Mongols ('Mongol Tartars'), as remembered by the Chinese
p.c: A popular Chinese tale, reported as such; not evidence of what happened in 1215.

p.h: A saint's mound that heals the sick
p.g: Half a verst from the ruins stood a large, dug-out burial mound where the local Tatars went on pilgrimage, saying a Muslim saint lay buried there. They told Pallas the saint still worked miracles, healed the sick and appeared to them in dreams. Pallas reports this as their belief and dismisses it as the fruit of imagination.
p.q: Obgedachte Tataren behaupten, daß der heilige noch itzt Wunder thue, Kranke heile, und ihnen zuweilen im Schlaf erscheine; womit es eben so, wie mit so vielen andern heiligen Erscheinungen und Wundern, welche die Einbildungskraft unter den Menschen in wenig aufgeklärten Zeiten so fruchtbar gebahr, beschaffen seyn wird.
p.s: Peter Simon Pallas (Reise, first edition, St Petersburg 1771-1776)
p.t: The said Tatars maintain that the saint still works miracles, heals the sick and sometimes appears to them in their sleep; which will be the same case as with so many other holy apparitions and miracles that imagination bore so fruitfully among men in unenlightened times.

p.h: Lost books blamed on 'Tatar lust for war'
p.g: Vambery laments that Uighur manuscripts on history and religion, such as those Rashid al-Din used for his great history, are lost for ever, destroyed by time and 'the even more devastating fire of Tatar lust for war'. Here 'Tatar' means the Mongol conquerors. It is a nineteenth-century scholar's explanation for missing sources, not evidence of a hidden civilisation.
p.q: Vieles hat der eiserne Zahn der Zeit und das noch mehr verheerende Feuer tatarischer Kriegslust zu Grunde gerichtet. Kostbare, unersetzliche Kleinodien der Geschichte jener fernen Gegenden Asiens, wie jene, deren Raschid-ed-Din noch bei Zusammenstellung seines Tag-et-tevarich's sich bediente, sind für uns auf ewig verschwunden
p.s: Hermann Vambery, introduction to his edition Uigurische Sprachmonumente und das Kudatku Bilik (Innsbruck 1870)
p.t: Much has been destroyed by the iron tooth of time and the even more devastating fire of Tatar lust for war. Precious, irreplaceable jewels of the history of those distant parts of Asia, such as those Rashid al-Din still used when compiling his Taj al-Tawarikh, are lost to us for ever.
p.c: Vambery's opinion; he gives no specific case of Mongols destroying Uighur books.

p.tg: lost books mongols rashid al-din uighur manuscripts

p.h: Remains of large 'Tartar ovens' near Chinggis's birthplace
p.g: In the Onon valley east of Lake Baikal, Cochrane passed Kondou, 'an ancient place' held to be the birthplace of the 'conqueror of China' (Chinggis Khan). There he saw 'many remains of large Tartar ovens', but gives no more detail, being more interested in a lively 93-year-old woman who cooked him dinner.
p.q: I saw many remains of large Tartar ovens, but nothing that excited my curiosity so much as an old lady of ninety-three years of age.
p.s: John Dundas Cochrane (1824)
p.c: Cochrane does not describe the 'ovens' or say how he knew they were Tartar. The Onon valley is indeed linked with Chinggis Khan's birth in Mongol tradition.

p.h: Skulls without sutures on the Kalmyk steppe
p.g: Riding back from Astrakhan, Hanway saw many human skulls lying about, as if on a battlefield, because the Kalmyks leave their dead unburied. He examined several and claims he could find no sutures in them. A footnote adds that surgeons doubted any race lacked sutures. A small, odd moment of amateur anatomy on the steppe.
p.q: I observed here many human sculls, as if the place had been a field of battle; for the Khalmucks always leave their dead uninterred. Upon examining several of these sculls, I could not discover any sutures,
p.s: Jonas Hanway (Historical Account, 1753)
p.c: Hanway's anatomical claim is his own impression; his footnote records that surgeons doubted it.

p.h: No poets on the flat steppe
p.g: Admiring the mountains near Thebes, Clarke argues that great poetry needs great scenery, and that flat countries like Scythia or Belgium never produced it. Even Homer, he says, would not have been a poet if raised in 'oriental Tartary'. It is a period prejudice, not an observation, but it shows how Tartary served as a byword for dull, flat emptiness.
p.q: Even Homer himself, if he had been a native of oriental Tartary, and had been cradled and brought up under the impressions made by such scenery, and under the influence of such a climate, would never have been a poet.
p.s: Edward Daniel Clarke (1816)
p.c: Clarke's own opinion and prejudice, not a report about any real people.

p.h: Rats that migrate 'like the wandering tartars'
p.g: Describing the root voles of Kamchatka, which store roots in neat many-roomed nests, Krasheninnikov compares their mass migrations to the moves of 'the wandering tartars'. When the rats left, the Kamchadals feared a wet year and poor hunting; when they came back, messengers ran to spread the good news. The simile shows that by the 1750s 'Tartar' was shorthand for nomads who move with the seasons.
p.q: These rats change their habitations like the wandering tartars, and sometimes for a certain number of years they all leave Kamtschatka, and go to some other place. This retirement is very alarming to the Kamtschadales, who think it forebodes a rainy season and a bad year for the chace
p.s: Stepan Krasheninnikov (translated by James Grieve, 1764)

p.h: Breath that froze on the beard
p.g: On Timur's last march toward China, Ibn Arabshah describes a winter so cold that a man's breath froze on his moustache and beard, and spittle turned to a frozen pellet before it hit the ground. It is a set piece of rhymed prose about the winter in which Timur died at Otrar.
p.q: وكان الرجل اذا تنفس جمدت انفاسه على سباله ولحيته … وان لفظ من فيه نخامة لا تصل الى الارض مع ما فيها من الحرارة الا وهي بندقة جامدة
p.s: Ahmad ibn Arabshah (Arabic text, print catalogued 1842)
p.t: When a man breathed out, his breath froze on his moustache and beard … and if he spat phlegm from his mouth, for all its warmth it did not reach the ground except as a frozen pellet.
p.c: Literary exaggeration; Ibn Arabshah was not on the campaign.
